Log each reading with an ISO 8601 timestamp to 'altitude_log.txt', flushing after every write. Handle all I2C read/write errors, sensor-absent conditions, and file-open failures gracefully with descriptive stderr messages. Clean up all resources (close the I2C handle, close the log file, terminate pigpio) on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to read temperature from an LM35 analog temperature sensor connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 10-bit ADC, wired via SPI0 (CE0, GPIO 8-11), using the pigpio library (not wiringPi or any deprecated library) for SPI communication. The LM35 output is 10 mV/°C; the MCP3008 VREF is 3.3 V. Use the MCP3008 SPI protocol: start bit (0x01), then single-ended mode bit plus channel number (channel 0 -> 0x80), then a don't-care byte, extracting the result as ((rx[1] & 0x03) << 8) | rx[2]. Read the temperature every 5 seconds, log each reading to the console in the format 'Temperature: XX.XX °C', and maintain a circular buffer of 120 float entries in memory; every 5 seconds overwrite the entire circular buffer to a binary file 'temp_log.dat' (opened with mode 'wb+') so the file always contains exactly 120 float values, with the oldest data overwritten when the buffer wraps. Check pigpio initialization, SPI open, and each SPI transfer; on SPI transfer failure, print an error and skip that reading rather than exiting; on file open failure, print an error and continue without logging to file. Use signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to close SPI, terminate pigpio, and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that logs ambient light and sound levels with timestamps to a file named "environmental_log.txt". Read ambient light from a BH1750 I2C sensor at address 0x23 on /dev/i2c-1, and read sound level from a MAX4466 analog microphone connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC over SPI using /dev/spidev0.0. Use the standard Linux i2c-dev API for I2C and the standard Linux spidev API for SPI; do not use the wiringPi library. Sample both sensors every 1 second and format each log entry as "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Light: [lux], Sound: [raw ADC value]". Handle I2C and SPI errors gracefully, including sensor-absent or bus-error conditions, without crashing. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, terminate gracefully and cleanly release all resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads a Keyes KY-026 flame sensor module connected to GPIO 17, using the libgpiod library. Initialize the GPIO line for input with pull-down enabled, then continuously poll the sensor every 1 second. The sensor's digital output is active HIGH when flame is detected (threshold adjustable via an onboard potentiometer) and operates at 3.3 V logic level. Log each timestamped HIGH/LOW reading to "flame_events.log" in CSV format: timestamp, pin, state. When flame is detected, print an alarm message to stdout. Use only the libgpiod API (gpiod_line_*, gpiod_chip_*) — not sysfs, wiringPi, or pigpio. Check every libgpiod call, print error messages to stderr, and exit with a non-zero status on failure. Clean up GPIO resources on normal exit and on SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads temperature from a TMP36 analog temperature sensor connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (CE0, mode 0, 500 kHz), converts the reading to Celsius, and outputs a proportional voltage via an MCP4725 I2C DAC at address 0x62 on bus 1. Linearly map the temperature range 0C to 50C to a DAC output of 0V to 3.3V. Use the pigpio library for all GPIO, SPI and I2C access. Check every initialization, SPI transfer, I2C write and file operation; handle sensor-absent or bus-error conditions gracefully with retries and clear error messages. Log each reading — timestamp, raw ADC value, temperature in C, and DAC voltage — to "temperature_log.txt" and also print it to stdout, sampling every 0.5 seconds. On SIGINT, shut down gracefully: close SPI and I2C, close the log file, and terminate pigpio. Do not use wiringPi or other deprecated APIs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads moisture levels from three DFRobot Soil Moisture Sensor v2.0 analog resistive sensors via an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (chip select CE0, SPI mode 0, 1 MHz clock), using the pigpio library. Read all three sensors on MCP3008 single-ended channels 0, 1 and 2, and convert each ADC value (0-1023) to a moisture percentage using moisture = (1.0 - (adc_value / 1023.0)) * 100.0, where 0% is dry and 100% is wet. Log timestamped readings ("YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS") to "soil_data.txt" in append mode, one line per sensor per cycle, with a 60-second sleep interval between cycles. If spiOpen or spiXfer fails, print an error message and exit with code 1; if a sensor read produces an invalid ADC value, print an error and continue. On SIGINT, close SPI, close the log file, terminate pigpio, and print a goodbye message, ensuring proper resource cleanup on all exit paths. Use only pigpio functions (spiOpen, spiXfer, spiClose, gpioInitialise, gpioTerminate, gpioDelay) — do not use wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library to sequentially activate and deactivate four Songle SRD-05VDC-SL relays connected to BCM GPIO pins 17, 22, 23 and 24, simulating a basic light sequencer. Use libgpiod calls (gpiod_line_set_value, gpiod_line_request_output, etc.) with error checking on every call. Initially set all relay pins inactive (LOW, assuming active-high relay modules). In a loop, activate each relay in sequence for 1 second, then deactivate it, with a 1-second delay between relays, repeating the full cycle indefinitely until interrupted. Install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that deactivates all relays and releases all GPIO lines before exiting. Include no SPI, ADC, temperature-sensor, or logging functionality — the task is relay sequencing only. Use only standard C libraries and libgpiod, not wiringPi or pigpio, and include clear comments explaining each step.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to read a Keyes KY-038 sound sensor's analog output through an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (chip select CE0 on GPIO8, mode 0, 1 MHz clock), reading MCP3008 channel 0. When the sound level exceeds a threshold of 500 (10-bit ADC value), turn on an LED connected to GPIO16, log the timestamp ("YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS") to "sound_events.log", and keep the LED on for 500 ms. Read the ADC every 10 ms in the main loop, applying a debounce delay after each trigger. Handle SPI transfer failures, invalid ADC channel selection, and GPIO initialization errors gracefully, checking every pigpio call and file operation. Install a signal handler for SIGINT to cleanly release resources on exit: close SPI, terminate pigpio, and turn off the LED. Use the pigpio library, not wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library for GPIO and SPI that reads a Seeed Studio Grove Rain Sensor (analog output) through an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (channel 0, 1 MHz, mode 0), and drives an L298N-based DC motor to automatically close a window when rain is detected. Wire the motor driver as IN1=GPIO17, IN2=GPIO18, ENA=GPIO27 with PWM (range 255, duty 150). Read the rain sensor with the standard 3-byte MCP3008 single-ended transfer: tx[0]=0x01, tx[1]=(0x08|channel)<<4, tx[2]=0x00, parsing the 10-bit result from the low 2 bits of rx[1] and all of rx[2]. Convert the ADC value (0-1023) to a rain level (0-10) so that ADC 1023 maps to rain level 0 (dry) and ADC 0 maps to rain level 10 (heaviest rain), since the sensor outputs higher voltage when dry. Poll every 1 second, and log each timestamped rain reading to "rain_log.txt" in append mode, flushing after every write. When the rain level is at or above a threshold of 5, close the window by driving the motor forward (IN1=1, IN2=0, PWM speed 150) for 3 seconds; when it drops below the threshold, open the window by driving the motor in reverse (IN1=0, IN2=1, PWM speed 150) for 3 seconds. The window starts in the open state. Handle pigpio initialization failures, SPI open failures, and log file open failures with clear error messages and proper cleanup, checking every init, syscall and I/O return value, and handling SPI transfer and log write failures without crashing. Install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag for graceful shutdown: stop the motor, close SPI, close the log file, and terminate pigpio, releasing all resources on every exit path. Use only the pigpio library, not wiringPi; the program should compile with gcc -o rain rain.c -lpigpio -lrt -lpthread.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library that implements a basic clap detector with a MAX9814 electret microphone amplifier (with AGC) whose output is read as an analog level on GPIO26 via pigpio's bit-banged ADC sampling. When the signal exceeds a threshold of approximately 0.7 x 3.3 V = 2.31 V, corresponding to a raw 10-bit ADC reading of about 700 out of 1023, turn on an LED on GPIO16 for 500 ms, print a timestamped detection message to the console, and apply a 50 ms debounce to avoid false triggers. Check the return values of pigpio initialization, ADC setup, and GPIO mode configuration, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error conditions gracefully. Install a SIGINT handler for clean shutdown that turns off the LED and terminates pigpio. Run continuously until interrupted with Ctrl+C, using C11 and avoiding deprecated APIs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads distance from a Sharp GP2Y0A21YK0F IR distance sensor using the sysfs GPIO interface on GPIO 17. Because the sensor's real output is analog and this exercise has no ADC available, treat GPIO 17 as a digital input reading 0 or 1, convert that to a placeholder voltage (0V for low, 3.3V for high), and then convert the voltage to distance using distance (mm) = A / voltage + B, with A = 26.0 and B = -6.0. Log each reading with a timestamp ("YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS") to "distance_log.txt" in append mode. Implement a proximity-based pet feeder activation: if the computed distance is below 200 mm, print "Feeder Activated" to the console; otherwise print "Feeder Idle". Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the libgpiod library, together with the standard Linux spidev SPI interface, to read analog soil moisture data from a Vegetronix VH400 sensor via an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (CE0, SCLK=GPIO11, MOSI=GPIO10, MISO=GPIO9), configured for single-ended mode on channel 0. Using calibrated ADC values of dry=800 and wet=300, if the moisture level drops below 30%, activate a 12V submersible water pump connected to GPIO17 through an active-high relay. Log each reading to "soil_moisture.log" with a timestamp, the moisture percentage, and the pump status (ON/OFF), sampling every 60 seconds continuously. Use only libgpiod and the standard Linux spidev SPI interface — do not use bcm2835 or wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads analog voltage from a DRV5055-A1 Hall-effect sensor via an external MCP3008 ADC over SPI, using the Linux spidev interface on /dev/spidev0.0 at 1 MHz, SPI mode 0, 8 bits per word, together with libgpiod (gpiochip0, line 8) to manually drive chip-select low during each SPI transfer and high afterward. Hardware wiring: MCP3008 VDD and VREF tied to the Pi's 3.3 V rail; MCP3008 DOUT to GPIO 10, DIN to GPIO 9, CLK to GPIO 11, and CS/SHDN to GPIO 8; DRV5055-A1 VOUT to MCP3008 channel 0, DRV5055 VCC to 3.3 V. The MCP3008 is a 10-bit ADC (0-1023) with VREF = 3.3 V, so compute Vout_mV = adc_value * 3300 / 1023. The DRV5055-A1 has a sensitivity of 100 mV/mT and a quiescent output of VCC/2 = 1650 mV, so compute the magnetic field B (mT) = (Vout_mV - 1650) / 100. Sample every 500 ms and append a CSV row to "magnetic_log.txt" as <unix_epoch>,<B_mt_two_decimals>. Use integer arithmetic internally for the field calculation and print the floating-point result with two decimal places in the log. Include all necessary headers such as stdint.h. Check every open, ioctl, SPI transfer, fopen, and fprintf call and propagate errors; if an ADC read fails, log the error to stderr, skip that sample, and continue the loop. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM cleanly, releasing the GPIO line, closing the gpiochip, closing the SPI file descriptor, and closing the log file on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library that reads analog voltage from a TI DRV5055VA Hall-effect sensor via an external MCP3008 ADC over SPI0 (CE0, GPIO 8, 9, 10, 11), with the sensor output wired to MCP3008 channel 0 (single-ended) and the sensor powered at 3.3 V. Initialize pigpio and SPI, handling initialization failures. Read the 10-bit MCP3008 value (0-1023) and convert it to voltage: V = ADC * 3.3 / 1023. Scale the voltage to magnetic field strength in mT using the DRV5055VA's ratiometric characteristics: quiescent output = VCC/2, and sensitivity at 3.3 V = 2.5 * 3.3/5 = 1.65 mV/mT, so field_mT = (voltage - VCC/2) * 1000 / sensitivity_mV_per_mT. Log each timestamped field-strength reading to "magnetic_log.txt" in append mode. If the field exceeds a threshold of 10.0 mT, turn on an LED on GPIO21; otherwise turn it off. Loop with a 100 ms delay between readings, using real ADC reads rather than simulated values. Handle SIGINT for graceful cleanup: close SPI, turn off the LED, and terminate pigpio. Check every SPI open, ADC read, and file open for errors. Use only pigpio for GPIO and SPI — do not use wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to monitor soil moisture with a DFRobot resistive soil moisture sensor connected to an MCP3008 ADC over SPI channel 0 (CE0, mode 0, 1 MHz), with the sensor's analog output wired to MCP3008 single-ended input channel 0. Initialize pigpio and open SPI with proper error handling. Every 60 seconds, read the ADC value using the MCP3008's single-ended protocol: start bit 0x01, single-ended mode bit 0x80, with the channel-selection bits in byte 1, and parse the 10-bit result from bits 1-2 of rx_buf[1] and all of rx_buf[2]. Log each reading with a timestamp ("YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS") and the raw ADC value to "moisture_log.txt" in append mode; on an ADC read failure (return -1), log an error line with a timestamp to the same file instead. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to gracefully close SPI, terminate pigpio, and exit. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using libgpiod for GPIO control (chip 0, line 17) and the Linux spidev SPI device (/dev/spidev0.0) for ADC communication, to read analog current values from a Melexis MLX91209 (the analog-output version) connected to BCM GPIO pin 17. The MLX91209 outputs an analog voltage proportional to current (0-5V range, sensitivity approximately 100 mV/A). Since the Raspberry Pi has no analog input, digitize the sensor output using an external MCP3008 ADC on channel 0 over SPI. Use signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean termination, releasing the GPIO line, closing the SPI handle, and closing the log file on exit. Do not use the sysfs GPIO interface or wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to read current from a Melexis MLX91211 analog-output current sensor via an MCP3008 SPI ADC. Wire the MCP3008 to the Pi's hardware SPI0 bus: CE0 on GPIO8, MOSI on GPIO10, MISO on GPIO9, SCLK on GPIO11, with MCP3008 VDD and VREF tied to the Pi's 5V rail and AGND/DGND tied to Pi GND. Wire the MLX91211 analog output to MCP3008 channel 0 (single-ended), with MLX91211 VDD from the Pi's 5V pin and GND to Pi GND. The MLX91211 output is ratiometric: 2.5V (VDD/2) at zero current and 5.0V (VDD) at full-scale +50A; linearly interpolate between those points. Initialize pigpio with gpioInitialise(), printing an error and exiting non-zero on failure. Open SPI0 (ce=0) at 1 MHz, mode 0 with spiOpen, terminating pigpio and exiting non-zero on failure. In a loop, read MCP3008 channel 0 with a 3-byte SPI transfer tx = {0x01, 0x80 | (channel<<4), 0x00} via spiXfer, computing the 10-bit result as ((rx[1] & 0x03) << 8) | rx[2]; on an SPI transfer error, print a diagnostic and skip that sample. Convert the raw code (0-1023) to voltage (0-5V), then to current using current = (voltage - 2.5) * (50.0 / 2.5); if voltage falls outside [0, 5V], print a warning and skip the sample. Every 100 ms (gpioDelay(100000)), append a timestamped line to "current_log.txt" in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS XX.XX A", flushing after each write; on file-open failure, close SPI, terminate pigpio, and exit non-zero. Install a SIGINT handler that sets a volatile flag so the loop exits cleanly; on exit, close the log file, call spiClose, and call gpioTerminate. Use only pigpio's spiOpen, spiXfer, and spiClose functions, include the necessary headers such as unistd.h, and comment the code clearly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 to interface with two Omron B5W-DB01 diffuse reflective sensors using the libgpiod library. Each sensor has a single digital output only — active-low, open-collector with an internal pull-up, where object present = LOW and no object = HIGH; the sensor has no analog light-intensity output. Connect sensor 1's output to GPIO4 and sensor 2's output to GPIO17. Check every libgpiod call (gpiod_chip_open_by_number, gpiod_line_request_input, etc.) and exit with a clear error message on failure. Debounce each read by sampling 5 times with 2 ms between reads and accepting the majority value. Log each sensor's state (0 = object present, 1 = no object) to the console once per second. If both sensors report object present simultaneously, print the warning "ALERT: Both sensors detect object". Handle SIGINT to release all GPIO resources (gpiod_line_release, gpiod_chip_close) and exit cleanly. Do not use pigpio, wiringPi, or any deprecated library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to periodically read analog moisture levels from a YL-69 soil moisture sensor via an MCP3008 ADC over SPI channel 0, CE0, at a 1 MHz baud rate, with the sensor on MCP3008 single-ended channel 0. Use the SPI command format: start bit 0x01, then a single-ended-plus-channel-select byte 0x80 | (channel << 4), then a dummy byte 0x00, reading the 10-bit ADC value as ((rx_buf[1] & 0x03) << 8) | rx_buf[2]. Calibrate so that ADC value 300 represents very dry soil and 800 represents very wet soil, converting to a moisture percentage with 100.0 - ((adc - 300) / (800 - 300)) * 100.0, clamped to [0, 100]. Every 60 seconds, append a reading to "soil_moisture_log.csv" in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,moisture_percentage" (e.g. "2025-03-15 14:30:00,45.23") and also print it to the console. Check every pigpio initialization, SPI open, SPI transfer, and file open call; on an SPI transfer failure, print an error and retry after a delay without exiting; on a file-open failure, print an error and continue. Use a volatile sig_atomic_t flag set by a SIGINT handler to close the SPI handle, terminate pigpio, and exit cleanly, releasing resources on every path — for example, if SPI open fails, terminate pigpio before returning. Include the headers pigpio.h, stdio.h, stdlib.h, unistd.h, time.h, signal.h, and string.h. Define constants SPI_CHANNEL (0), SPI_BAUD (1000000), MCP3008_CHANNEL (0), READ_DELAY (60), MIN_ADC (300), MAX_ADC (800), and LOG_FILE ("soil_moisture_log.csv"). Implement functions read_mcp3008(int channel), calculate_moisture_level(int adc_value), log_data(double moisture_level), signal_handler(int signal), and spi_setup(spi_config_t config); in main, initialize pigpio, open SPI, register the signal handler, loop until the termination flag is set reading the ADC, calculating moisture, logging data, and delaying 60 seconds each cycle, then close SPI and terminate pigpio on cleanup.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm, using the pigpio library, that detects motion via an HC-SR501 PIR sensor connected to BCM GPIO17 and triggers a camera snapshot via the libcamera-still command-line utility. Initialize pigpio and verify success; configure GPIO17 as input with a pull-down resistor, and poll it every 50 ms. After a state change, apply a 200 ms debounce delay and re-read the GPIO to confirm the state. On motion detection, capture a 1280x720 JPEG image with an ISO 8601 timestamp filename, saved to /home/pi/security_cam/; construct the output path safely with snprintf and verify the target directory exists before capture. Execute libcamera-still via fork and execvp (never system()), checking the child's exit status and treating a non-zero exit as a capture error. Log all key events — startup, motion detected, capture success or failure, and shutdown — to syslog. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, stop the main loop, release pigpio resources, and close syslog. Do not use wiringPi or placeholder camera functions.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that captures grayscale images from an Arducam OV5647 CSI camera module using the V4L2 API — the kernel interface exposed through libcamera's V4L2 compatibility layer, not libcamera's C++ API directly. Save each frame as a raw grayscale .pgm file, named sequentially (image_0001.pgm, image_0002.pgm, etc.). Open the V4L2 device given on the command line, defaulting to /dev/video0. Set the format to 640x480 using V4L2_PIX_FMT_GREY (8-bit grayscale), and use memory-mapped (V4L2_MEMORY_MMAP) streaming with a single buffer. Handle every open(), ioctl(), mmap(), fwrite(), and close() call, printing strerror(errno) on failure, and handle EAGAIN gracefully when dequeuing buffers using select() with a 2-second timeout to avoid infinite loops. Implement clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM to stop streaming and unmap buffers safely. The program should capture frames continuously until a signal is received or a fatal error occurs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that captures an MJPEG video stream from a USB webcam connected at /dev/video0. Configure the video capture for a resolution of 640x480, using the V4L2 API directly rather than the libv4l2 wrapper library. For every captured frame, log its timestamp in microseconds to a file named "frame_log.txt", writing each entry in the format "seconds.microseconds". Use memory-mapped (MMAP) buffers for frame capture, and handle input and output asynchronously with select() so the program never blocks indefinitely waiting for a frame. Implement robust error handling for every V4L2 ioctl call, every file operation, and every memory mapping, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including a graceful shutdown triggered by SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi (Broadcom BCM2711, e.g. Pi 4) that captures video from the CSI camera, exposed as /dev/video0 via V4L2, and streams it over UDP to a target IP address and port given as command-line arguments (./program <server_ip> <server_port>). Use V4L2 MMAP streaming with 4 buffers at 640x480 YUYV format. Fragment each frame into UDP datagrams of at most 65000 bytes, each prefixed with a small header containing the frame index, fragment index, total fragment count, and payload size, so the receiver can reassemble frames. Handle errors at every syscall — open, ioctl, mmap, socket, and sendto — and exit gracefully on failure. Run until SIGINT or SIGTERM is received, then cleanly stop streaming, munmap all buffers, and close all descriptors.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi to capture a single 1920x1080 JPEG image from a USB camera at /dev/video0 and save it to "image.jpg", using the V4L2 API with memory-mapped (MMAP) buffers. Open the device in blocking mode (O_RDWR without O_NONBLOCK) so VIDIOC_DQBUF blocks until a frame is ready. Query device capabilities and verify V4L2_CAP_VIDEO_CAPTURE and V4L2_CAP_STREAMING are supported. Request the format V4L2_PIX_FMT_MJPEG at 1920x1080 with V4L2_FIELD_NONE, request 4 MMAP buffers, and query, mmap, and queue each one. Start streaming, dequeue one frame, verify buf.bytesused > 0, and write the raw MJPEG bytes directly to disk with no re-encoding. Implement clean resource release on all exit paths: stop streaming, munmap all mapped buffers, free the buffer array, close the file, and close the device fd. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so Ctrl+C cleanly tears down streaming and releases resources. Check every ioctl, open, mmap, and fopen return value, printing a descriptive error via perror/errno on failure. Do not use any external image libraries.

Write a C program using the libgpiod library to control a camera pan-tilt system with two hobby servos on a Raspberry Pi: the pan servo is connected to GPIO4 and the tilt servo to GPIO5. Four push-buttons, wired active-low with internal pull-ups enabled, control movement: GPIO6 moves tilt up, GPIO7 moves tilt down, GPIO8 moves pan left, and GPIO9 moves pan right. Generate software PWM through libgpiod with a 50 Hz period (20 ms) and pulse widths between 1 and 2 ms, expressed as duty values of 50 to 100 out of 1000. Start both the pan and tilt servos at the mid-position value of 75. Each button press increments or decrements the corresponding servo's position by 5 units, clamped to the range [25, 125], polling all four buttons every 50 ms. Check the return value of every libgpiod call, handling chip-open and line-request failures, and cleanly release all GPIO resources when SIGINT is received.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi (Bookworm, 64-bit) that captures a single frame from a USB camera at /dev/video0, applies a 5x5 box-blur filter, and saves the result as a JPEG. Use the V4L2 MMAP API correctly: request buffers, mmap, queue, streamon, dequeue, streamoff, munmap, free buffers, and close the fd. Set the format to 640x480 YUYV, and use select() with a 2-second timeout for frame readiness. Convert the captured YUYV frame to RGB24, then apply a 5x5 box blur (kernel radius 2) with edge clamping. Save the blurred result as a JPEG at quality 75 using libjpeg, with an output filename of the form capture_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS.jpg. Handle SIGINT cleanly. Check every syscall and allocation; on error, print to stderr and clean up all resources. Do not use wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi, running a 32-bit or 64-bit kernel with the V4L2 subsystem active, that queries a connected CSI camera at /dev/video0 and prints its supported resolutions, frame rates, and whether autofocus is supported. Use the V4L2 API: open the device, query capabilities with VIDIOC_QUERYCAP, enumerate frame sizes with VIDIOC_ENUM_FRAMESIZES, and enumerate frame intervals with VIDIOC_ENUM_FRAMEINTERVALS. For autofocus support, query the V4L2_CID_FOCUS_AUTO control via VIDIOC_QUERYCTRL. Check every ioctl return value, and handle the cases where the device node does not exist or cannot be opened, where the camera does not support frame-size or interval enumeration, and where the focus control is not present. Print a clear summary to stdout and exit with a non-zero code on fatal errors.

Write a C program using the pigpio library to control a camera pan-tilt system with two standard hobby servos on a Raspberry Pi: pan servo on GPIO4, tilt servo on GPIO5. Four push-buttons, active-low and wired to ground with internal pull-ups enabled, control movement: UP on GPIO6, DOWN on GPIO7, LEFT on GPIO8, RIGHT on GPIO9. Servos expect a 50 Hz PWM signal with pulse widths between 1000 microseconds and 2000 microseconds; initialize both servos to the center position of 1500 microseconds. While a button is held, increment or decrement the corresponding servo position by 10 microseconds per loop iteration (50 ms loop delay), clamped to the 1000-2000 microsecond range. Initialize the pigpio library and check its return value, printing an error and exiting if it fails. Configure internal pull-up resistors on all button pins, and use gpioServo() for PWM output. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler to cleanly stop PWM on both servo pins and call gpioTerminate() before exiting. Print a startup message showing the pin assignments and the center position. Use only pigpio — not wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to detect motion via an HC-SR501 PIR sensor connected to GPIO17 (physical pin 11). Initialize pigpio and configure GPIO17 as input with a pull-down resistor, checking and handling initialization failures; poll it every 100 ms, applying a 2-second debounce after each motion event. When motion is detected, capture a timestamped JPEG snapshot (640x480, quality 85) using the Raspberry Pi Camera Module v2 via the libcamera-still command-line tool, saving it to a directory named "motion_captures" (creating it if it does not exist, handling EEXIST gracefully). The program takes a server IP and port as command-line arguments and sends a JSON payload containing the filename, an ISO 8601 timestamp with microseconds, the motion status, and the GPIO pin number to http://<server_ip>:<server_port>/upload using libcurl. Call curl_global_init exactly once at startup and curl_global_cleanup at exit. Check all system calls, libcurl operations, and file operations for errors, printing diagnostic messages to stderr. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean shutdown, calling gpioTerminate() and curl_global_cleanup().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses a PIR motion sensor (HC-SR501) connected to BCM GPIO17 (physical pin 11) to trigger the Raspberry Pi Camera Module v2 to capture and save a timestamped JPEG image to /home/pi/images. Use libgpiod (v2) for GPIO input and invoke the libcamera-still CLI utility for image capture. Open the GPIO chip and claim GPIO17 as input with edge-falling or edge-rising detection, applying a 50 ms debounce via a falling-edge wait with timeout. On motion detection, generate a timestamped filename in the format YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS_mmm.jpg and run libcamera-still with "-o <filename> --width 640 --height 480 -q 85 --timeout 2000 --nopreview" (assume the images directory already exists), checking its return code and logging failures. Log all events, with timestamps, to /home/pi/motion_capture.log. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM cleanly by releasing all libgpiod resources and closing file descriptors. Do not use wiringPi, and do not use ZeroMQ or any network publishing — save to the local file system only.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi (32-bit or 64-bit) that captures a single frame from a USB UVC camera at /dev/video0 using the V4L2 API, crops a specific region, and saves the result as a raw YUYV file — V4L2 only, no libgpiod, pigpio, or wiringPi. Open /dev/video0 read/write and verify it is a V4L2 video capture device via VIDIOC_QUERYCAP. Negotiate format 640x480, V4L2_PIX_FMT_YUYV, V4L2_FIELD_NONE, and use memory-mapped streaming with one buffer (VIDIOC_REQBUFS, VIDIOC_QUERYBUF, mmap, VIDIOC_QBUF). Start streaming, then use select() with a 2-second timeout to wait for the frame, handling EINTR retries in ioctl calls. Dequeue the buffer and verify the captured width, height, and pixel format match the requested values before processing. Crop the region starting at (100, 50) with size 200x150 from the YUYV frame, copying complete 4-byte YUYV macroblocks (Y0, U, Y1, V) to avoid color corruption, and save the cropped frame to cropped.yuv (200*150*2 bytes). Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so Ctrl-C cleanly stops streaming, munmaps buffers, closes the fd, and frees memory. Check every syscall, ioctl, mmap, fopen, and fwrite return value, printing errno via perror on failure and exiting with EXIT_FAILURE.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to control two SG90 servo motors connected to GPIO17 (pan) and GPIO18 (tilt), forming a basic pan-tilt camera mount. Read user input from stdin — arrow keys for up, down, left, right — to adjust pan and tilt angles in 5-degree increments, enforcing limits of 0 to 180 degrees, with initial angles of 90 degrees (neutral). Use pigpio's hardware PWM at 50 Hz, with pulse widths ranging from 500 microseconds (0 degrees) to 2500 microseconds (180 degrees). Handle pigpio initialization failure gracefully by printing an error and exiting with code 1. On SIGINT (Ctrl+C) or a 'q' input, set both servos to the neutral position and terminate pigpio cleanly. Validate all angle inputs and PWM settings, printing clear error messages for out-of-range angles or PWM failures. Include a 100 ms delay between commands to prevent excessive CPU usage. Use only pigpio functions — not wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that displays real-time CPU temperature, read from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp, and CPU usage percentage, computed from /proc/stat, on a 128x64 I2C OLED screen using the SSD1306 driver. Use the pigpio library for I2C communication on bus 1, addressing the SSD1306 at 0x3C. Implement a basic 5x7 bitmap font to render the temperature and usage text on the display, updating the display once per second. Handle file read errors by returning specific error strings to the display instead of the missing values, and handle I2C communication failures by logging a message to stderr and exiting gracefully, checking every I2C write operation for an error return. Include signal handling for SIGINT so that all resources are released cleanly on exit.
code:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

#define OLED_WIDTH 128
#define OLED_HEIGHT 64
#define OLED_I2C_ADDR 0x3C
#define I2C_BUS 1

#define SSD1306_DISPLAYOFF 0xAE
#define SSD1306_SETDISPLAYCLOCKDIV 0xD5
#define SSD1306_SETMULTIPLEX 0xA8
#define SSD1306_SETDISPLAYOFFSET 0xD3
#define SSD1306_SETSTARTLINE 0x40
#define SSD1306_CHARGEPUMP 0x8B
#define SSD1306_MEMORYMODE 0x20
#define SSD1306_SEGREMAP 0xA0
#define SSD1306_COMSCANDEC 0xC8
#define SSD1306_SETCOMPINS 0xDA
#define SSD1306_SETCONTRAST 0x81
#define SSD1306_SETPRECHARGE 0xD9
#define SSD1306_SETVCOMDETECT 0xDB
#define SSD1306_DISPLAYALLON_RESUME 0xA4
#define SSD1306_NORMALDISPLAY 0xA6
#define SSD1306_DISPLAYON 0xAF
#define SSD1306_SETENTRYMODE 0x40
#define SSD1306_SETCOLUMN 0x21
#define SSD1306_SET 0x00
#define SSD1306_DISPLAYDATA 0x40

#define SSD1306_PAGESCROLLRIGHT 0x00
#define SSD1306_PAGESCROLLLEFT 0x01
#define SSD1306_PAGE 0x02

#define SSD1306_CMD 0x00
#define SSD1306_DATA 0x40

static volatile sig_atomic_t running = 1;

static void signal_handler(int sig) {
    (void)sig;
    running = 0;
}

static int oled_command(int handle, unsigned char cmd) {
    char buf[2] = { (char)SSD1306_CMD, (char)cmd };
    return i2cWriteDevice(handle, buf, 2);
}

static int oled_command2(int handle, unsigned char cmd, unsigned char arg) {
    char buf[3] = { (char)SSD1306_CMD, (char)(cmd + 1), (char)arg };
    return i2cWriteDevice(handle, buf, 3);
}

static int oled_init(int handle) {
    int rc;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_DISPLAYOFF);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_SETDISPLAYCLOCKDIV);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, 0x80);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_SETMULTIPLEX);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, OLED_HEIGHT - 1);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_SETDISPLAYOFFSET);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, 0x00);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_SETSTARTLINE | 0x00);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_CHARGEPUMP);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, 0x14);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_MEMORYMODE);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, 0x00);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_SEGREMAP | 0x01);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_COMSCANDEC);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_SETCOMPINS);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, 0x12);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_SETCONTRAST);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, 0x8F);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_SETPRECHARGE);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, 0xF1);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_SETVCOMDETECT);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, 0x40);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_DISPLAYALLON_RESUME);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_NORMALDISPLAY);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_DISPLAYON);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;

    char buf[3] = { (char)SSD1306_CMD, (char)(cmd + 1), (char)arg };
    return i2cWriteDevice(handle, buf, 3);
}

static int oled_init(int handle) {
    int rc;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_DISPLAYOFF);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_SETDISPLAYCLOCKDIV);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, 0x80);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_SETMULTIPLEX);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, OLED_HEIGHT - 1);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_SETDISPLAYOFFSET);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, 0x00);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_SETSTARTLINE | 0x00);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_CHARGEPUMP);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, 0x14);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_MEMORYMODE);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, 0x00);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_SEGREMAP | 0x01);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_COMSCANDEC);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_SETCOMPINS);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, 0x12);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_SETCONTRAST);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, 0x8F);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_SETPRECHARGE);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, 0xF1);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_SETVCOMDETECT);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, 0x40);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_DISPLAYALLON_RESUME);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_NORMALDISPLAY);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    rc = oled_command(handle, SSD1306_DISPLAYON);
    if (rc < 0) return -1;
    return 0;
}

static int oled_clear(int handle) {
    unsigned char buffer[1 + OLED_WIDTH];
    memset(buffer, 0, sizeof(buffer));
    buffer[0] = SSD1306_DISPLAYDATA;
    for (int page = 0; page < OLED_HEIGHT / 8; page++) {
        if (oled_command2(handle, SSD1306_SET, page + 1) < 0) return -1;
        if (oled_command(handle, SSD1306_SETENTRYMODE) < 0) return -1;
        if (oled_command(handle, 0x00) < 0) return -1;
        if (oled_command(handle, SSD1306_SETCOLUMN) < 0) return -1;
        if (oled_command(handle, OLED_WIDTH) < 0) return -1;
        if (oled_command(handle, SSD1306_DISPLAYDATA) < 0) return -1;
        memcpy(buffer + 1, memset(buffer + 1, 0, OLED_WIDTH), OLED_WIDTH);
        if (oled_command2(handle, SSD1306_SET, page + 1) < 0) return -1;
        if (oled_command(handle, SSD1306_SETENTRYMODE) < 0) return -1;
        if (oled_command(handle, 0x01) < 0) return -1;
        if (oled_command(handle, SSD1306_SETCOLUMN) < 0) return -1;
        if (oled_command(handle, OLED_WIDTH) < 0) return -1;
        if (oled_command(handle, SSD1306_DISPLAYDATA) < 0) return -1;
        memcpy(buffer + 1, memset(buffer + 1, 0xFF, OLED_WIDTH), OLED_WIDTH);
    }
    return i2cWriteDevice(handle, buffer, sizeof(buffer));
}

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library exclusively (no wiringPi) to display real-time wind speed and direction on a 16x2 LCD (PCF8574 I2C backpack at address 0x27, bus 1), updating every 500 ms. Write a C program using the libgpiod library for a Raspberry Pi to create a wave-like animation on an 8x8 common-anode LED matrix. Implement a scanning display function that lights one row at a time — row HIGH and column LOW lights an LED (common-anode logic) — using a scan delay of 800 microseconds per row. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with an STMicroelectronics VL53L3CX Time-of-Flight multi-target sensor via I2C using the pigpio library. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 to interface with an E18-D50NK IR proximity sensor via GPIO using the libgpiod library. The E18-D50NK outputs LOW when an object is detected within its calibrated range of 10-30 cm, and HIGH otherwise. Use GPIO line 4 (physical pin 7) for the sensor input and GPIO line 17 (physical pin 11) for an LED output, polling every 100 ms. When an object is detected (sensor reads LOW), blink the LED for 100 ms (ON then OFF) and log a timestamped event to "proximity.log" in ISO 8601 UTC format, e.g. "2024-01-15T12:34:56Z Object detected" — log only on the falling edge (HIGH to LOW transition, object entering range) to avoid duplicate entries while the object remains in range. Open the GPIO chip by name "gpiochip4" (the Raspberry Pi 5 default); if that fails, fall back to gpiod_chip_open_by_name("gpiochip0") — do not use gpiod_chip_open_lookup without arguments. Check all libgpiod calls and handle file I/O errors, ensuring clean resource release — releasing GPIO lines and closing the chip — on all exit paths, including SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library over I2C bus 1 (default address 0x60) to read proximity (PS1) and ambient light (ALS_VIS) data from a Silicon Labs Si1145 sensor. On startup verify the PART_ID register (0x00) returns 0x45, then write 0x17 to HW_KEY (0x07), set CH_LIST (0x4F) to enable the PS1 and ALS_VIS channels, configure the measurement rates, and use the COMMAND register (0x30) with 0x06 (ALS_FORCE) and 0x07 (PS_FORCE) to trigger measurements. Read PS1 data from registers 0x18-0x19 and ALS_VIS data from registers 0x22-0x23, little-endian. Check every I2C read/write return code and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully. Once per second, in an infinite loop, log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp, proximity value, and ambient light value to a CSV file named 'biometric_data.log', flushing the file after every write. Install a SIGINT handler that closes the I2C handle, closes the log file, and calls gpioTerminate() for clean shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the libgpiod library to drive an HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor for a proximity-based plant watering reminder. Use TRIGGER on GPIO 17 (BCM, output) and ECHO on GPIO 27 (BCM, input). Because the HC-SR04 echo pin outputs 5V logic and the Pi's GPIO is only 3.3V-tolerant, use a voltage divider (e.g. 1kOhm/2kOhm) on the echo line to protect the input. Generate a 10 microsecond trigger pulse, measure the echo pulse width using libgpiod edge events with CLOCK_MONOTONIC, and compute distance as (pulse_seconds * 34300) / 2 cm. Check every libgpiod call, apply a 30 ms timeout on each phase, treat an echo that never rises as sensor-absent and an echo stuck high as a timeout, and reject readings outside 2-400 cm. Log every measurement, including error and timeout entries, with an ISO-8601 timestamp to 'distance_log.txt', polling every 60 seconds. If the measured distance is below 15 cm, log a 'Time to water the plant!' reminder. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, releasing all libgpiod resources and closing the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to continuously read an Adafruit APDS9960 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x39. On startup verify the sensor ID register (0x92) equals 0xAB, then configure ENABLE (0x80) to 0x03, ATIME (0x81) to 0xDB, WTIME (0x83) to 0xF6, PPULSE (0x8E) to 0x87, CONTROL (0xF1) to 0x03, and CONFIG2 (0x90) to 0x01. Every 100 ms read the 16-bit raw RGB color values from registers 0x96-0x9B and the 8-bit proximity value from register 0x9C, logging both with a timestamp to a CSV file named 'color_proximity_log.csv' only when proximity exceeds a threshold of 200. On I2C communication errors, re-open the bus and re-initialize the sensor rather than aborting. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and the CSV file and releasing all pigpio resources. On any I2C communication error, close and reopen the I2C bus and fully re-initialize the sensor's configuration registers before resuming, rather than aborting the program.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface to interface with a Silicon Labs Si1182-A-GMR optical sensor and measure heart rate. Open /dev/i2c-1, set the 7-bit slave address 0x5A via ioctl(I2C_SLAVE), and perform register reads and writes with i2c_smbus_* helpers, checking every return code and aborting on error. On startup, read the PART_ID register (0x00) and verify it returns the expected Si1182 part identifier; if the read fails or the ID mismatches, print a diagnostic and exit non-zero. Configure continuous proximity measurement by writing the MEAS_RATE0 register (0x08) with an appropriate rate value, then issue a reset/start command via the COMMAND register (0x47). Every 100 ms, read the 16-bit proximity data registers PS_DATA0 (0x24) and PS_DATA1 (0x25), combine them little-endian, and compute a placeholder BPM from the proximity signal. Log each sample as 'timestamp,bpm' with an ISO-8601 timestamp to 'heartrate.csv', calling fflush after every write. If an I2C read fails mid-loop, print a warning to stderr, skip that sample, and continue rather than crash. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that sets a volatile running=false flag so the loop exits cleanly, then closes the I2C file descriptor, closes the CSV file, and returns 0.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to interface with an Adafruit VL53L0X Time-of-Flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x29; do not use wiringPi. Configure GPIO 17 (BCM numbering) with a pull-up and trigger a single distance measurement on each falling edge detected there. Verify sensor presence at 0x29 before initialization. To range, write 0x01 to SYSRANGE_START (register 0x00), poll bit 0 of RESULT_INTERRUPT_STATUS (register 0x13) until it sets, with a timeout of about 100 ms, then read the 14-byte result block starting at RESULT_RANGE_STATUS (register 0x14) and extract the 16-bit distance from bytes 10-11, and finally clear the interrupt by writing 0x01 to SYSTEM_INTERRUPT_CLEAR (register 0x0B). Apply robust error handling to every I2C transaction and to sensor-absent and timeout paths. Log each timestamped distance measurement, in millimetres, to 'distance_log.txt' in CSV format as 'timestamp,distance_mm'. Handle SIGINT for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and log file and releasing pigpio resources on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library over I2C bus 1 to measure distance with a TDK CH101 ultrasonic sensor at its default address 0x45. Trigger a measurement, wait about 50 ms, then read the 16-bit distance result in millimetres. Sample every 200 ms, logging each reading as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, <distance_mm>' to 'distance_log.txt' and also printing it to stdout. Check pigpio initialization, the I2C open call, every write and read, and the file open for errors; on I2C errors print a diagnostic and continue to the next sample rather than crashing. Use a fixed-size local buffer for the timestamp so no malloc/free happens per iteration. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl-C) gracefully by stopping the loop and closing the I2C handle, log file, and pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with two TCRT5000 IR reflective sensors on GPIO 17 and GPIO 18 (BCM numbering) to detect object proximity. Every 100 milliseconds, read both sensors and log the readings (0 or 1) with a timestamp to 'obstacle_log.txt'. Apply robust error handling for GPIO setup failures; if a sensor read fails, log an error message to stderr and continue rather than stopping. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for graceful shutdown and ensure all resources are properly released on exit. If a sensor read fails, log a clear error message to stderr and continue polling rather than terminating the program, and ensure all GPIO and file resources are released on every exit path, including SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library for both I2C and GPIO control to interface with a TDK InvenSense ICU-20201 Ultrasonic Time-of-Flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x6A. Every 100 ms, read a distance measurement and log it with an ISO-8601 timestamp to 'distance_log.txt'. Turn on an LED connected to BCM GPIO 17 when the distance falls below 20 cm, and turn it off otherwise. Check all pigpio, I2C, and file operations for errors, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully. Ensure clean resource release of the I2C handle, GPIO, and pigpio library on all exit paths, handling SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Silicon Labs Si1182-GMR Optical Proximity and Ambient Light Sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x60. Every 500 ms, read the 16-bit proximity data from register 0x18 and the 16-bit ambient light data from register 0x16, logging the timestamped readings to a file named 'biometric_log.txt'. Check the return value of every I2C read/write operation, retry failed reads up to 3 times, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for clean resource release: close the I2C handle and log file and terminate pigpio before exiting. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for clean resource release by closing the I2C handle and the log file and terminating pigpio cleanly before the process exits, rather than leaving any handle open.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library for both I2C communication and GPIO control to interface with a TDK InvenSense ICU-20201 ultrasonic Time-of-Flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x6A. Continuously read distance measurements every 50 ms, logging each reading with a timestamp to 'tof_log.txt', and turn on an LED connected to GPIO 17 whenever the measured distance falls below a configurable threshold, default 100 mm, passed as the first command-line argument. Verify the sensor's WHO_AM_I register during initialization, check all I2C read/write return codes, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error conditions gracefully without crashing. Ensure clean resource release of the I2C handle, GPIO, and pigpio library on all exit paths via a SIGINT handler.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (open/ioctl/read/write on /dev/i2c-1) to interface with an Omron B5L-LD50-07050 3D TOF sensor at its default 7-bit address 0x50; do not use wiringPi. To request a distance measurement, write the 4-byte command frame {0x50, 0x0A, 0x00, 0x01} to the sensor, wait at least 10 ms, then read a 15-byte response frame, validating that byte 0 of the header equals 0x50. The distance in millimetres is a 16-bit big-endian value located at bytes 11 and 12 of the response frame. Sample the sensor 10 times per cycle, calculate the average distance, and if it is less than 1000 mm, log the event, along with a timestamp and the average distance, to 'intrusion_log.txt' to detect intrusions within a 1-meter range. Check all I2C open, ioctl, read, and write calls for failures, and handle sensor-absent (I2C NACK) and bus-error paths gracefully. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to close the I2C file descriptor and any open log files, with clean resource release on all exit paths. Use a 100 ms delay between sampling cycles.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to periodically read distance from an Adafruit VL53L0X Time-of-Flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x29. Initialize pigpio and open the I2C device, checking every call for errors and printing strerror(errno) on failure. Verify the sensor is present by reading the model ID register 0xC0 and confirming it equals 0xEE; if the read fails or the ID mismatches, print an error and exit cleanly. Perform a single-shot ranging loop: write 0x01 to SYSRANGE_START (register 0x00) to begin a measurement, poll RESULT_INTERRUPT_STATUS (register 0x13) until bit 0 is set, with a timeout of about 100 ms, then read the 16-bit distance from RESULT_RANGE_STATUS (register 0x14, two bytes, little-endian) and clear the interrupt by writing 0x01 to SYSTEM_INTERRUPT_CLEAR (register 0x0B). Print each reading to stdout as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS Distance: <N> mm' every 500 ms. On any I2C read/write error during the loop, print a warning to stderr and continue to the next iteration rather than crashing. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully by closing the I2C handle, calling gpioTerminate(), and exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to periodically read proximity data from a Silicon Labs Si1182 optical sensor connected on I2C bus 1 (GPIO2 SDA / GPIO3 SCL) at its default 7-bit address 0x39, logging the 16-bit values to the console. Initialize the sensor by writing 0x01 to the CONFIG register (0x18) to enable proximity mode, then poll bit 0 of the IRQ status register (0x25) to detect data-ready before reading the 16-bit proximity result from registers 0x2A (LSB) and 0x2B (MSB), printing the value every 500 ms. Check every pigpio and I2C call, detect sensor-absent as a NACK on the initial write, and handle bus errors gracefully without crashing. Install a SIGINT handler so Ctrl+C cleanly closes the I2C handle and calls gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the Linux I2C userland API (i2c-dev / ioctl SMBus commands), not wiringPi, to read distance data from a Melexis MLX75030 Time-of-Flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default 7-bit address 0x4C, logging the distance in millimetres to stdout every 500 ms. Open /dev/i2c-1 with error checking, set the slave address via ioctl I2C_SLAVE, and verify the device responds; if the sensor is absent at startup, print an error and exit with status 1. Read the 16-bit distance register at offset 0x00, little-endian (low byte first, then high byte), and convert the raw value to millimetres using the factor 0.125 mm per count. Loop reading every 500 ms using nanosleep; on I2C read failure, print a diagnostic to stderr and retry on the next cycle rather than exiting. Print each reading as 'Distance: <value> mm'. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so Ctrl-C cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and exits with status 0.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Texas Instruments OPT3101 Time-of-Flight distance sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x44. Every 500 ms, log channel 0 distance readings, ambient light data, and any error flags to the console. Apply robust error handling for I2C communication failures such as a sensor being absent or bus errors, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown on SIGINT (Ctrl+C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to periodically read distance from an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor connected with trigger on GPIO 17 (BCM) and echo on GPIO 18 (BCM). Send a 10 microsecond trigger pulse, measure the echo pulse width using gpioTick() for microsecond precision, and compute distance in cm using the formula (pulse_us * 0.0343) / 2. Log each reading with a timestamp to the console once per second. Handle errors for pigpio initialization failure, an echo rising-edge timeout of 200 ms, an echo falling-edge timeout of 200 ms, and invalid pulse durations (<= 0 or > 38 ms, the HC-SR04's maximum range timeout). Use a 1 kOhm resistor in series on the echo line for protection, and note in a comment that the HC-SR04 operates at 5V while the Pi GPIO is only 3.3V tolerant. Shut down gracefully on SIGINT/SIGTERM, calling gpioTerminate() on all exit paths. Note in a code comment that gpioTick() returns a monotonically increasing microsecond counter, and ensure the trigger, echo timing, and logging steps repeat once every second until a shutdown signal is received.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to interface with a Texas Instruments IWR1443 mmWave radar sensor over UART (/dev/serial0), using the POSIX termios library for UART initialization and the pigpio library for GPIO control. The radar outputs a range profile of 64 range bins with a range resolution of 0.0486 meters per bin. Each data frame begins with an 8-byte magic word header (0x02 0x01 0x04 0x03 0x06 0x05 0x08 0x07), followed by 128 bytes of raw range profile data as 64 little-endian 16-bit integers. Implement basic intrusion detection: trigger an alert if a target appears within a distance threshold of 1.0 meters, activating an LED on GPIO 17 (BCM) for 2 seconds. Log each detected intrusion, with an ISO 8601 timestamp and the distance in meters, to a comma-separated file named 'intrusion_log.csv'. Handle UART initialization errors via termios, validate all I/O operations, handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths through SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the libgpiod library, not the deprecated sysfs interface, to read obstacle detection data from an E18-D80NK IR sensor connected to GPIO 17. The sensor is active-low, outputting 0 when an obstacle is within the threshold distance and 1 otherwise. When an obstacle is detected, activate a buzzer on GPIO 18 (active-high); when the obstacle is removed, deactivate the buzzer. Poll the sensor every 100 ms and log every state transition with an ISO 8601 timestamp to 'obstacle_log.txt'. Check all libgpiod return values and handle errors robustly, including chip open failure, line request failure, and read/write errors. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, releasing all GPIO lines and closing the chip.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with a TDK Chirp ICU-20201 Ultrasonic Time-of-Flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x69. Continuously read distance measurements by combining the 16-bit distance value from registers 0x31 (high byte) and 0x32 (low byte), sampling every 100 ms. Log each reading with an ISO 8601 timestamp to 'distance_log.txt', and trigger a GPIO alert on physical pin 17 (BCM 17) if the distance falls below 10.0 cm. Handle all I2C read/write errors, check for sensor absence, and manage log file creation errors. Cleanly release all resources -- I2C handles, GPIO, and pigpio -- on SIGINT/SIGTERM. Structure the main loop so that every sample first checks for a signal-requested shutdown, then performs the I2C read, then writes the log entry, so that no partial or corrupted log line is ever produced even if an error occurs mid-sample.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a parking-assistance system using an STMicroelectronics VL53L1X Time-of-Flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x29, using the pigpio library (not wiringPi). Verify the sensor is present by reading the model ID register 0x010F and checking it equals 0xEA. Perform a software reset by writing 0x00 to register 0x0000 and waiting 2 ms. Write 0x01 to the SYSTEM__MODE_START register 0x007 to begin continuous back-to-back ranging, then poll the SYSRANGE__START register 0x000 bit 0 until it self-clears, with a timeout of 100 ms. In a loop every 100 ms, poll bit 0 of the RESULT__INTERRUPT_STATUS register 0x013 for data-ready, read the 16-bit distance from RESULT__RANGE_STATUS + 10 (register 0x078, big-endian), clear the interrupt by writing 0x01 to the SYSTEM__INTERRUPT_CLEAR register 0x014, and append each reading as 'timestamp,distance_mm' to distance_log.csv, writing the header row 'timestamp,distance_mm' only when creating a new file. Print a parking guidance message to stdout based on thresholds: below 300 mm print 'STOP', 300-600 mm 'APPROACH', 600-1200 mm 'SLOW', and above 1200 mm 'CLEAR'. Check every pigpio, I2C, and file return code, and handle SIGINT/SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, releasing all resources -- I2C handle, log file, pigpio -- on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) for both I2C and GPIO to interface with a TDK InvenSense CH201 ultrasonic Time-of-Flight sensor over I2C bus 1 (GPIO 2/3 for SDA/SCL) at its default address 0x45, and blink an LED on GPIO 18 (with a 330 Ohm current-limiting resistor to 3.3V) faster as the measured distance decreases. Sample distance every 100 ms. Map distance linearly to blink frequency: 50 mm maps to 10 Hz, 500 mm maps to 1 Hz, clamped outside this range. Each loop iteration should perform one half-cycle of the LED blink (on or off) so the blink continues smoothly across samples. Log timestamped distance and blink frequency to stdout. Check every pigpio and I2C call, retry failed I2C reads or writes up to 3 times with 10 ms delays between attempts, and handle sensor-absent (I2C open failure) or bus-error paths gracefully. Install SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers for clean shutdown: close the I2C handle, turn off the LED, and terminate pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Melexis MLX75030 Time-of-Flight sensor over I2C bus 1, continuously reading distance data and appending it to a comma-separated 'distance_log.csv' file formatted as 'timestamp,distance_cm'. Assume the sensor requires a write command to trigger a measurement, followed by a delay, then a 2-byte read returning the distance in centimeters, sampled at a 100 ms interval. Apply robust error handling for I2C communication failures -- sensor absent, bus errors, read/write timeouts -- with retry logic for transient errors, logging errors to stderr. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful termination via SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to interface two TCRT5000 IR obstacle avoidance sensors on GPIO 17 (physical pin 11) and GPIO 27 (physical pin 13). Each TCRT5000 outputs LOW (0) when an obstacle is detected and HIGH (1) when the path is clear. Poll both sensors every 10 ms with a 50 ms software debounce per sensor, and log every state transition with an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp, the sensor ID (1 or 2), and the event type -- 'DETECTED' for a HIGH-to-LOW transition, 'CLEARED' for LOW-to-HIGH -- to 'proximity_log.txt'. Check the return values of gpioInitialise(), gpioSetMode(), gpioRead(), and all file I/O operations. Ensure clean resource release, closing the log file and calling gpioTerminate(), on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface, with no third-party GPIO libraries like wiringPi, to interface with a TDK CH-101 Time-of-Flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default 7-bit address 0x49, for use in a smart parking system. Use /dev/i2c-1 and standard open(2), ioctl(I2C_SLAVE), read(2), and write(2) system calls, and implement a helper that performs an I2C register read using a combined write-then-read transaction. Trigger a single range measurement by writing 0x01 to the MEAS_TRIGGER register (0x04), then poll the MEAS_STATUS register (0x06) until bit 0 (data-ready) is set, with a timeout of 50 ms. Read the 16-bit distance from registers DIST_HIGH (0x08, MSB) and DIST_LOW (0x09, LSB), combined as (DIST_HIGH << 8) | DIST_LOW, in millimetres. Check every open, ioctl, write, read, and fopen call; on I2C failure print a diagnostic to stderr with errno and skip that sample rather than crashing. Log the data with ISO-8601 timestamps to a CSV file named 'distance_log.csv' with columns timestamp,distance_mm, sampling every 500 ms between successful measurements. Perform a clean shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM: close the I2C file descriptor and flush and close the CSV file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface directly (open/ioctl on /dev/i2c-1), not wiringPi and not any external VL53L5CX driver library, to periodically read distance data from a VL53L5CX ToF sensor at I2C address 0x29. Configure the sensor for an 8x8 zone grid (64 zones), implementing the I2C register reads and writes manually with standard Linux file I/O. Every 500 ms, log all 64 zone distances to the console. Apply robust error handling for I2C communication and sensor initialization, with clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT. Structure the zone read as a loop over all 64 zones, printing each zone's distance value clearly labeled by zone index, and repeat this full 64-zone read every 500 ms until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to interface with a Melexis MLX75030 ToF sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x4C. Every 100 ms, read a distance measurement and log it to the console with a millisecond timestamp. Check the return values of all pigpio initialization and I2C read/write calls, retry failed I2C transactions up to 3 times with a 10 ms delay between retries, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully. Ensure clean resource release, closing the I2C handle and terminating pigpio, on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown on SIGINT (Ctrl+C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to read distance data from a VL53L4CX time-of-flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x29. Initialize pigpio and open the I2C bus, with full error checking on every call. Perform the startup sequence: write 0x00 to register 0x7FFF (soft reset), wait 10 ms, then write 0x00 to register 0x0009 to begin ranging, checking the return value of every I2C write and aborting cleanly on failure. Every 500 ms, poll the interrupt status register 0x0046; if bit 0 is set, read the 16-bit distance result from registers 0x0096 (high byte) and 0x0097 (low byte) and log it to the console with a microsecond-precision timestamp in the format 'Timestamp: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.uuuuuu, Distance: N mm'. If the interrupt status bit is not set after the poll, skip that cycle without reporting an error. On I2C communication failures, print an error message to stderr and continue to the next cycle for transient errors, or abort cleanly for initialization failures. Install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM so Ctrl+C triggers a graceful shutdown: close the I2C handle, call gpioTerminate(), and exit with return 0. Use the specified registers exactly, not placeholder addresses, and ensure all resources are released on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with a single VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x29. Configure the sensor for continuous ranging mode, using registers SOFT_RESET (0x0001), I2C_SLAVE__DEVICE_ADDRESS (0x0001), SYSTEM__MODE_START (0x0007), and RESULT__FINAL_CROSSTALK_CORRECTED_DISTANCE_MM (0x0096). Trigger distance readings every 500 ms and activate an active buzzer connected to GPIO 22 if the measured distance is below 100 mm. Handle I2C errors gracefully -- sensor absent, bus errors -- by logging the error and skipping the iteration. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including handling SIGINT for graceful shutdown. Ensure the continuous ranging configuration is applied exactly once at startup and re-applied automatically if a re-initialization is required after an I2C error, and confirm the buzzer is switched off again as soon as the measured distance rises back above the 100 mm threshold, rather than staying latched on.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to implement a parking-assist system with a single HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor -- trigger on GPIO 23, echo on GPIO 24, both BCM -- and an SG90 servo controlled on GPIO 17 (BCM) that rotates between -90 degrees (closest, about a 1 ms pulse) and +90 degrees (farthest, about a 2 ms pulse) to indicate the measured distance. Initialize pigpio and check for failure, configure trigger as output and echo as input, and measure distance by sending a 10 microsecond trigger pulse and timing the echo pulse width using a speed of sound of 343 m/s. Handle sensor timeouts -- echo stuck low or high for more than 50 ms -- by returning a sentinel error value and skipping that reading. Map valid distances from 2 to 400 cm to servo angle so that 2 cm maps to -90 degrees and 400 cm maps to +90 degrees. Log each reading with a timestamp to sensor_data.log, appending, once every 200 ms until interrupted. Install SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers for graceful shutdown that stop the servo (pulse 0), release resources, and call gpioTerminate() on all exit paths, including when the main loop exits due to a signal, ensuring no GPIO operations occur after termination. Use only valid BCM GPIO numbers on the Pi 4, and do not use GPIO 28.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to interface with a VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x29. Verify the sensor model ID equals 0xEA at register 0x010F during initialization, perform a software reset by writing 0x00 then 0x01 to register 0x0000, configure the sensor for a 50 ms timing budget, and start ranging by writing 0x01 to register 0x0080. Every 50 ms, poll the data-ready bit (bit 0 of register 0x0089) before reading the 16-bit distance from registers 0x0096-0x0097, and activate a buzzer connected to GPIO23 if the measured distance falls below 100mm. Handle all I2C read/write errors gracefully, with robust error handling for I2C communication failures and sensor absence. Log distance readings using a POSIX message queue. Ensure clean resource release of the I2C handle, message queue, GPIO, and pigpio on SIGINT. Structure the initialization sequence so that the model-ID check, the software reset, and the timing-budget configuration all complete successfully before ranging begins, and treat a failure at any of these steps as a fatal startup error.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to implement an interrupt-driven parking sensor with a single HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor on GPIO 17 (trigger, BCM) and GPIO 27 (echo, BCM), with a buzzer on GPIO 22 (BCM). Send a 10 microsecond HIGH trigger pulse and use gpioSetAlertFuncEx for interrupt-driven measurement of the echo pulse width, computing distance using a speed of sound of 34300 cm/s divided by 2 for the round trip, and handling pigpio's 32-bit tick wraparound correctly. Valid readings range from 2 cm to 400 cm. Display the distance in centimeters on the console every 100 ms. Activate the buzzer continuously while the distance is less than 30 cm, and turn it off once the distance returns to 30 cm or above. Check pigpio initialization, GPIO mode configuration, and alert registration for errors, and detect and clearly report sensor-absent (timeout/no echo) and invalid reading (out-of-range) conditions. Perform a clean shutdown on SIGINT that turns off the buzzer and calls gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to control a gate with a VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x29 and an SG90 servo motor on GPIO18 (BCM, hardware PWM). Automatically open the gate when an object is detected within 20 cm and close it when the path is clear. Implement full bare-metal I2C initialization for the VL53L1X: software reset, wait for boot, start ranging, and read the 16-bit distance. Log all gate events with timestamps to 'gate_log.txt'. Handle I2C communication errors and sensor-absent paths gracefully, with retries. Support remote control using the paho-mqtt v2 callback API, handling force_open, force_close, and status_request commands. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths via signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to measure distance with an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor: TRIG on GPIO 23 (physical pin 16, BCM, output, initially LOW) and ECHO on GPIO 24 (physical pin 18, BCM, input with a pull-down resistor). Initialize pigpio with full error checking, printing a diagnostic and exiting non-zero on failure. Generate a 10 microsecond trigger pulse to start each measurement cycle, and register an alert callback on ECHO that captures both rising and falling edge timestamps as pigpio tick values in microseconds. Compute pulse duration as (falling_tick - rising_edge_tick), accounting for pigpio's 32-bit tick wraparound every roughly 72 minutes, and calculate distance using a speed of sound of 343 m/s (0.0343 cm/us), dividing by 2 for the round trip. Validate the pulse width: reject readings below 100 microseconds as noise or above 30000 microseconds as a timeout/no object detected, logging rejected readings as warnings. Log valid readings with an ISO 8601 timestamp to both stdout and an append-mode file named 'distance_log.txt', flushing after each write. Measure every 200 ms (5 Hz); if no valid echo is received within 60 ms of triggering, log a timeout warning and continue. Note in a comment that the HC-SR04's ECHO output is 5V, exceeding the Pi's 3.3V GPIO tolerance, and assume a voltage divider or logic-level converter is present on the ECHO line. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean shutdown: close the log file, release GPIO resources via gpioTerminate(), and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) for all GPIO, PWM, and I2C operations to implement a smart parking gate with a VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor on I2C bus 1 (GPIO2/SDA, GPIO3/SCL) at address 0x29 and a servo motor gate actuator. Connect the VL53L1X shutdown pin to GPIO23 (BCM) and its interrupt pin to GPIO24 (BCM); generate the servo PWM signal on GPIO18 (BCM, hardware PWM). Open the gate when an object is detected within 50 cm and close it when the distance exceeds 60 cm, applying hysteresis. Log all gate state changes with timestamps and distances to 'parking_log.txt'. Verify the sensor model ID during initialization, check all I2C read/write operations, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handlers.
