prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to control a gate actuator based on a VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor connected via I2C bus 1 at address 0x29. The gate should open (GPIO 18 HIGH, GPIO 19 LOW) when the sensor detects an object within 20 cm (200 mm), and close (GPIO 18 LOW, GPIO 19 HIGH) otherwise. Properly initialize the VL53L1X with a soft reset, configure its timing budget, and start ranging, polling the sensor every 500 ms and reading the 16-bit distance from the correct data registers. Use the pigpio I2C functions i2cWriteI2CBlockData and i2cReadI2CBlockData for 16-bit register access, since the VL53L1X uses 16-bit register addresses; do not use i2cReadBlockData or i2cWriteBlockData for register reads or writes. Log every open/close event with an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp to 'gate_events.log'. Check all pigpio and I2C return codes, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully by logging the error. Ensure clean resource release -- close the I2C handle, reset GPIO, close the log file, call gpioTerminate -- on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with a single VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x29. Trigger a distance reading on the rising edge of GPIO24 using a pigpio ISR. Follow this VL53L1X register sequence: write 0x00 to register 0x0000 (soft reset), wait 1 ms, write 0x01 to register 0x0000 (start measurement), poll register 0x0089 until bit 0 is set (data ready), then read the 16-bit distance from registers 0x0096-0x0097. Based on the measured distance, control a small DC motor via GPIO17 (forward) and GPIO18 (backward): below 100 mm (10 cm) drive forward, above 300 mm (30 cm) drive backward, otherwise stop. Check all pigpio and I2C return values, retry failed I2C transactions with exponential backoff, and stop the motor safely if the sensor is absent or a bus error occurs. Log distance readings and motor state changes to the console. Ensure clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM: close I2C handles, stop the motor, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses libgpiod for GPIO control and the Linux I2C interface (/dev/i2c-1 via ioctl), not wiringPi, to implement a proximity-based interactive art installation with a single MPR121 capacitive touch sensor at I2C address 0x5A. Monitor the 12 electrodes ELE0-ELE11 by polling the touch status registers 0x00 and 0x01 every 50 ms, and trigger distinct 4-bit LED patterns on GPIO 17, 18, 27, and 22 (BCM) based on which electrode detects proximity. On startup, perform a soft reset by writing 0x63 to register 0x80, verify the sensor is present by reading back a known register, then initialize it: stop mode (ELECONFIG0 = 0x00), baseline filtering (MHDR = 0x01, NHDR = 0x01, NCLR = 0x0E, FDLR = 0x00), auto-configuration thresholds (register 0x5A = 0x0B, 0x5D = 0xC8, 0x5E = 0x82, 0x5F = 0xB4), and enable all 12 electrodes in run mode (ELECONFIG0 = 0x0C). Validate all I2C reads and writes and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully. Log all proximity events to the console with timestamps. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths -- releasing all GPIO lines and closing the I2C and log file descriptors -- using signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM. Ensure the electrode-to-LED-pattern mapping is applied consistently every polling cycle, so that only one 4-bit pattern is ever active at a time, and log a clear message whenever the touch status registers indicate no electrode is currently active.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library for both I2C and GPIO control to implement a capacitive touch-based proximity detector with an MPR121 sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x5A. Configure electrode 0 with a touch threshold of 0x0A and a release threshold of 0x05. Verify the MPR121 is present by reading its device ID, and properly initialize all required MPR121 registers: FFI, SFI, ESI, debounce, AFE config, and baseline filtering. When proximity is detected on electrode 0, turn on an LED connected to GPIO 27 for 1 second and log the event with a timestamp to 'proximity.log'. Handle I2C errors gracefully, and cleanly release all resources on SIGINT/SIGTERM. Ensure the touch and release thresholds are written before any other MPR121 configuration register, and confirm the LED is switched off again automatically after its 1 second interval elapses.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the libgpiod library, not sysfs or wiringPi, to measure distance with an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor: trigger on GPIO17 (BCM, output), echo on GPIO18 (BCM, input). Open the trigger line as output and the echo line as input using gpiod_line_request_output/input with proper error checking on every call. Run the trigger sequence: hold trigger low for 5 microseconds, pulse high for 10 microseconds, then low. Wait for the echo rising edge with a 30 ms timeout, then measure the echo pulse width with a 30 ms timeout, computing distance as (pulse_us * 0.0343) / 2.0 cm using a speed of sound of about 343 m/s at 20 degrees C. Reject readings outside 2-400 cm and log an error line instead. Handle sensor-absent (echo never rises) and timeout paths explicitly. Every second, log the reading with an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp to 'distance_log.txt', flushing the file after each write. Install a SIGINT handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag; on SIGINT release all libgpiod resources, close the log file, and exit cleanly. Use libgpiod bulk or per-line requests and do not leak resources on any exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses pigpio to measure distance with an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor: TRIG on GPIO17 and ECHO on GPIO18 (BCM), with a 1 kOhm/2 kOhm voltage divider stepping the 5V echo signal down to about 3.3V for the Pi's input. Use pigpio's interrupt-driven ISR callback (gpioSetISRFuncEx) to measure the echo pulse width on EITHER_EDGE transitions. Fire a 10 microsecond trigger pulse once per second, compute distance in meters as pulse_us * 343 / 2e6, and append each reading with a timestamp to 'distance_log.txt'. Check pigpio initialization and the file open for errors, validate that an echo was actually received -- pulse width greater than 0 and within a sane range such as 58 microseconds to 25 milliseconds, roughly 1 cm to 4 m -- and handle tick-wraparound in the pulse-width calculation. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler for clean shutdown that disables the ISR, closes the log file, and calls gpioTerminate(). Do not include any UDP networking; focus purely on local logging.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with a VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x29, using GPIO27 as an active-low trigger to the sensor's XSHUT pin. Configure GPIO27 as an output and set it high at startup to enable the sensor. Initialise the sensor by writing 0x00 to register 0x0018 (continuous mode), 0x00 to register 0x0019 (no timeout), and 0x01 to register 0x0020 (start ranging). In an infinite loop, read the 2-byte little-endian distance from register 0x0014 and the 1-byte status from register 0x0016, and log the timestamp, distance in mm, and status to the systemd journal via syslog, using LOG_INFO for successful reads and LOG_ERR for failures; on a read failure, log the error and continue without crashing. Wait 100 ms between readings. Verify pigpio initialisation and the I2C device open. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that close the I2C handle, terminate pigpio, and exit cleanly on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to interface with a VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x29 and control a gate actuator on GPIO24 (active high to open). Initialise the sensor by reading the model ID from register 0x010F (expect 0xEA), setting the ranging mode to short via register 0x0021 = 0x00, and starting ranging via register 0x0015 = 0x01. Read the distance from the 16-bit register pair 0x0089-0x008A and convert it from mm to cm. Every 100 ms, open the gate when the distance is less than 20 cm and close it otherwise; the gate must start closed (GPIO24 low) at startup. Log every distance reading, gate state change, and error with a timestamp to 'gate_log.txt'. Check all I2C operations, sensor initialisation, and file operations for errors. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that closes the I2C handle, closes the log file, and terminates pigpio for a graceful shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to measure distance with an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (trigger on GPIO23, echo on GPIO24) and pan an SG90 servo (signal on GPIO18, hardware PWM-capable) to track it. Drive the trigger high for 10 us then low, and measure the echo pulse width with a pigpio alert callback using the 32-bit tick counter with wrap-around handling, applying a 30 ms timeout. Convert pulse width to distance using speed of sound = 34300 cm/s, valid range 2-400 cm, and apply a 5-sample moving average. Map distance to a servo angle of 0-180 degrees using a non-linear (logarithmic) mapping, convert the angle to a pulse width of 500-2500 us, and command it via gpioServo(). Trigger every 100 ms. Write timestamp, distance in cm, and servo angle in degrees to 'distance_log.csv' with a header row, flushing after each write. Check pigpio initialisation, alert registration, servo command return codes, and file open; on an invalid reading (out of range or no echo), log -1.0 and default the servo to 90 degrees. Protect the pulse-width data shared between the alert callback and the main thread with a flag-based handshake. On SIGINT, using a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, stop the servo, close the CSV file, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with a VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x29. Initialise the sensor using the recommended STMicroelectronics sequence: set the default configuration, enable the signal rate check, configure cross-talk compensation, and start ranging. Continuously read distance measurements in millimeters every 50 ms and store the last 10 readings in a circular buffer. If any reading falls below 200 mm, set GPIO17 HIGH to activate a warning LED, otherwise set it LOW. Check every I2C read/write operation, handle sensor initialisation failures, and on a read error print the error and continue rather than crashing. Install a SIGINT handler that turns off the LED, closes the I2C handle, and terminates pigpio, and release all resources on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Silicon Labs Si1102 proximity sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x60, and configures GPIO27 to raise an interrupt on a rising edge when proximity exceeds a configurable threshold (default 1000). Initialise pigpio and I2C with error checking. Read the 16-bit proximity value from registers 0x08 (high byte) and 0x09 (low byte). On each interrupt, read the proximity value, compare it to the threshold, and log to 'proximity.log' a timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS), the proximity value, and a status of 'SAFE' if at or below the threshold or 'ALERT' if above it. Support command-line arguments -a <i2c_address> (hex or decimal) and -t <threshold>. The interrupt handler must be thread-safe, with no blocking calls, using a flag or queue to hand data to the main loop. Check all I2C operations, GPIO setup, and file operations, printing errors to stderr. Handle SIGINT for clean shutdown: close the I2C handle, close the log file, and terminate pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to build a theremin-like instrument: an 8-ohm speaker on GPIO18 (PWM0) produces a tone whose pitch is controlled by the distance measured from an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (trigger on GPIO23, echo on GPIO24). Use pigpio's hardware-timed PWM to generate the tone, with frequency ranging from 200 Hz to 2000 Hz at 50% duty cycle. Drive the HC-SR04 using pigpio's gpioTrigger() and gpioWaveTxBusy() for precise timing, with a 10 us trigger pulse and a 200 ms timeout. Map the measured distance (2 cm to 200 cm) to frequency using the logarithmic formula f = 200 * exp(distance / 50) Hz. If the distance is out of range or the echo times out, keep the previous frequency rather than producing an error tone. Include robust error checking for every pigpio call. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that cleanly stop the PWM output and terminate pigpio, with proper resource cleanup on exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to synthesize a theremin-like instrument on a piezo buzzer connected to GPIO18 (PWM0), with pitch controlled by distance read from an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (trigger on GPIO23, echo on GPIO24). Set trigger low initially, send a 10 us high pulse, and measure the echo pulse width with microsecond precision using gpioDelay for timing and pull-down resistors on the echo pin; treat a pulse over 100 ms as a timeout, report the error, and reuse the last valid distance. The sensor's full range is 2 cm to 400 cm, but map the practical range of 5 cm to 50 cm linearly to a PWM frequency between 200 Hz and 2000 Hz using frequency = MIN_FREQ + (MAX_FREQ - MIN_FREQ) * (MAX_DIST - distance) / (MAX_DIST - MIN_DIST), clamped to that range, driven through pigpio's gpioHardwarePWM (not sysfs PWM) so the tone changes smoothly and continuously. Check pigpio initialisation and confirm GPIO modes are set correctly, handling sensor read failures gracefully. Print distance and frequency to the console each loop iteration, with a 10 ms delay between readings. Install a SIGINT handler that stops the PWM output and terminates pigpio cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to measure distance with an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor connected to GPIO17 (trigger) and GPIO18 (echo). Initialise pigpio, set the trigger pin as output (initially low) and the echo pin as input. Every 500 ms, send a 10 us trigger pulse and measure the echo pulse width with a 50 ms timeout, computing distance in cm as pulse_width / 2 / 29.1 (speed of sound = 29.1 cm/us). Reject readings below 2 cm or above 400 cm, printing 'Invalid reading' for those; otherwise print the distance as 'Distance: X.XX cm', and if it is below 10 cm also print 'Too close!'. Check pigpio initialisation and handle a timeout (-1) returned from the echo pulse measurement, ensuring that all resources are released cleanly on every exit path, not only on the normal one. Handle SIGINT by setting a flag to exit the loop, terminating pigpio, and exiting cleanly. The program should run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with a TDK InvenSense ICU-20201 ultrasonic time-of-flight sensor over SPI (mode 0, 1 MHz clock, chip select on GPIO8 / CE0), for a robotic obstacle-avoidance application. Initialise the sensor by writing 0x01 to register 0x01 (continuous measurement mode), 0x00 to register 0x02 (5 m range), and 0x01 to register 0x00 to trigger a measurement; read the distance from registers 0x0C (low byte) and 0x0D (high byte) using spiXfer, since pigpio has no spiWriteRead function. Continuously read distance in millimeters (range 200-5000 mm) with a 100 ms delay between readings, and log each reading with a timestamp to 'distance_log.csv' opened in append mode, closed properly on exit. Handle SPI communication errors, sensor initialisation failures, and sensor-absent conditions gracefully, logging errors to stderr and continuing to run indefinitely. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that close the SPI handle, release resources, and flush the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the standard Linux I2C ioctl interface (no third-party C libraries) to interface with a Silicon Labs Si1175 ambient light and proximity sensor at its default I2C address 0x60. Read the 16-bit visible ambient light value from registers 0x22 (low byte) and 0x23 (high byte) every 5 seconds. Log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to a CSV file named 'proximity_log.csv' with the header row 'timestamp,als_visible'. Check every I2C open/read/write call for errors, handling both sensor-absent conditions and bus-error paths without terminating unexpectedly, and cleanly release the I2C file descriptor and the log file on all exit paths, including those triggered by SIGINT and SIGTERM. Include <stdint.h> for the uint8_t and uint16_t types used to hold the register bytes and the combined light reading.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read ambient light (ALS) and proximity (PS1) data from a Silicon Labs Si1120 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x60. Reset the sensor by writing 0x01 to register 0x30, then verify the part ID at register 0x00 equals 0x41. Read ALS data from registers 0x22 (low byte) and 0x23 (high byte) and proximity data from registers 0x18 (low byte) and 0x19 (high byte), combining each pair into a 16-bit little-endian value. Sample every 500 ms until SIGINT (Ctrl+C) is received, logging each reading together with a timestamp in YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS format to 'si1120_log.txt', which the program opens in append mode so earlier readings are preserved across runs. Retry I2C operations up to 3 times with a 10 ms delay between attempts before giving up on that reading, check the return value of every initialisation call and syscall, print descriptive errors to stderr so a failure can be diagnosed, and release all resources (I2C handle, log file, pigpio) on any failure path as well as on normal exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses standard Linux I2C ioctl calls (open, ioctl, read, write) on /dev/i2c-1 to interface with a Silicon Labs Si1182-A-GM optical sensor at I2C address 0x39. Initialise the sensor by verifying the part ID register (0x00) and configuring the measurement rate register (0x08) to 0x07. Every 100 ms, read ambient light data from registers 0x22-0x23 and proximity data from registers 0x24-0x25, each as a 16-bit little-endian value; convert ambient light to lux using lux = raw * 0.1, and log proximity as the raw value with no conversion. Log each timestamped reading (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.mmm) to 'biometric_log.txt' in CSV format as timestamp,lux,proximity, and print the same reading to stdout. Check every I2C read/write operation for errors, handle sensor absence (a failed part ID read) gracefully, and report I2C bus errors such as NACK with appropriate messages. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that close the I2C file descriptor and log file, and ensure all resources are released on every exit path, including error exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library's I2C functions (gpioInitialise, i2cOpen, i2cWriteByteData, i2cReadByteData, i2cClose, gpioTerminate) to continuously read proximity data from a Silicon Labs Si1145 sensor at I2C address 0x60. Initialise the sensor with the following write sequence: 0x03 to register 0x07 (hardware key), 0x02 to register 0x06 (MEAS_RATE, 2 ms), 0x00 to register 0x1A (no interrupt), 0x0B to register 0x21 (ALS_VIS_IR_ADC_COUNTER), 0x00 to register 0x24 (ALS_VIS_ADC_GAIN), 0x49 to register 0x22 (PS_ADC_COUNTER, 16-bit, 1/15 gain), 0x03 to register 0x0C (PS_LED21, 180 mA), 0x0F to register 0x0F (PS_LED3, 180 mA), 0x03 to register 0x11 (PS_ADC_MISC, small IR), 0x07 to register 0x0D (PS_ADC_GAIN, 7.7x), and 0x03 to register 0x80 (COMMAND, PS_FORCE). After initialisation, continuously read the proximity value from registers 0x16 (PS1_DATA0, low byte) and 0x17 (PS1_DATA1, high byte), combining them into a 16-bit unsigned integer, and append each reading with a timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS) to 'proximity_log.txt'. Check every I2C write/read operation for errors; on a communication failure, log the error together with a timestamp and retry up to 3 times before exiting, and handle sensor initialisation failures by reporting a clear, specific error message rather than failing silently. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to measure distance with an interrupt-driven HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (trigger on GPIO17, echo on GPIO18) and activate a buzzer on GPIO27 when the distance falls below 20 cm. Configure the trigger pin as output, the echo pin as input with a falling/rising edge alert callback, and the buzzer pin as output. Generate a 10 us trigger pulse on GPIO17, then measure the echo pulse width using an interrupt handler that records the rising and falling edge timestamps, computing distance in cm as round-trip time * 0.0343 / 2 (speed of sound = 0.0343 cm/us). Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) by terminating pigpio and exiting, with proper resource cleanup on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to implement a parking assist system with an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (trigger on GPIO4, echo on GPIO17) and an SG90 servo motor (signal on GPIO18). Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to interface with a VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x29 and control a servo-actuated gate on GPIO18 (hardware PWM-capable). Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to implement a parking assist system with an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (trigger on GPIO23, echo on GPIO24, measuring 2 cm to 400 cm) and an SG90 micro servo (signal on GPIO18, powered from 5V with a common ground) that visually indicates distance by rotating from 0 degrees (closest) to 180 degrees (farthest). Map distances below 20 cm to 0 degrees, above 200 cm to 180 degrees, and values in between linearly, controlling the servo via gpioServo() with pulse widths of 500 us for 0 degrees and 2500 us for 180 degrees. Print distance and angle each cycle, with a 100 ms delay between measurements. Initialise pigpio with error checking, exiting with a clear message on failure; check every pigpio call, handle sensor timeout, and avoid division by zero or invalid angles. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) by stopping the servo (gpioServo with 0) and terminating pigpio cleanly. Use only pigpio, not wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Silicon Labs Si7005 I2C humidity and temperature sensor at I2C bus 1, address 0x40, logging readings to the console every 2 seconds. Write 0x00 to the CONFIG register (0x03) to select the internal temperature sensor and disable the heater, waiting 10 ms afterward. After writing the register address to read, wait 10 ms for conversion, then read the temperature register (0x01) and the humidity register (0x02). Convert readings using T = (175.72 * raw) / 65536.0 - 46.85 and H = (125.0 * raw) / 65536.0 - 6.0. Verify pigpio initialisation, the I2C bus open, and every I2C read/write operation; if a transaction fails, close and re-open the I2C handle to attempt recovery. Handle SIGINT for a graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and terminating pigpio on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to periodically read raw accelerometer and gyroscope data from a TDK InvenSense MPU-6050 over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x68 (SDA on GPIO2, SCL on GPIO3), logging it to the console. Every 100 ms, read the 14-byte data block starting at register 0x3B (accelerometer XYZ, temperature, gyroscope XYZ) using i2cReadI2CBlockData, parse the big-endian int16 values, and print them to stdout. Handle I2C read/write errors and sensor-absent conditions without terminating the loop unexpectedly. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by closing the I2C handle and calling gpioTerminate() before exiting, and print a brief startup message when the program begins along with a clean-shutdown message when it terminates.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to periodically read temperature and humidity from an Adafruit SHT40 I2C sensor connected to I2C bus 1 at address 0x44, logging readings to the console every 5 seconds. To trigger a high-repeatability measurement, send command 0xFD, wait at least 10 ms, then read 6 bytes: 2 bytes temperature, 1 CRC byte, 2 bytes humidity, 1 CRC byte. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for a graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and terminating pigpio on exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the Linux I2C character device interface via /dev/i2c-1 to read ambient and object temperatures from a Melexis MLX90614ESF-BAA infrared temperature sensor at its default address 0x5A, for a contactless food safety monitoring system. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to periodically sample temperature from a Sensirion STS30-DIS sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x4A. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Sensirion SDP810-125Pa differential pressure sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25, simulating a simple ventilation system monitoring application. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including handling SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses standard Linux I2C ioctls on /dev/i2c-1 to interface with a Sensirion SHT40 humidity and temperature sensor on I2C bus 1 (SDA on GPIO2, SCL on GPIO3) at the 7-bit address 0x44, simulating a smart greenhouse environment monitor. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (gpioInitialise/gpioTerminate, i2cOpen/i2cClose, i2cWriteDevice/i2cReadDevice) to periodically read differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP31 (±500 Pa) sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x28. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to read temperature and humidity from a Silicon Labs Si7015 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x40. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Si7021 humidity and temperature sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x40, and control a cooling fan on GPIO18 (active-high). Handle SIGINT cleanly: turn off the fan, close the I2C handle, and call gpioTerminate() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Sensirion SCD40 CO2 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x62 (standard 100 kHz clock-stretching compatible settings), for monitoring indoor air quality in a smart ventilation system. Check every return value from pigpio initialisation, I2C open, and command send; if any step or the CRC check fails, print a descriptive stderr message and retry or exit appropriately. Convert the reading to degrees Celsius using Temperature = 4215 - (2143 * TH / TL). Log each valid reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to 'temperature_log.txt' in append mode, sampling once every 5 seconds. Check pigpio initialisation and file open results; detect sensor-absent or stuck-line conditions via a 50 ms timeout on each edge wait; guard against division by zero if TL is zero; flag readings outside the valid range -40 to +150 °C as errors; and after 3 consecutive failures, log a 'SENSOR MALFUNCTION' entry to the log file. Log data in ISO-8601 UTC format to 'environmental_data.txt' every 5 seconds. Implement robust error handling for pigpio initialisation, I2C open/read/write, and file open. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and terminating pigpio cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the standard Linux I2C i2c-dev interface to interface with a Sensirion SDP810-125Pa differential pressure sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x25. Log the timestamp, pressure, and temperature to a CSV file named 'airflow.csv' every 1 second. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (open(), ioctl(), read(), write()) to periodically read temperature and humidity from an Adafruit Si7021 sensor at I2C address 0x40 on bus 1 (GPIO 2/3), simulating a greenhouse monitoring system. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP810-500Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25, for a simplified HVAC airflow monitoring system. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to read differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25, for a DIY ventilation system. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to read differential pressure from a Honeywell Zephyr HAF Series HAFBLF0100A2AX5 digital airflow sensor over I2C bus 1 at 7-bit address 0x28, and drives a PWM fan on GPIO18 (a hardware-PWM-capable pin) at 25 kHz based on the computed flow rate. Implement robust error handling for I2C communication failures, logging errors to stderr without crashing. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read pressure and temperature from an STMicroelectronics LPS33HW sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x5D. On startup, read the WHO_AM_I register (0x0F) and abort if it does not equal 0xB1. Configure CTRL_REG1 (0x10) to 0xB0 for block data update, 10 Hz output rate, and active mode. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to read an STLM75 digital temperature sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x48, reading temperature register 0x00 once per second. The STLM75 returns a 16-bit two's-complement word with 9-bit resolution (sign bit, 8 data bits, and the low 7 bits always 0); because pigpio's i2cReadWordData returns bytes in little-endian order, swap the two bytes before extracting the value, then right-shift by 7 and divide by 2 to get degrees Celsius. Store each reading in a 10-element circular buffer in memory and compute the running average. Turn on an LED on GPIO 17 when the average temperature exceeds 28.0 °C and turn it off otherwise. Install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM so the program shuts down cleanly, turning off the LED, closing the I2C handle, and calling gpioTerminate() before exiting.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (gpioInitialise, i2cOpen, i2cClose, i2cReadDevice, i2cWriteDevice, gpioTerminate) to interface with a Sensirion SCD30 CO2 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x61. Set the measurement interval to 2 seconds and start continuous measurement with ambient pressure compensation disabled (0). Before each read, poll the data-ready flag with command 0x0202, then read the measurement with command 0x0300, returning 18 bytes (3 values of 4 data bytes plus 2 CRC bytes each). Implement the SCD30 CRC-8 checksum (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF) for every write command that carries arguments and verify the CRC on every value read. Log CO2 (ppm), temperature (°C), and humidity (%RH) with ISO 8601 UTC timestamps as comma-separated values to air_quality.log, flushing after each write, and drive a simulated ventilation system from the CO2 reading: OFF below 800 ppm, LOW between 800 and 1199 ppm, and HIGH at 1200 ppm or above. Handle every error path — pigpio initialization failure, I2C open/write/read failures, sensor non-response, data-not-ready, and CRC mismatches — by logging the error and continuing the loop rather than crashing. In a mocked or emulated environment where the I2C hardware may be absent, initialize pigpio and open the I2C bus, and if sensor initialization or reads fail, log the error and exit gracefully with code 0 rather than crashing or returning a nonzero status.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to periodically read differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP32 (±125 Pa) sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x21. Send the continuous-measurement command bytes 0x36, 0x2F to start the sensor, then poll 9 bytes per reading: pressure MSB, pressure LSB, pressure CRC, temperature MSB, temperature LSB, temperature CRC, scale-factor MSB, scale-factor LSB, and scale-factor CRC. Verify the CRC-8 checksum on the pressure, temperature, and scale-factor words, and convert the raw pressure using pressure_pa = raw_pressure / scale_factor. Implement robust error handling for I2C communication failures, including sensor-absent and bus-error paths; if the sensor is not physically connected, detect the I2C read/write failures and exit with a clear diagnostic message rather than crashing. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths through signal handling, and make sure the program compiles and runs cleanly in a mocked or emulated environment, exiting with code 0 when terminated by SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to periodically read differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP810-125Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 (SDA on GPIO 2, SCL on GPIO 3) at address 0x25. Validate the CRC-8 (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF) on each 3-byte data word, then convert the raw values using the per-reading scale factors returned by the sensor: raw_pressure / scale_factor_pressure for pressure, and raw_temperature / 200.0 for temperature. Log the results to stdout every 1 second. Check pigpio initialization, the I2C bus open, and every read and write, and handle CRC mismatches and sensor-absent or bus-error paths without crashing. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and calling gpioTerminate() on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running a 64-bit kernel to periodically read temperature and humidity from a Texas Instruments HDC1000 sensor on I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1, GPIO 2 = SDA, GPIO 3 = SCL) at its default 7-bit address 0x40, using the Linux i2c-dev API (open(), ioctl(), read(), write()) rather than the deprecated wiringPi library. Configure the Configuration Register (pointer 0x02), setting bit 12 to enable a combined temperature-and-humidity measurement at 14-bit resolution. To read a sample, write the temperature register pointer 0x00 to the sensor, wait at least 20 ms for the 14-bit conversion (the DRDYn pin is not connected, so rely on this fixed delay), then read 4 bytes — 2 bytes temperature followed by 2 bytes humidity — in a single I2C read transaction. Convert the raw 16-bit values using Temperature (°C) = (raw / 65536.0) * 165.0 - 40.0 and Humidity (%RH) = (raw / 65536.0) * 100.0. Check the return value of every open(), ioctl(), read(), and write() call, and handle the sensor-absent path where the device file cannot be opened or the sensor fails to acknowledge. Log readings to the console every 5 seconds in the format "Temperature: XX.XX C, Humidity: XX.XX %"; on a read failure, print an error to stderr and continue the loop without exiting. Install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM so the program closes the I2C file descriptor and exits cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to periodically read temperature from a Silicon Labs Si7051 sensor over I2C bus 1 (GPIO 2/3 for SDA/SCL) at its default 7-bit address 0x40. Log the temperature in degrees Celsius to the console every 5 seconds. Implement robust error handling for I2C communication failures, including sensor-absent conditions, bus errors, and read/write timeouts, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to periodically read pressure values from a Melexis MLX90833 absolute pressure sensor connected over I2C bus 1 at its manufacturer-default 7-bit address 0x60. Log each reading to the console every 500 ms with a timestamp. Check all pigpio initialization and I2C read/write operations, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to periodically read pressure and temperature from a TDK ICP-10101 barometric pressure sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x63. On startup, read the 4 calibration coefficients from the sensor's OTP memory with command 0x50 (8 bytes) and compute the scale_factor_lut, scale_factor_h, and scale_factor_p scaling factors per the datasheet. Every 5 seconds, trigger a high-precision measurement with command 0x40, wait 7 ms, then read 6 bytes — 2 bytes temperature followed by 4 bytes pressure — and apply the datasheet compensation formulas to convert the raw values to Celsius and Pascals. Log each reading to stdout with an ISO-8601 timestamp, for example "2024-01-15T14:30:00 - Temperature: 22.45 C, Pressure: 101325.00 Pa". Check the return value of every pigpio I2C call, detect a sensor-absent condition when a read returns a negative value or all bytes are 0xFF, and log such errors to stderr without crashing. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and calling gpioTerminate() on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the Linux i2c-dev interface (open() and ioctl() on /dev/i2c-1) to periodically read pressure values from a Melexis MLX90819 (digital I2C version) sensor on I2C bus 1 at 7-bit address 0x60. Trigger a measurement and read the 16-bit raw pressure value from the sensor's pressure registers, MSB at 0xAA and LSB at 0xAB, once per second. Convert the raw value to kPa using a linear scaling factor of 0.1. Log each reading to stdout with a timestamp. Handle I2C communication failures, including read/write errors and a sensor-absent condition, by printing to stderr and continuing. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so the program exits cleanly on Ctrl+C, closing the I2C file descriptor.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (open() and ioctl()) rather than the deprecated wiringPi library to interface with a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa differential pressure sensor connected on I2C bus 1, with SDA on GPIO 2 and SCL on GPIO 3, at address 0x25, for a do-it-yourself HVAC airflow monitoring system. Validate each word's CRC-8 (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF), then convert the raw values using pressure = raw / 60.0 (Pa) and temperature = raw / 200.0 (C). Log the timestamp, differential pressure, and temperature as comma-separated values to pressure_log.txt. Handle I2C open/write/read errors and sensor-absent paths gracefully, and release all resources cleanly on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to read differential pressure data from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25. Use the continuous-measurement command bytes 0x36, 0x2F to trigger readings, wait at least 8 ms for the measurement to complete, then read 3 bytes: 2 data bytes plus 1 CRC byte. Verify the CRC-8 checksum (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF) of the data bytes, and convert the raw 16-bit signed value to pressure in Pa using raw / 60.0. Check every pigpio I2C call, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully. Log the pressure reading and a timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS) once per second as comma-separated values to a CSV file named airflow_log.csv, writing a header row if the file is newly created. Include the necessary POSIX headers, such as unistd.h for access()/F_OK, so the code compiles cleanly with gcc -Wall -Wextra. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown on SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (i2cOpen, i2cReadI2CBlockData, i2cClose) to interface with a Melexis MLX90821 relative pressure sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x40, simulating a tire pressure monitoring system. Read the 16-bit big-endian pressure output register (0x00) every 1 second, convert the raw unsigned value to kPa using a scale factor of 0.01, and flag a warning to stderr whenever the pressure falls outside the safe tire range of 200-250 kPa. Log each reading with a UTC timestamp to a CSV file named pressure_log.csv with the header row "timestamp,pressure_kPa", writing the header only if the file is newly created (size 0). Check pigpio initialization, the I2C bus open, every I2C read, and the file open; on an I2C read failure, close and reopen the I2C handle and retry once before continuing. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to cleanly close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and call gpioTerminate() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to read temperature and humidity from a Honeywell HIH6130 I2C sensor at address 0x27 on I2C bus 1. Follow the HIH6130 measurement protocol: write 0x00 to trigger a measurement, wait about 40 ms, then read 4 bytes, validating the sensor's status bits. Convert the raw values using temperature = raw_T * 165.0/16383.0 - 40.0 and humidity = raw_H * 100.0/16383.0. Do not manipulate any GPIO pins for pull-up control; rely on the bus pull-ups. Sample every 5 seconds and log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to a rolling file environmental_data.log, truncating it when it exceeds 1 MB. Check every I2C return code and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths robustly. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library for GPIO timing to read pressure data from a Melexis MLX90824 SENT pressure sensor connected to GPIO 4 (BCM), for an automotive brake pressure monitoring system. Implement the SENT protocol with a tick time of 3 us: a synchronization pulse of 56 ticks, followed by a status nibble, 3 data nibbles, and a checksum nibble, where a valid nibble pulse width is 12 to 271 ticks (36-813 us). Validate the checksum as the sum of the nibbles modulo 16, and convert the 12-bit raw value to pressure using the linear transfer function raw * scale + offset. Detect sensor-absent (timeout) and bus-error (checksum or pulse-width) conditions, logging errors to stderr without crashing. Log each pressure reading with a timestamp to pressure_log.txt in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Pressure: XXXX.XX Pa". Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean resource release.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to monitor a greenhouse with an Adafruit TMP117 High Precision Temperature Sensor over I2C bus 1 at the default address 0x48. On startup, verify the sensor's device ID register reads 0x0117. Read the temperature register 0x00 (2 bytes, signed, LSB = 0.0078125 °C) every 60 seconds and append each reading as a 4-byte little-endian float to a binary file named greenhouse_temps.dat. Handle I2C communication failures gracefully without crashing, and ensure clean resource release — the I2C handle, the file stream, and the pigpio library — on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to read temperature and humidity from an Adafruit SHT40 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x44, simulating a smart greenhouse environment monitor. Issue the high-precision measurement command 0xFD, wait at least 8.5 ms for the conversion, then read 6 bytes: 2 bytes temperature, 1 CRC byte, 2 bytes humidity, 1 CRC byte. Validate both CRC-8 checksums (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF), then convert the raw values using Temperature = -45 + 175 * (raw_temp / 65535.0) °C and Humidity = -6 + 125 * (raw_hum / 65535.0) %RH. Log each reading with a timestamp to environmental_data.txt in append mode, flushing after each write. Check pigpio initialization, the I2C bus open, the I2C write, the I2C read, and CRC validation, and handle file-operation errors as well. Handle SIGINT gracefully by closing the I2C handle, terminating pigpio, and closing the log file. Read the sensor every 5 seconds indefinitely.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to periodically sample temperature from a Texas Instruments TMP117 high-accuracy sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x48. Read the 2-byte big-endian temperature register 0x00 every 5 seconds and convert it using the 0.0078125 °C LSB resolution. Store readings in a rolling circular buffer in memory and persist the entire buffer to a binary file named temperature_log.dat on every sample and on exit. Check that pigpio initialization and I2C handle creation succeed. If a read fails, log the error, skip that sample, and continue running rather than crashing. Implement graceful shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM that flushes the buffer to the file and releases all resources — the I2C handle and pigpio — on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses pigpio to read temperature and humidity from a Sensirion SHTC3 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x70, for an indoor air quality monitoring system. The SHTC3 operates at 1.8 V but tolerates 3.3 V on SDA/SCL; wire VDD to 3.3 V (Pin 1), VSS to GND (Pin 2), SDA to GPIO 2 (Pin 3), and SCL to GPIO 3 (Pin 4). Validate each pair with CRC-8 (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF), then convert using T = 175 * raw / 65535 - 45 and RH = 100 * raw / 65535, rejecting readings outside -40 to 125 °C or 0 to 100 %RH. Log valid readings every 5 seconds to shtc3_environment.log in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,Temperature(C),Humidity(%)" with two decimal places, printing valid readings to stdout and errors to stderr. Handle I2C write/read errors, CRC failures, out-of-range values, and file-open errors gracefully without crashing. On SIGINT, close the I2C handle, call gpioTerminate(), and exit cleanly.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Silicon Labs Si7202 I2C Hall-effect sensor at address 0x40 on I2C bus 1, for a precise rotational speed measurement system. Every 1 second, read the sensor and convert the raw values using field_gauss = raw_value * 0.1 and temp_celsius = raw_value * 0.01 - 25.0, then log the magnetic field (Gauss) and temperature (Celsius) as comma-separated values to mag_temp_log.csv, writing a header row if the file is newly created. Handle errors from I2C initialization, sensor communication, and file I/O; if a sensor read fails, log an entry with NaN values and continue running. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) gracefully by closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and terminating pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library for I2C communication (do NOT use wiringPi) to continuously read temperature from a Texas Instruments TMP117 high-accuracy sensor at its default address 0x48 on I2C bus 1. Check the return value of every I2C call, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and reinitialize the I2C handle up to 3 times on consecutive failures before exiting. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and terminating pigpio cleanly on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to read airflow data from a Honeywell HAF Series HAFUHH0025PA3 flow sensor over I2C bus 1 at its 7-bit address 0x49, for real-time ventilation system monitoring. Sample every 1 second and log the timestamped flow rate (SLPM) and temperature (°C) to flow_log.txt. Handle the first two reads after power-up gracefully, since the datasheet notes they may return stale data. If a read fails, log the error to the file and attempt to re-initialize the I2C handle. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths: handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to close the I2C handle, close the log file, and terminate pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses pigpio (gpioTick for microsecond timing, gpioRead, gpioWrite, gpioSetMode) to bit-bang the single-wire protocol of a DHT11 temperature/humidity sensor connected to GPIO 4 (physical pin 7, BCM numbering). Pull the line low for at least 18 ms, release it, then read the sensor's 80 us low plus 80 us high response followed by 40 data bits; each bit begins with a 50 us low pulse, and the following high-pulse duration determines its value (about 26-28 us for a '0', about 70 us for a '1'). Validate the 8-bit checksum (the sum of the first 4 bytes modulo 256 must equal the 5th byte); DHT11 readings are integer-only, with humidity in byte 0 and temperature in byte 2, while bytes 1 and 3 (the decimal parts) are always 0. Sample every 2 seconds. Detect and handle timeouts on every phase — the start signal, the sensor's response, and the data bits — plus checksum failures and sensor-absent conditions where the line is stuck high or low, logging all errors with timestamps and status codes to a file. Log temperature and humidity with ISO-8601 timestamped entries to dht11_readings.txt. On SIGINT/SIGTERM, release the GPIO resources, call gpioTerminate(), and close any open file handles before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (do NOT use wiringPi) to read temperature and humidity from an Adafruit SHT31-D sensor over I2C bus 1 (GPIO 2 = SDA, GPIO 3 = SCL) at its default address 0x44, for an automated greenhouse environment. Validate each CRC-8 (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF), then convert the raw values using temperature = -45 + 175 * raw / 65535 and humidity = 100 * raw / 65535. Log readings every 5 seconds to sht31d_data.log with ISO-8601 timestamps in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,temperature,humidity". Check pigpio initialization, the I2C bus open, the file open, the I2C write, the I2C read, and CRC validation, retrying a failed I2C transaction up to 3 times; on persistent sensor failure, log the error with a timestamp and continue running. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, and terminating pigpio.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (i2cWriteI2CBlockData/i2cReadI2CBlockData or similar block reads) to interface with two Analog Devices ADPD105 photometric front-end sensors on I2C bus 1, at addresses 0x64 and 0x65 (the default 7-bit address is 0x64; the second sensor uses an alternate address pin). On each sensor, verify the device ID register at 0x00 reads 0x2A, then read the 16-bit little-endian red, green, and blue channel data registers at 0x64, 0x66, and 0x68. Compute the Correlated Color Temperature (CCT) for each sensor using McCamy's formula, and log the average of the two CCT values every 1 second to a CSV file named cct_log.csv, writing the header "Timestamp,Average_CCT" if the file is newly created. Check every I2C read and write operation, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths by logging the error to stderr and skipping the log entry for that cycle. Ensure clean resource release — the I2C handles, file streams, and pigpio termination — on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to interface with a Melexis MLX90824 absolute pressure sensor over I2C bus 1 at 7-bit address 0x60, simulating a tire pressure monitoring system. Every 2 seconds, read the RAW pressure register at 0x0A2C (2 bytes, big-endian) and the RAW temperature register at 0x0A2E (2 bytes, big-endian), and log the results with an ISO-8601 timestamp to pressure_log.txt. Convert raw pressure to kPa using pressure_kPa = (raw - output_min) * (pmax_kPa - pmin_kPa) / (output_max - output_min), with output_min=0, output_max=32768, pmin=0 kPa, pmax=800 kPa; convert raw temperature using temp_C = raw * 0.01 - 40. Check every pigpio and I2C call; if a read fails, log the error with a timestamp rather than skipping silently, and continue running. Run the program indefinitely until interrupted, performing clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT and SIGTERM: close the I2C handle, close the log file, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library for both I2C and GPIO (not wiringPi) to interface with an STMicroelectronics LM75B temperature sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x48. Every 1 second, read the 2-byte temperature register 0x00 and convert it using the LM75B's signed 9-bit format (0.5 °C resolution, using bits D9-D1, with D0 always 0). Store each reading in a 60-element circular buffer in memory and compute the running average. Control a cooling fan on GPIO 18 (BCM numbering) with hysteresis: turn it on when the running average exceeds 28.0 °C and off when it falls below 26.0 °C. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown: stop the fan, close the I2C handle, and terminate pigpio cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (do NOT use wiringPi) to read differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP810-500Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25, simulating a basic HVAC airflow monitoring system. Send the continuous-measurement command 0x362F, wait 45 ms for the first measurement, then read 9 bytes containing 3 words — pressure, temperature, and status — each followed by a CRC8 byte. Validate every CRC using the Sensirion CRC-8 polynomial 0x31 (initial value 0xFF), then convert the raw pressure (int16) using scale factor 60 and the raw temperature (int16) using scale factor 200. Log the timestamp, differential pressure (Pa), and temperature (°C) to airflow.log in CSV format once per second, and print a warning to stderr whenever the pressure exceeds 5.0 Pa. Handle I2C read/write failures, CRC mismatches, and sensor-absent conditions robustly. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean shutdown: close the I2C handle, close the log file, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads an STTS2004 temperature sensor over I2C (default slave address 0x4A) using the Linux i2c-dev interface, and drives an LED on GPIO 17 (BCM numbering) using the libgpiod C API (no wiringPi for either). Read the 16-bit temperature value from register 0x00, combine the MSB and LSB, right-shift the result by 4 bits, and convert to Celsius using 0.0625 °C/LSB. Log the temperature to stdout once per second. Drive the LED high when the temperature exceeds 28 °C and low when it falls below 27 °C, implementing this hysteresis band. Check every I2C read and every libgpiod GPIO operation; on repeated I2C failures, log the errno details and exit cleanly. Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM to release all libgpiod resources (lines and chips), close the I2C file descriptor, and turn the LED off before exiting.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library for I2C communication to read differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25. Send the continuous-measurement command 0x362F, wait at least 45 ms, then read 9 bytes: 2 bytes differential pressure plus 1 CRC byte, 2 bytes temperature plus 1 CRC byte, and 3 bytes of scale-factor data. Validate CRC-8 (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF) for the pressure and temperature readings. Convert the raw differential pressure by dividing by the scale factor, taken as a signed integer from the last 16 bits of the read data, and convert the raw temperature by dividing by 200. Log each reading with a timestamp to flow_data.txt. Handle I2C communication errors and sensor-absent scenarios gracefully. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths using SIGINT signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to read temperature and humidity from an Adafruit Si7021 sensor over I2C bus 1 (GPIO 2/3 for SDA/SCL) at address 0x40. Use i2cReadDevice/i2cWriteDevice for raw byte transfers, since the Si7021 protocol uses single-byte commands followed by 2-byte reads rather than register-addressed access: issue 'Measure Relative Humidity, No Master Hold' (0xF5) and 'Measure Temperature, No Master Hold' (0xF3), or read temperature from the previous RH measurement via command 0xE0, waiting at least 20 ms after a no-hold command before reading the result. At startup, validate the sensor is present by reading its electronic ID or firmware revision; if absent, log an error and exit with a non-zero status. Sample every 60 seconds and log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp, in CSV format timestamp,temperature_c,humidity_pct, to environment.log (flushing after every write) and to stdout. Log errors with timestamps to both the log file and stderr. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean shutdown, closing the I2C handle and calling gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read temperature and humidity from a TI HDC1080 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x40, initializing pigpio and opening the I2C bus with error checking. Configure the HDC1080's configuration register (0x02) for 14-bit temperature and 14-bit humidity resolution. Read both values in a single measurement by writing the pointer to register 0x00, waiting at least 20 ms for conversion, then reading 4 bytes: 2 bytes temperature followed by 2 bytes humidity. Convert the raw values using temperature = (raw_temp / 65536.0) * 165.0 - 40.0 and humidity = (raw_humidity / 65536.0) * 100.0. Every 5 seconds, log a valid reading with a timestamp to enviro_log.txt in the format "timestamp,temperature_C,humidity_percent". Handle I2C communication failures and sensor-absent scenarios gracefully, skipping the log entry on error. Run in an infinite loop until interrupted, implementing clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM: close the I2C handle and terminate pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the Linux I2C ioctl interface (no wiringPi) to read temperature from a Sensirion STS40 sensor at address 0x44 on /dev/i2c-1, for a simulated greenhouse environment monitor. Open the I2C adapter with open() and set the slave address via ioctl(I2C_SLAVE). Send the single-shot high-repeatability measurement command bytes 0x2C, 0xE0 with a combined write() call, wait 10 ms for conversion, then read 3 bytes (2 data bytes plus 1 CRC8 byte) with read(). Validate the CRC8 using the Sensirion polynomial 0x31, then convert the raw ticks to Celsius using T = -45 + 175 * raw / 65535.0. Log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to temperature_log.txt every 5 seconds in an infinite loop. Handle every error path — open, ioctl, write, read, CRC mismatch, and file open — with a descriptive stderr message and continue looping rather than exiting. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler for clean shutdown that closes the file descriptor and the log file.

Develop a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (NOT wiringPi) to monitor air duct pressure in a simulated HVAC system, reading a Sensirion SDP810-500Pa differential pressure sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25. Send the continuous-measurement command 0x3615, wait at least 50 ms, then read 9 bytes: 2 bytes pressure plus 1 CRC, 2 bytes temperature plus 1 CRC, and 3 bytes of scale factor. Validate every I2C read/write and each CRC-8 (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF), then convert raw pressure using pressure/scale_factor and raw temperature using temperature/200.0. Check every initialization call (gpioInitialise, i2cOpen, fopen) and exit with an error message if any fails. Sample once per second, logging valid readings as comma-separated values — timestamp, pressure_Pa, temperature_C — to hvac_pressure_log.txt; on an I2C or CRC error, log an error line with the timestamp and continue. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) gracefully: close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Sensirion SCD40 CO2 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x62. Initialize pigpio and open the I2C bus with error checking. Send the start-periodic-measurement command 0x21B1 and wait at least 1 second before reading. Every 5 seconds in the main loop, read CO2, temperature, and humidity with command 0xE000, which returns 9 bytes as three 2-byte-plus-CRC values; validate the CRC-8 (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF) for each, and if a CRC check or I2C transaction fails, log the error and skip that reading. Convert the values with CO2 in ppm, temperature = -45 + 175 * raw / 65535, and humidity = 100 * raw / 65535. Store each valid reading (timestamp, CO2, temperature, humidity) in a thread-safe circular buffer of capacity 100. Spawn a separate thread that every 60 seconds writes the entire buffer to a timestamped CSV file, with a header row, in /var/log/scd40_data/ (creating the directory if needed). Use a volatile sig_atomic_t running flag and handle SIGINT gracefully: stop the main loop, send the stop-periodic-measurement command 0x3F86, join the logging thread, flush any remaining buffer data to a final CSV file, close the I2C handle, and terminate pigpio. Log all errors with timestamps to /var/log/scd40_error.log, ensuring no resource leaks on any exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (NOT wiringPi) to read differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP810-500Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25, for a basic HVAC airflow monitoring application. Send the continuous-measurement command 0x362F (mass flow, no clock stretching), wait at least 45 ms, then read 9 bytes: 2 bytes differential pressure plus CRC, 2 bytes temperature plus CRC, and 2 bytes scale factor plus CRC. Validate each CRC-8 (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF), then convert using pressure_Pa = raw_pressure * scale_factor / 1000 and T = -45 + 175 * raw_temp / 65535. Log each reading with a timestamp to sdp810_log.txt in CSV format (timestamp, pressure_Pa, temperature_C) once per second. Handle I2C open/write/read errors and CRC failures gracefully by logging the error and continuing. On SIGINT, close the I2C handle, terminate pigpio, close the log file, and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with a TDK ICP-10110 pressure sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x63, for a simulated weather station. Initialize pigpio and open the I2C bus with error checking. Verify the sensor identity by reading the WHO_AM_I register at 0x08 and checking for the value 0x08, then read the 4 calibration coefficients from registers 0x05-0x08 using i2cReadI2CBlockData. In a loop, trigger a measurement by writing 0x00 to register 0x00, wait 10 ms, then read 6 bytes of pressure and temperature data from register 0x00, converting them to hPa and Celsius using the ICP-10110 datasheet formulas. Sample every 5 seconds, logging each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to environmental_data.txt in append mode (flushing after each write) and printing it to stdout. Handle I2C read/write errors by printing to stderr and skipping the sample. Handle SIGINT gracefully: set a flag to exit the loop, close the I2C handle, close the file, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads a TDK ICP-10125 barometric pressure sensor over I2C using the standard Linux I2C interface (open(), ioctl(), read(), write() on <linux/i2c-dev.h>) at the sensor's default address 0x63, and drives a warning LED using the libgpiod API, without using wiringPi. Read the 4 calibration coefficients from OTP memory register 0x66, then trigger a measurement by writing command 0x4011 (high-accuracy mode). After a 20 ms delay, read 6 bytes — 2 bytes pressure, 2 bytes temperature, and 2 bytes CRC — verifying the CRC, and apply the official InvenSense ICP-10125 conversion formulas to compute pressure in Pascals and temperature in Celsius. Poll the sensor once per second. Using libgpiod, request an LED line on GPIO 17 (BCM numbering) as output and blink it at 1 Hz (500 ms on, 500 ms off) under normal conditions; when the pressure drops below 95000 Pa, indicating high altitude, blink it at 5 Hz (100 ms on, 100 ms off) as a warning. Check every I2C syscall, handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths, and verify the CRC on every read. Handle SIGINT to release the GPIO line and close the I2C file descriptor cleanly on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library for both I2C and GPIO to read ambient and object temperatures from a Melexis MLX90614ESF-BAA infrared temperature sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x5A. Read ambient temperature from RAM register 0x06 and object temperature from RAM register 0x07, converting each raw 16-bit value to Celsius using temp = raw * 0.02 - 273.15. Every 2 seconds, log the timestamped readings to temperature_log.txt, skipping the log entry if a reading is invalid. Control a cooling fan on GPIO 18 with hysteresis: turn it on when the object temperature exceeds 30 °C and off when it falls below 28 °C. Validate pigpio initialization, the I2C bus open, and every I2C read/write; retry a failed read up to 3 times with a 10 ms delay between attempts. Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM cleanly by closing the I2C handle, turning off the fan, and terminating pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to stream live temperature and humidity data from a Sensirion SHT40 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x44 to a local HTTP web server listening on port 8080. To read the sensor, send measurement command 0xFD (high repeatability, clock stretching enabled), wait at least 10 ms, then read 6 bytes and convert the raw data using T = -45 + 175 * (raw_T / 65535) and RH = -6 + 125 * (raw_RH / 65535), clamping humidity to 0-100%. Accept incoming HTTP connections and respond with a simple HTML page showing the current temperature and humidity. Implement robust error handling for I2C communication, including sensor-absent and bus-error cases, with up to 3 retries, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT and SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read temperature from a Texas Instruments TMP102 I2C sensor at address 0x48 on I2C bus 1, simulating a smart greenhouse climate monitoring system. Every 5 seconds, read the 12-bit two's-complement value, left-justified in two bytes, from register 0x00, shift it right by 4 bits, and multiply by 0.0625 to get degrees Celsius. Log each reading to a timestamped CSV file named temperature_log.csv in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,XX.XX'. If a read fails, log the error to stderr and skip the CSV entry. Check all initialization and I/O calls, and include standard headers such as errno.h and stdint.h so the code compiles without warnings. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) cleanly by closing the I2C handle, terminating pigpio, and exiting gracefully.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to read temperature and humidity from a Texas Instruments HDC2010 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x40, logging the values to the console every 5 seconds. Before each reading, trigger a one-shot temperature and humidity measurement by writing 0x01 to the MEASUREMENT_CONFIG register (0x0E), keeping the CONFIG register (0x0F) set for heater disabled and 14-bit resolution. Poll MEASUREMENT_CONFIG until bit 0 clears, or time out after about 500 ms, before reading temperature from registers 0x00-0x01 and humidity from registers 0x02-0x03. Convert using temperature = raw/65536*165 - 40 and humidity = raw/65536*100. Check every pigpio call, detect sensor-absent (NAK) and bus-error paths, and enforce a maximum retry count for transient I2C failures. Handle Ctrl+C cleanly with a signal handler using a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, closing the I2C handle and calling gpioTerminate() for graceful shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to periodically read differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25. Use continuous measurement command 0x362F to trigger readings, then, after the measurement completes (about 45 ms), read 6 bytes: 2 bytes pressure plus 1 CRC byte, and 2 bytes temperature plus 1 CRC byte. Log the raw 16-bit pressure and temperature values to the console every 500 ms. Check pigpio initialization, I2C open, and every write/read call, and verify the CRC-8 checksums for both data words using polynomial 0x31 with initial value 0xFF, handling sensor-absent and bus-error paths gracefully. Use SIGINT signal handling for clean shutdown, closing the I2C handle and calling gpioTerminate() on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a PID-controlled reflow oven using a MAX6675 thermocouple over SPI0 (CE0/CE1) and a solid-state relay on GPIO17, reading a target temperature profile from profile.txt (lines of time_seconds,target_temp_celsius). Use libgpiod for GPIO control and spidev for SPI communication. The MAX6675 returns a 16-bit word where bit 2 is the open-circuit flag and bits 3-14 hold the 12-bit temperature; read it at 1 Hz. The PID controller's output, from 0.0 to 1.0, sets the solid-state relay's duty cycle over each 1-second period. Log temperature data to reflow_log.csv. Implement robust error handling for SPI communication and GPIO control, including sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths through signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a PID-controlled greenhouse heater. Read temperature from a DS18B20 sensor on GPIO4 (physical pin 7) via the w1-gpio kernel module through sysfs at /sys/bus/w1/devices/, validating the CRC in each reading. Control a 12V heater using a relay on GPIO17 (physical pin 11) for enable/disable and a hardware PWM signal on GPIO18 (physical pin 12) for duty cycle modulation, using libgpiod for all GPIO control (not wiringPi). Accept command-line arguments for setpoint temperature and PID gains Kp, Ki, Kd. Every 5 seconds, log timestamp, average temperature, setpoint, PID output, and PWM duty cycle to greenhouse.log. Check all I/O operations and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths. Ensure clean resource release — turn off the relay, set PWM to 0, close the GPIO lines, close the chip, and close the log file — on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library to read humidity from an AHT20 sensor over I2C bus /dev/i2c-1 at address 0x38, activating a dehumidifier relay on GPIO 17 (active-high) when humidity exceeds 60% and turning it off when humidity falls below 55%. Perform the AHT20 initialization sequence (0xBE 0x08 0x00) once at startup, then in a loop send the measurement trigger command (0xAC 0x33 0x00), wait 80 ms, and read 6 bytes of data, verifying the status byte indicates the sensor is calibrated and not busy before reading. Retry failed I2C transactions up to 3 times with a 10 ms delay between retries, and poll every 5 seconds. Log each reading to the console with a timestamp. If the sensor is absent or I2C communication fails after all retries, print an error to stderr and continue the loop rather than crashing. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM cleanly by releasing the GPIO line, closing the I2C file descriptor, and exiting with code 0.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads relative humidity from an HTU21D sensor over I2C at address 0x40 on /dev/i2c-1 every 60 seconds, and POSTs the reading as JSON to http://api.example.com/humidity. Use the standard Linux I2C dev interface (linux/i2c-dev.h with open(), ioctl(), read(), write()) rather than the bcm2835 library. Implement robust error handling for I2C communication failures — NACKs, bus errors, CRC mismatches, sensor absence — and for HTTP failures. Implement the HTTP POST client using standard POSIX sockets rather than an external library such as libcurl, and use syslog for logging. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, closing all file descriptors cleanly.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to monitor a Bosch BMP280 pressure sensor over I2C-1 at address 0x76. Verify the chip ID equals 0x58 at register 0xD0 before proceeding, then read the 24-byte calibration block starting at 0x88 and apply the Bosch compensation formulas. Configure ctrl_meas (register 0xF4) for 1x oversampling on temperature and pressure in forced mode (0x27), triggering a measurement by writing the forced mode bits (0x01) each loop, and wait about 10 ms for conversion completion before reading 6 bytes of raw data from register 0xF7. Sample every 2 seconds and log timestamped pressure threshold breaches — above 1020 hPa or below 980 hPa — to pressure_log.txt. Handle I2C errors gracefully with up to 3 retry attempts that re-open the bus and re-verify the chip ID. Use signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to shut down cleanly, closing the I2C handle and calling gpioTerminate() on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4B that logs temperature from a TMP117 sensor (I2C address 0x48, temperature register 0x00, 16-bit signed big-endian, LSB = 0.0078125 °C), humidity from an AHT20 sensor (I2C address 0x38, init command 0xBE 0x08 0x00, measure command 0xAC 0x33 0x00, 7-byte response with busy bit in data[0] bit 7, 20-bit humidity and temperature raw values), and motion detection from a PIR sensor on GPIO 17, into daily timestamped CSV files. Use libgpiod for GPIO access (gpiochip4, line 17, input direction) and the standard Linux I2C interface (/dev/i2c-1) via ioctl for the sensors. Sample every 1 second, handle I2C errors with up to 3 retries and a 10 ms backoff, and check sensor presence at startup — print a warning but continue if a sensor is absent. Create a new log file each day at midnight with CSV header 'Timestamp,Temperature(C),Humidity(%),MotionDetected'. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling. Build with: gcc -o logger logger.c -lgpiod -lrt.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 using the libgpiod library, through the Linux GPIO character-device interface, to monitor a YL-83 rain sensor connected on GPIO17, reading it as an active-low digital output where a value of 0 means rain has been detected, polling the line every 2 seconds. When rain is detected, close a window by driving an L298N motor driver board, with its enable line ENA on GPIO22, its first direction input IN1 on GPIO23, and its second direction input IN2 on GPIO24, so that the motor runs forward for 5 seconds and then stops. Check the return value of every libgpiod call, and explicitly handle the case where the GPIO chip cannot be opened at startup. Ensure the motor is stopped and every requested GPIO line is released back to the system on program exit, whether that exit is triggered by SIGINT or SIGTERM signal handling, and log each event with a timestamp to stdout. Do not include any DHT22 or humidity-sensing code in this program — the scope is limited strictly to the rain sensor and the motor control it drives.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library, and not wiringPi, to modulate a common-anode RGB LED, whose Red, Green, and Blue cathodes are wired to GPIO 17, 22, and 27 respectively, so that its color visually represents the current CPU load. Use hardware PWM through pigpio to control the brightness of each channel, clamping every PWM value to the 0-255 range. Map CPU load, computed by reading /proc/stat and comparing successive samples, onto a color gradient: 0% load renders Green (0,255,0), 50% load renders Yellow (255,255,0), and 100% load renders Red (255,0,0), sampling and updating every 500 ms. Handle any pigpio initialization failure by printing an error message to stderr and exiting with status code 1. Install handlers for both SIGINT and SIGTERM that turn the LED fully off, which for a common-anode LED means driving all channels to full off, and then cleanly call gpioTerminate() before the process exits. Do not include any temperature-sensor code in this program; the scope here is CPU load alone.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to read temperature and pressure from a Bosch BMP280 sensor over I2C-1 (SDA=GPIO2/pin3, SCL=GPIO3/pin5) at address 0x76, sending the data as a JSON string over UDP to 192.168.1.100:5000 every 5 seconds. Verify the chip ID equals 0x58 at register 0xD0 before proceeding, read the 24-byte calibration block at 0x88-0xA1, and apply the Bosch 64-bit compensation formulas. Use forced mode (write to register 0xF4) for low power, waiting for the measurement to complete before reading 6 bytes from register 0xF7. Handle all I2C read/write errors, sensor-absent paths, and UDP send failures gracefully. Ensure clean resource release of the I2C handle, UDP socket, and pigpio library on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to dynamically control a PWM-driven cooling fan on GPIO18 (BCM) based on temperature readings from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier over SPI0 (CE0, GPIO8). Initialize pigpio and open SPI channel 0 at 500 kHz, mode 0. Every 1 second, read the 32-bit MAX31855 register, extracting the signed 14-bit thermocouple temperature at 0.25°C resolution and checking the fault bit (bit 16) plus fault type bits OC (bit 0), SCG (bit 1), and SCV (bit 2). Drive the fan via hardware PWM on GPIO18 at 1 kHz with a 0-255 duty range, using a piecewise curve: 0% below 25°C, a linear ramp of 0-50 between 25-40°C, a steeper ramp of 50-200 between 40-60°C, and 100% above 60°C. Log each valid reading — timestamp, temperature, PWM duty cycle — into a 20-entry circular buffer. On SPI transfer errors or MAX31855 faults, print a diagnostic message to stderr and skip the fan update for that cycle. Handle SIGINT gracefully: stop PWM, close SPI, print the full buffer contents, and terminate pigpio before exiting. Check every pigpio call, including gpioInitialise, spiOpen, spiXfer, and gpioPWM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library. Configure GPIO2 as a falling-edge triggered interrupt, with the internal pull-up enabled, to toggle data logging on and off from a BMP180 sensor connected over I2C bus 1 at address 0x77. Use oversampling setting OSS=3 for pressure. Log timestamped pressure (Pa) and temperature (Celsius) readings to altitude_log.txt in CSV format (timestamp,temperature,pressure), polling the main loop at 1-second intervals. Handle I2C read and write errors at every step and verify the calibration data reads. Ensure graceful exit on SIGINT by closing the I2C handle, closing the file, and releasing the GPIO.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads temperature from a MAX31865 RTD-to-digital converter over SPI0 (CE0, GPIO8, 1 MHz) and logs readings with timestamps to rtd_log.csv, every 5 seconds. Use the libgpiod library for chip-select line management and the standard Linux spidev interface for SPI communication (do not use wiringPi).
