Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library for both I2C communication and SPI output to control an APA102 RGB LED strip's overall brightness based on ambient light from up to three BH1750 I2C light sensors on I2C bus 1, at addresses 0x23 (ADDR low) and 0x5C (ADDR high); attempt to open both addresses and gracefully skip any sensor that is not present. The APA102 strip connects via hardware SPI: MOSI on GPIO10 and SCLK on GPIO11. Initialize each BH1750 using the One-Time High-Resolution Mode 2 command (0x21), wait approximately 180 ms for the conversion to complete, and read 2 bytes of data. Average the lux readings across available sensors, ignoring any that report read errors, and map the average lux to a global brightness level (0-31) for the strip, where lower ambient light yields higher brightness. Smoothly fade the strip's global brightness to the new target over 500 ms, looping continuously with a 100 ms delay between cycles. Check all pigpio initialization and I2C/SPI calls for errors, and handle sensor-absent and I2C bus-error paths gracefully. Use a SIGINT signal handler for clean resource release: turn off the LED strip, close all I2C handles, close the SPI handle, and terminate pigpio on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library for GPIO and the standard Linux i2c-dev interface for I2C (not wiringPi or any deprecated library) to control the brightness of a WS2812B LED strip based on readings from a VEML7700 ambient light sensor at I2C address 0x10. Initialize the VEML7700 with configuration register 0x00 set to 0x0000 (integration time 100 ms, gain 1/8) and read the ALS data from register 0x04 (16-bit). Convert the raw value to lux using lux = raw * 0.0036 * (1/gain) * (100ms/integration_time), which for the default settings reduces to lux = raw * 0.0288. Map the lux value (range 0 to 120000) to LED brightness (0-255) using gamma correction: brightness = 255 * pow(lux / 120000.0, 1.0/2.2). Drive the WS2812B strip via a single GPIO18 pin, bit-banging with libgpiod: toggle the pin at a high frequency such as 800 kHz with duty cycle proportional to brightness, or fall back to threshold-based on/off control if bit-banging is not feasible. Gracefully handle I2C errors, such as sensor absence or bus errors, by retrying up to 3 times with a 100 ms delay between retries, then logging an error and continuing. Use signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to cleanly release GPIO lines, close I2C file descriptors, and turn off the LED strip. Run in an infinite loop with a 200 ms delay between iterations, printing the current lux and brightness values to stdout.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library (gpiod_line_* functions; no sysfs, no wiringPi, no pigpio) to interface with a KY-026 flame sensor (digital output, active-low) on GPIO4. Upon flame detection (sensor output LOW), activate a buzzer on GPIO17 and an LED on GPIO18. On startup, run a self-test: blink the LED twice (500 ms on, 500 ms off) with the buzzer off, then read the flame sensor 5 times at 100 ms intervals; if it consistently reads LOW (flame detected) all 5 times, treat it as a sensor fault. On self-test failure, signal the error with a distinct pattern -- the LED blinking rapidly (100 ms on/off) for 5 cycles, then the buzzer sounding a short-short-long-short pattern (200 ms, 200 ms, 600 ms, 200 ms) repeated 3 times -- then exit with code 1. After self-test passes, poll the flame sensor every 50 ms in the main loop; when flame is detected (LOW), activate the buzzer and LED continuously until the sensor reads HIGH for at least one sample, then deactivate them. Log all events (flame detected, flame gone, errors) with timestamps. Check every gpiod call, including line requests and value reads/writes, and handle failures gracefully with clear error messages. Clean up all GPIO lines on normal exit and on SIGINT (Ctrl+C) using a signal handler.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the Linux i2c-dev interface (not sysfs) to read ambient light from a BH1750 digital light sensor at I2C address 0x23 on /dev/i2c-1, initialized in continuous high-resolution mode (command 0x10). Read the 2-byte raw value every 1 second and convert it to lux using lux = raw / 1.2. Store the last 60 lux readings in a circular buffer and compute the average lux over the buffer. Control an LED on GPIO17 (BCM numbering) via sysfs GPIO, blinking it at a rate proportional to the average lux, from 0.5 Hz (dark) to 5 Hz (bright, 1000+ lux), using the linear mapping rate = 0.5 + (avg_lux / 1000) * 4.5, clamped to [0.5, 5.0]. The blink pattern is a 50% duty cycle square wave (on for half period, off for half period). If an I2C read fails, print an error, skip that sample, and retry on the next loop iteration. On program exit (Ctrl+C), cleanly release the GPIO (unexport) and close the I2C file descriptor, using signal(SIGINT) for graceful shutdown. Use only standard POSIX and Linux kernel headers, no external libraries beyond those.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that uses libgpiod to display the digit '5' on a common-cathode seven-segment display driven by a 74HC595 shift register, blinking it on and off every second (500 ms on, 500 ms off). Use GPIO17 as the data pin, GPIO18 as the clock pin, and GPIO27 as the latch pin. The 74HC595 outputs connect to the display segments in the order Q0=a, Q1=b, Q2=c, Q3=d, Q4=e, Q5=f, Q6=g, Q7=dp (dp unused). Initialize libgpiod, set all three pins as outputs, and implement a robust shift-out function that sends 8 bits MSB-first with proper clock and latch timing. Include error checking for gpiod line requests and handle cleanup on exit by releasing the lines and closing the chip. Loop to blink the digit indefinitely.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi (any model with a 40-pin GPIO header) that uses libgpiod to blink an LED connected to BCM GPIO17 (physical pin 11) with a 2-second period (1 second on, 1 second off). Open GPIO chip 0, request the LED line as output initially low, and request a momentary push button on BCM GPIO18 (physical pin 12) as input with an internal pull-up and falling-edge event detection. In a loop, toggle the LED while monitoring for button events using gpiod_line_event_wait() with a 1-second timeout. On a falling edge (button press), stop the blinking immediately, turn off the LED, print a message, and exit cleanly. Include robust error checking for every libgpiod call, including chip open, line request, event request, and line set/get, and release all resources (lines, chip) on all exit paths. Use signal handling for SIGINT to allow graceful termination with Ctrl+C. Compile with: gcc -o blink_button blink_button.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (no wiringPi) to blink an LED connected to GPIO5 (physical pin 29) with a periodic delay of 750 ms. Initialize pigpio and check for failure, exiting with a non-zero code if initialization fails, then set GPIO5 as an output. In an infinite loop, turn the LED on (gpioWrite GPIO5 high), print 'LED ON' to stdout, wait 750 ms using time_sleep or gpioDelay, turn the LED off (GPIO5 low), print 'LED OFF', and wait another 750 ms, flushing stdout after each print so output is visible immediately. Handle SIGINT gracefully: cleanly turn off the LED, terminate pigpio, and exit with code 0, ensuring all pigpio resources are released on exit, including on error paths. The program should run successfully in both real and emulated Raspberry Pi environments, exiting cleanly with code 0 on SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that uses the libgpiod library (no wiringPi, no pigpio) to control an LED and read a button. The LED anode is connected to GPIO24 (physical pin 18) through a 330-ohm resistor to ground, and a button is connected between GPIO22 (physical pin 15) and 3.3V, with a 10k-ohm pull-down resistor to ground (or the internal pull-down if available). Open the gpiochip0 device, configure GPIO24 as output initially low and GPIO22 as input with an internal pull-down. Continuously monitor the button: while it is pressed, blink the LED in a repeating 500 ms on, 500 ms off pattern; when the button is released, turn the LED off immediately and keep it off until pressed again. Check every gpiod call, including chip open, line get, direction set, and value read/write, printing descriptive error messages to stderr, and handle the case where the gpiochip device is not found or a line is busy. On program exit, including via SIGINT or SIGTERM, release all gpiod resources (lines and chip) gracefully. Run indefinitely until terminated by Ctrl+C.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library (not wiringPi or pigpio) to control a common-cathode RGB LED by randomly changing its color every 100 ms, using software PWM via a simple timing loop (no hardware PWM). Wire Red to GPIO24 (physical pin 18), Green to GPIO23 (physical pin 16), and Blue to GPIO18 (physical pin 12) (BCM numbering). Drive each channel with a 100 Hz PWM signal (10 ms period) with a duty cycle from 0 to 100. Initialize all three GPIOs as outputs; generate random RGB values (0-100) using rand() seeded with time(NULL) and set the PWM duty cycles accordingly. Use gpiod_line_set_value() in a busy-wait PWM loop, avoiding sleep calls shorter than 1 ms and using clock_nanosleep for precision. Check gpiod_chip_open_by_number(), gpiod_chip_get_line(), and gpiod_line_request_output() for each line, handling failures with descriptive messages. Run indefinitely until Ctrl+C, which should cleanly release GPIO lines via a SIGINT signal handler and exit, ensuring proper resource cleanup on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library for both I2C and GPIO to interface with an Adafruit LSM303DLHC accelerometer at I2C address 0x19 on bus 1, detecting sudden impacts exceeding a configurable G-force threshold (default 2.0G, set via a -t command-line argument). Configure the sensor with CTRL_REG1_A=0x27 (enable all axes, 100 Hz) and CTRL_REG4_A=0x00 (2G full-scale, sensitivity 16384 LSB/G), and use multi-byte reads with the auto-increment bit (0x80) starting at OUT_X_L_A (0x28). Continuously poll the accelerometer at 10 Hz, calculate the total G-force magnitude, and when the threshold is exceeded, pulse GPIO17 (set as output) HIGH for 50 ms and log timestamped accelerometer data to 'impact_log.txt'. Check every I2C read/write, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release (I2C handle, GPIO, pigpio library) on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to interface with an Analog Devices ADPD188BI optical sensor over I2C bus 1 at 7-bit address 0x39. Initialize the sensor by writing 0x01 to register 0x0D (MODE) to enter normal operation mode. Read ambient light (ALS) data from 16-bit registers 0x64 (LSB) and 0x65 (MSB), combining them into a 16-bit unsigned value, and read color (RGB) data from 16-bit registers 0x66 (Red), 0x68 (Green), and 0x6A (Blue). Log each timestamped reading (ALS, R, G, B) to a CSV file named 'color_log.csv' with a header row. Simulate a smart lighting system by adjusting LED brightness on GPIO18 (hardware PWM) using pigpio: map the ALS value (0-65535) to a PWM duty cycle (0-255), so brighter ambient light increases LED brightness. Handle I2C errors, such as failed writes/reads or sensor absence, by logging to stderr and retrying after 100 ms. Use signal handling (SIGINT/SIGTERM) for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle, turning off the LED, and closing the CSV file. Sample every 500 ms.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses pigpio for I2C (never wiringPi) to interface with an Adafruit FXOS8700CQ 6-axis accelerometer/magnetometer at I2C address 0x1F on bus 1, detecting sudden impacts by computing the acceleration magnitude. On startup, verify the sensor by reading WHO_AM_I (register 0x0D) and checking it equals 0xC7, aborting with a clear error if it does not match. Initialize the sensor: place it into standby (clear CTRL_REG1 bit 0), configure XYZ_DATA_CFG (0x0E) for ±2g mode (0x00), then activate by setting CTRL_REG1 (0x2A) bit 0 (active mode, 200 Hz ODR). Read 6 bytes of acceleration starting at OUT_X_MSB (0x01); the data is 14-bit left-justified, so shift right by 2, then convert using sensitivity 4096 counts/g for the ±2g range and multiply by 9.81 for m/s^2. Compute magnitude = sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2); if it exceeds the 2g (19.62 m/s^2) threshold, log the timestamp, x, y, z, and magnitude to 'impact_log.txt' in append mode as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,x,y,z,magnitude' with 3 decimal places. Sample every 50 ms. Check every pigpio I2C call's return value; on a read error, print a diagnostic to stderr and continue the loop rather than crashing. Implement graceful shutdown via SIGINT (Ctrl+C): close the I2C handle, call gpioTerminate(), and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the Linux i2c-dev ioctl interface (/dev/i2c-1 character device) to read angular velocity from a GY-50 L3G4200D gyroscope at I2C address 0x69 (SA0 tied high) on bus 1. Configure CTRL_REG1 (0x20) to 0x0F (normal mode, all axes enabled, 100 Hz ODR) and CTRL_REG4 (0x23) to 0x00 (250 dps full-scale, continuous update). Read the 6-byte OUT_X_L..OUT_Z_H block starting at register 0x28 using an auto-increment read, and convert the raw 16-bit signed values to degrees per second using a sensitivity of 0.00875 dps/LSB. Perform a 100-sample stationary calibration at startup to compute X/Y/Z zero-rate offsets. Log the calibrated X, Y, Z readings with ISO-8601 timestamps to 'gyro_log.txt' at 20 Hz (50 ms period). If any axis exceeds 50 dps, print a warning to stderr and append an alert line to the log. Check every open, ioctl, read, and write call; detect sensor absence via WHO_AM_I (register 0x0F, expected 0xD3) and handle I2C bus errors. Cleanly release the I2C file descriptor and log file on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read acceleration data from an ADXL345 accelerometer over I2C bus 1 at address 0x53. Configure the sensor for full-resolution, ±2g range, and verify the DEVID register (0x00) reads 0xE5 before proceeding. Read the 6 bytes of X/Y/Z data starting at register 0x32 every 100 ms (10 Hz). Log each sample to 'accel_log.txt' as 'timestamp,x,y,z' in g units with 3 decimal places. Turn on an LED connected to GPIO17 (active-high) when the absolute acceleration on ANY axis exceeds 2.0 g, otherwise turn it off. Check every pigpio/I2C call, and handle I2C read failures without writing garbage to the log. Ensure clean resource release (I2C handle, GPIO, log file) on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses pigpio for I2C to read magnetometer and accelerometer data from a GY-51 LSM303DLHC over I2C bus 1 (accelerometer address 0x19, magnetometer address 0x1E) and calculate a tilt-compensated heading. Initialize the accelerometer with CTRL_REG1_A (0x20) set to 0x27 (50 Hz, all axes enabled) and the magnetometer with MR_REG_M (0x02) set to 0x00 (continuous-conversion mode). Read 6 bytes from each sensor: accelerometer data from OUT_X_L_A (0x28) with the auto-increment bit, and magnetometer data from OUT_X_H_M (0x03). Log timestamped heading, acceleration (x, y, z in g), and magnetic field (x, y, z in gauss) to 'compass_log.txt', writing a CSV header if the log file is new. Check every I2C call and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths. Sample every 100 ms. Use SIGINT/SIGTERM for graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handles and terminates pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses pigpio to continuously read distance from an Adafruit VL6180X Time-of-Flight sensor via I2C bus 1 at address 0x29, simulating a proximity-based automated door opener. Perform the VL6180X's mandatory initialization sequence before use (read register 0x016, write 0x0207 to register 0x000, and the remaining sequence steps). Sample every 100 ms, reading the range status register (0x04d) to detect errors such as overrange or signal failure. If the measured distance is less than 100 mm, log 'DOOR_OPEN'; otherwise log 'DOOR_CLOSED'. Log timestamped readings to 'distance_log.txt'. Check all I2C read/write return values and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths by attempting re-initialization. Handle SIGINT for clean resource release.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses pigpio to sample data from two STMicroelectronics IMP23ABSU ultrasonic MEMS microphone sensors on I2C bus 1, simulating a bat echolocation analysis system. The two sensors have distinct I2C addresses: sensor 1 at 0x68 and sensor 2 at 0x69, each exposing a 16-bit data register at 0x01 and a control register at 0x00 that must be written with 0x80 to enable continuous measurement. Read 16-bit signed audio samples from both sensors, timestamp them using CLOCK_REALTIME, compute a basic Time Difference of Arrival (TDOA) by subtracting the two samples, and log the data as CSV to 'audio_log.dat' with columns sec, nsec, sensor1, sensor2, tdoa. Use a 10 ms sampling interval. Verify all pigpio initialization and I2C communication calls; handle sensor-absent or bus-failure paths gracefully by skipping the sample and retrying. Ensure clean resource release (I2C handles, log file, pigpio termination) on all exit paths via a SIGINT signal handler.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface over SPI with an Analog Devices ADIS16488A IMU on SPI channel 0 (CE0 on GPIO8) at 1 MHz, SPI mode 3 (CPOL=1, CPHA=1), using pigpio SPI flags 0b11000000000 (bit 9 = CPHA, bit 10 = CPOL, bit 8 = aux SPI off) and 16-bit words. The ADIS16488A read protocol sends a 16-bit word whose MSB is 0 followed by the 7-bit register address; the requested register's data is returned on the next 16-bit transfer, so implement a dummy read or stall of at least 40 microseconds between the request and the data-retrieval transfer. Continuously read gyroscope X, Y, Z from registers X_GYRO=0x04, Y_GYRO=0x06, Z_GYRO=0x08 and accelerometer X, Y, Z from X_ACCEL=0x0A, Y_ACCEL=0x0C, Z_ACCEL=0x0E every 100 ms, converting with sensitivities 0.005 deg/sec/LSB for gyroscope and 0.00025 g/LSB for accelerometer, and log each sample with a millisecond-precision timestamp to a CSV file named "imu_data.csv" whose header row is "timestamp,gyro_x,gyro_y,gyro_z,accel_x,accel_y,accel_z". Check the return values of gpioInitialise, spiOpen and fopen; if spiXfer returns less than 0, log the error to stderr and skip that sample rather than aborting. Use a non-blocking sampling delay that checks a running flag every few milliseconds so the program responds promptly to signals, and implement a cleanup() helper registered with atexit() that closes the SPI handle and CSV file and terminates pigpio on SIGINT, SIGTERM and every other exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads an Analog Devices ADIS16448 IMU over SPI bus 0, chip-select CS0 on GPIO8, SPI mode 3, at up to 1 MHz. Because libgpiod has no SPI API, perform the SPI transfers through the Linux spidev ioctl interface and use libgpiod only for the chip-select/GPIO line. Use the ADIS16448 single-register read protocol: send the 8-bit register address with bit 7 set (0x80) in the first 16-bit SPI cycle, then read the 16-bit data response in the second cycle. Read gyroscope X, Y, Z from XGYRO_OUT=0x04, YGYRO_OUT=0x06, ZGYRO_OUT=0x08 and accelerometer X, Y, Z from XACCL_OUT=0x0A, YACCL_OUT=0x0C, ZACCL_OUT=0x0E, applying scale factors of 0.02 dps/LSB for gyroscope and 0.00025 g/LSB for accelerometer, and log the values to the console every 100 ms. Include robust error handling for SPI initialization, ioctl transfers and data reads, and handle SIGINT/SIGTERM for clean resource release by closing the SPI device file and the libgpiod chip.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with an Analog Devices ADIS16448 IMU over SPI channel 0 (CE0/GPIO8) at 1 MHz, SPI Mode 0. The ADIS16448 requires a two-cycle SPI read: send the read command (register address with bit 15 set) in the first 16-bit transfer, wait at least 40 microseconds of stall time, then send a dummy 0x0000 in the second transfer to clock out the 16-bit data. Periodically read gyroscope x, y, z from X_GYRO_OUT=0x04, Y_GYRO_OUT=0x06, Z_GYRO_OUT=0x08 and accelerometer x, y, z from X_ACCL_OUT=0x0A, Y_ACCL_OUT=0x0C, Z_ACCL_OUT=0x0E, scaling with 0.05 deg/sec/LSB for gyroscope and 0.00025 g/LSB for accelerometer, and print the formatted values to the console every 100 ms. Include robust error handling for pigpio initialization, SPI open, and transfer failures, and handle Ctrl+C cleanly by closing the SPI handle and calling gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a TDK MPU-6886 6-axis IMU over I2C bus 1 at address 0x68 using the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (open/ioctl/read/write), not wiringPi. Verify the sensor is present by reading the WHO_AM_I register (0x75) and checking it returns 0x86, then initialize the sensor by waking it (PWR_MGMT_1 = 0x00) and setting ACCEL_CONFIG (0x1C) and GYRO_CONFIG (0x1B) to 0x00 for the +-2g and +-250 dps ranges. Every 50 ms, read raw accelerometer data from registers 0x3B-0x40 and gyroscope data from registers 0x43-0x48, and print the raw 16-bit signed values to the console. Check every I2C syscall, retry transient read failures up to 3 times, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths gracefully, ensuring clean resource release by closing the I2C file descriptor on all exit paths including SIGINT (Ctrl+C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library for I2C and GPIO to interface with an Adafruit ADXL345 accelerometer on I2C bus 1 at address 0x53, configured for full-resolution mode at the +-2g range (scale factor 256 LSB/g), to detect sudden impacts. Verify the ADXL345 device ID by reading register 0x00 and checking it equals 0xE5. Poll the sensor every 10 ms; if the total acceleration magnitude exceeds 2.5g, turn on a red LED connected to GPIO17 for 500 ms and append a timestamped entry containing the magnitude and X/Y/Z components to "impact_log.txt". Check every I2C read/write call, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release of the I2C handle, LED, log file, and pigpio on all exit paths including SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library for all I2C operations to read accelerometer and gyroscope data from a TDK InvenSense ICM-20602 IMU on I2C bus 1 at address 0x68. Initialize the device by waking it from sleep (PWR_MGMT_1 = 0x00), setting the accelerometer to +-2g (ACCEL_CONFIG = 0x00) and the gyroscope to +-250 dps (GYRO_CONFIG = 0x00), and before the main loop verify the sensor is present by reading the WHO_AM_I register (0x75) and checking for the expected value 0x12. Use burst reads (i2cReadI2CBlockData) to fetch the 6 accelerometer bytes starting at 0x3B and the 6 gyroscope bytes starting at 0x43 efficiently, and log timestamped raw x, y, z accelerometer and gyroscope values to a CSV file named 'imu_log.csv' at 10 Hz (100 ms interval). Check the return value of every I2C operation and print failures to stderr, and handle Ctrl+C (SIGINT) gracefully by closing the I2C handle, terminating pigpio, and closing the CSV file before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads X, Y, and Z acceleration data from a GY-45 MMA8451Q accelerometer over I2C bus 1 at address 0x1D, using the Linux i2c-dev ioctl interface for I2C access (libgpiod has no I2C API) and libgpiod for the LED GPIO line on GPIO17 (BCM numbering) — never wiringPi. Verify the sensor's identity by reading the WHO_AM_I register (0x0D) and checking it equals 0x1A before operation. Poll the sensor every 100 ms and trigger the LED if the magnitude of acceleration on any axis exceeds a threshold of 2.0g, given the sensor's default +-2g range where 1g = 1024 counts; when an impact is detected, turn the LED on for 500 ms and append a timestamped entry to 'impact_log.txt'. Handle I2C read/write errors gracefully, and cleanly release all resources — the I2C bus, GPIO lines, and file handles — on SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads X, Y, and Z magnetic field data from a Texas Instruments TMAG5273 I2C 3D Hall-Effect sensor at its default address 0x35, using the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface directly (open/ioctl/read/write) rather than wiringPi, to simulate an industrial robotic arm joint position feedback system. Use 16-bit little-endian reads for the X, Y, and Z result registers at 0x10, 0x11, and 0x12, sampling once per second, and log the data with timestamps to 'magnetic_field_log.csv', writing the CSV header row on startup if the file does not already exist. Check every syscall (open, ioctl, read, write, fopen, etc.) and handle errors gracefully; if an I2C read fails, log an error to stderr and continue the loop. Implement a signal handler for SIGINT/SIGTERM that cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and the CSV file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a SparkFun ADXL345 I2C accelerometer on /dev/i2c-1 at address 0x53 via the Linux i2c-dev ioctl interface, and uses libgpiod (never wiringPi) to request a falling-edge interrupt on GPIO17 (physical pin 11), connected to the ADXL345 INT1 pin, to detect freefall events. Put the sensor in standby before register writes, then configure it: set THRESH_FF (0x0A) to ~300 mg, TIME_FF (0x20) to ~100 ms, enable the freefall interrupt via bit 2 of INT_ENABLE (0x2E), map it to INT1 via INT_MAP (0x2F = 0x00), and enter measurement mode by setting POWER_CTL (0x2D) to 0x08. On each interrupt, read INT_SOURCE (0x30) to verify the freefall bit (bit 2) is set, then read 6 bytes from DATAX0 (0x32) in a single I2C block read; reading INT_SOURCE also clears the interrupt. Log timestamped X, Y, Z acceleration values only during a freefall event to 'freefall_log.csv' in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.mmm,X,Y,Z' (with milliseconds), writing a header row on creation and flushing after each write. Check every I2C syscall and GPIO call, verify the device ID (register 0x00 should read 0xE5) at startup, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths. Use a poll-based loop on the libgpiod event file descriptor rather than threads, and on SIGINT/SIGTERM disable the sensor's interrupts, close the I2C file descriptor, release the GPIO lines, close the chip, and close the log file.

Log timestamped readings in CSV format to 'motion_log.txt' and implement a basic fall-detection state machine (IDLE -> FREEFALL -> IMPACT) using an acceleration-magnitude threshold below 0.2g for freefall and above 2.5g for impact within a 1.0 second window. Handle I2C read/write errors, a sensor-absent condition via a WHO_AM_I check, and bus errors gracefully, and ensure clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to continuously read X, Y, and Z angular velocities from a GY-50 L3G4200D gyroscope over I2C bus 1 at address 0x69. Configure the sensor for normal mode with all axes enabled (CTRL_REG1 = 0x0F) and +-250 dps full-scale range (CTRL_REG4 = 0x00). Read all 6 data bytes starting at OUT_X_L (0x28) in a single block read, and convert raw values to degrees per second using sensitivity 8.75 mdps/LSB (i.e., divide by 114.285). Log each sample with a nanosecond-precision timestamp to 'gyro_log.csv' with a header row 'Timestamp,X,Y,Z', sampling every 10 ms. Retry I2C writes up to 3 times during initialization, check every I2C call, verify the WHO_AM_I register (0x0F) reads 0xD3 before proceeding, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths. Use signal handling for graceful termination, performing clean resource release on SIGINT by closing the I2C handle, closing the file, and calling gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that initializes the pigpio library and reads a KY-026 Flame Sensor Module's digital output connected to GPIO17 (physical pin 11), enabling the internal pull-up resistor on GPIO17 so the input is deterministic when the sensor's open-collector output is off. The DO line is active-LOW: it reads LOW (0) when a flame is detected and HIGH (1) when no flame is present. Check for pigpio initialization failure, then open 'flame_events.log' in append mode and verify the file handle is valid. In a main loop, poll the sensor every 500 ms; on each poll, log a timestamped line of the form 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS - Flame detected: YES|NO' to the log file and immediately flush it, and when a flame is detected (LOW), print 'FLAME DETECTED!' to the console to simulate a fire alarm. Install a SIGINT handler so Ctrl+C sets a flag that stops the loop cleanly, and on any exit path close the log file if open and call gpioTerminate(). Handle sensor read errors (gpioRead returning PI_BAD_GPIO) by logging an error line rather than a false positive.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that interfaces with an Omron D7S-0001 vibration sensor over I2C at slave address 0x53 on bus /dev/i2c-1, using the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface directly (open/read/ioctl) rather than wiringPi, to simulate a structural integrity monitoring system. The D7S-0001 exposes acceleration in registers 0x28-0x2D (X_LSB, X_MSB, Y_LSB, Y_MSB, Z_LSB, Z_MSB); combine each axis as signed 16-bit (MSB<<8 | LSB). Sample the sensor every 100 ms and log X, Y, and Z axis acceleration data to a CSV file named 'vibration_log.csv' with header 'Timestamp,X,Y,Z' and ISO-8601 UTC timestamps. Check every open/ioctl/read call, detect sensor-absent paths (e.g. an I2C read returning 0xFF or failing), and handle bus errors gracefully without crashing; if a read fails, print a diagnostic to stderr and skip that sample rather than terminating. Install a SIGINT handler so Ctrl+C cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and the CSV file before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses libgpiod (v1.6+ API) to monitor a conveyor belt safety system by reading the digital output of two TI DRV5032 digital Hall-Effect sensors connected to GPIO17 and GPIO27, configured as inputs with internal pull-ups enabled via bias flags. Log timestamps with millisecond precision and the sensor states to 'conveyor_log.txt' every 50 ms, and if both sensors read logic 1 (triggered), halt the conveyor, simulated with a print statement. Include robust error handling for GPIO access (chip opening, line requests, reads) and log file I/O, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, releasing all libgpiod resources cleanly on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running a 64-bit OS that interfaces with a GY-45 MMA8452Q 3-axis accelerometer over I2C using the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (no third-party GPIO/I2C libraries such as wiringPi). The sensor's SA0 pin is tied high, so use I2C address 0x1D on bus /dev/i2c-1. Verify the sensor identity by reading the WHO_AM_I register (0x0D) and checking it equals 0x2A, printing an error and exiting if it does not match. Initialize the sensor by reading CTRL_REG1 (0x2A), clearing bit 0 to place it in standby mode, setting the data rate to 100 Hz (bits 3-5 = 0b010), and then setting bit 0 to switch to active mode. Continuously poll the accelerometer at roughly 100 Hz (10 ms loop interval), reading the six data registers (0x01-0x06) in a single I2C block read for atomic sampling, combining MSB/LSB and right-shifting by 4 to form signed 12-bit values, and compute the tilt angle of the X-axis relative to gravity using atan2(x, sqrt(y*y + z*z)). When the absolute tilt angle exceeds 45 degrees, log a timestamped line containing the raw 12-bit X, Y, Z values to fall_log.txt, opened once in append mode at startup. Handle all I2C syscall failures (open, ioctl, read, write) by printing strerror(errno) and exiting or skipping the iteration as appropriate. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that closes the I2C file descriptor and the log file before exiting, keeping the log file open for the program's lifetime and flushing after each entry rather than reopening it on every write.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with an Adafruit LIS3MDL Triple-Axis Magnetometer over I2C on /dev/i2c-1 at address 0x1E, using the Linux i2c-dev ioctl interface for I2C access since libgpiod has no I2C API. Configure the sensor for continuous-conversion mode at 80 Hz ODR with high-performance mode on all axes (CTRL_REG1=0x70, CTRL_REG4=0x0C, CTRL_REG3=0x00), and verify the sensor is present by reading WHO_AM_I (0x0F) and checking it equals 0x3D. Continuously read the 6-byte little-endian X/Y/Z magnetic-field output registers starting at 0x28, apply fixed offset/scale calibration constants, convert to milliGauss using the +-4 gauss sensitivity of 0.146 mG/LSB, and append comma-separated X,Y,Z values to 'magnetic_log.txt' at 10 Hz. Check every I2C read/write for errors and retry initialization up to 3 times; handle SIGINT/SIGTERM cleanly by closing the I2C file descriptor and the log file, which should be opened once and flushed after each write. Include a simple metal-detector threshold alert printed to stderr when the total field magnitude exceeds 800 mG.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library over SPI channel 0 (CE0/GPIO8), 1 MHz clock, SPI Mode 0, to read acceleration data from an Analog Devices ADXL354B accelerometer. The ADXL354B outputs 20-bit signed acceleration data in 3 consecutive bytes per axis (XDATA at 0x08, YDATA at 0x0B, ZDATA at 0x0E); use the +-2g range sensitivity of 3.9 microg/LSB (0.0000039 g/LSB). SPI reads use bit 7 = 1 for read and bit 6 = 1 for multi-byte. Implement a proper device reset sequence: write 0x52 to the RESET register (0x1F), wait 1 ms, then set the measurement mode by clearing the RUN bit in POWER_CTL (0x2D), waiting for the STABLE bit in STATUS (0x04), then setting the RUN bit. Log X, Y, and Z axis readings with timestamps every 100 ms to a file named 'vibration_log.txt'. Handle SPI communication errors with retries, check sensor presence by reading PARTID (0x01, expected 0x1D), and implement graceful shutdown via SIGINT/SIGTERM with proper resource cleanup: close the SPI handle, close the file, and terminate pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library's spiOpen and spiXfer APIs (not deprecated wiringPi) to interface with an Analog Devices ADIS16362 IMU over SPI channel 0 (CE0/GPIO8), baud rate 1 MHz, SPI Mode 3 (active-high clock, sampled on trailing edge). The ADIS16362 read protocol sends the register address with the MSB set followed by a dummy byte, with the requested register's data returned on the next 16-bit transfer; implement a robust read function that sends the address, waits for the conversion, and retrieves the data, handling stall/error returns from spiXfer. Continuously read 3-axis gyroscope from X_GYRO=0x04, Y_GYRO=0x06, Z_GYRO=0x08 and 3-axis accelerometer from X_ACCL=0x0A, Y_ACCL=0x0C, Z_ACCL=0x0E, scaling with 0.05 deg/sec/LSB for gyroscope and 0.0025 g/LSB for accelerometer, sampling at approximately 100 Hz (10 ms delay between reads). Log timestamped readings to a comma-separated file 'imu_log.csv' starting with the header 'Timestamp,X_Gyro,Y_Gyro,Z_Gyro,X_Accel,Y_Accel,Z_Accel', using high-precision UNIX epoch timestamps (seconds.nanoseconds). Check pigpio initialization, SPI open, file open, and spiXfer return codes; if spiXfer fails, print an error to stderr and skip the logging iteration. Implement graceful shutdown via SIGINT (Ctrl+C) using a signal handler that safely closes the SPI handle, flushes and closes the log file, and calls gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library (not the deprecated sysfs interface, and not wiringPi) to read an E18-D80NK IR obstacle sensor connected to GPIO17. The E18-D80NK outputs LOW (0) when an obstacle is detected within its detection range, adjustable up to about 80 cm and configured here for roughly 30 cm, and HIGH (1) when the path is clear. Open the gpiochip device for GPIO17 on the Raspberry Pi 5 (gpiochip4) and request the line for input direction using modern libgpiod APIs such as gpiod_chip_open_by_name, gpiod_line_open, gpiod_line_request_input, and gpiod_line_get_value. Poll the sensor every 1 second; when an obstacle is detected (line reads LOW), trigger a simulated "self-parking" sequence logged to the console with timestamps ("Self-parking sequence started" / "completed"). Check all libgpiod calls, handle the case where the gpiochip or line is unavailable and exit gracefully, and handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for clean shutdown, releasing the GPIO line and closing the chip on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses libgpiod (v2 API) to interface with two Keyes KY-032 IR obstacle avoidance sensors connected to GPIO17 and GPIO27 (physical pins 11 and 13, BCM numbering). The KY-032 output is active-low: the sensor reads 0 when an obstacle is detected and 1 when the path is clear. Use a single gpiochip and request both lines together for input, reading both lines in a single call via the libgpiod v2 bulk-read API gpiod_line_request_get_values. Poll both sensors every 100 ms and log the obstacle detection status to the console with a timestamp, simulating a basic collision avoidance system for a small robot, running in an infinite loop until interrupted. Check every libgpiod call, handle the case where the gpiochip or lines are unavailable, and ensure clean release of all resources on all exit paths including SIGINT (Ctrl+C). Compile cleanly with -Wall -Wextra against libgpiod >= 2.0.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the modern libgpiod library for SPI chip-select line control together with the Linux spidev interface for SPI communication (not the deprecated bcm2835 or wiringPi libraries) to periodically read gyroscope data from an Analog Devices ADIS16266 connected on SPI0 (CE0 on GPIO8), configured for SPI Mode 3, MSB first, at a 1 MHz clock speed. Initialize the SPI device (/dev/spidev0.0) and a libgpiod line for the CS pin, write to the MSC_CTRL register (0x24) to enable data ready mode, then periodically read the X, Y, and Z angular rate output registers (0x04, 0x06, 0x08) using the ADIS16266 two-transfer read protocol (send the address with the MSB set, then read 2 bytes). Convert the raw 16-bit signed values to angular rates using the scale factor of 0.02 deg/sec/LSB and log the results to the console every 100 ms. Include robust error handling: check all SPI and GPIO initialization calls, handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT, running in a loop until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses only the pigpio C API, not wiringPi, to read accelerometer and gyroscope data from an STMicroelectronics LSM6DSR connected via I2C bus 1 at the 7-bit address 0x6B. Initialize the pigpio library and open the I2C bus, then verify the sensor is present by reading the WHO_AM_I register and checking it returns 0x6B. Configure the accelerometer for +-2g full-scale at 104 Hz (CTRL1_XL = 0x42) and the gyroscope for +-250 dps at 104 Hz (CTRL2_G = 0x42). Every 100 ms, burst-read 12 bytes starting at OUTX_L_G (0x22) covering gyro X/Y/Z then accel X/Y/Z, convert to physical units using gyro sensitivity mdps/LSB = 8.75 (i.e. 0.00875 dps/LSB) and accel sensitivity mg/LSB = 0.061 (i.e. 0.000061 g/LSB), and print one line to stdout. Handle all error paths: pigpio init failure, I2C open failure, WHO_AM_I mismatch, register write failures, and short or failed burst reads, printing to stderr and exiting non-zero; check every I2C call's return value and never use hard-coded sleeps that ignore errors. Install a SIGINT handler so Ctrl+C triggers a clean shutdown that closes the I2C handle and calls gpioTerminate() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to read accelerometer and magnetometer data from an Adafruit FXOS8700 breakout board over I2C at address 0x1D on bus 1 (GPIO2/GPIO3 for SDA/SCL). Initialize the sensor into hybrid mode by configuring CTRL_REG1 (0x2A), CTRL_REG2 (0x2B), M_CTRL_REG1 (0x5B), and M_CTRL_REG2 (0x5C) so both the accelerometer and magnetometer produce data. Every 100 ms, read the 12-byte combined data block starting at register 0x01 (OUT_X_MSB), which contains 6 bytes of 14-bit left-aligned accelerometer data followed by 6 bytes of 16-bit magnetometer data, and log the raw X, Y, and Z values for both sensors to the console each cycle. Handle I2C communication errors robustly: check every pigpio I2C call, verify the sensor is present by reading the WHO_AM_I register (0x0D, expected value 0xC7) before initialization, and retry on transient read failures. Clean up all resources — close the I2C handle and terminate pigpio — on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that interfaces with an ADXL345 accelerometer over I2C at address 0x53 using the Linux i2c-dev interface via /dev/i2c-1, not wiringPi, since libgpiod itself has no I2C API. Read X, Y, Z data from registers 0x32-0x37, calculate tilt angles using atan2, and log events with timestamps every 100 ms. Log tilt events exceeding a threshold of 30.0 degrees to '/var/log/tilt_events.log'. Include robust error handling for I2C communication failures, explicitly handling sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for Ctrl+C.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library, and no wiringPi, to monitor ambient noise levels via a KY-038 sound sensor connected to GPIO17 (physical pin 11). The KY-038 OUT pin is active-high and pulses when sound exceeds its onboard comparator threshold. Accept a single command-line argument — an integer threshold representing the minimum number of high-readings per 5-second window required to trigger an alert — and validate it, rejecting non-numeric or non-positive values. Continuously sample GPIO17 every 1 ms for 5 seconds, counting how many times the pin reads high; at the end of each 5-second window, print a timestamped ALERT to stdout if the high-reading count exceeds the threshold, otherwise print a normal status line. Run in a continuous loop until signaled to stop, with a 1-second pause between monitoring windows. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully, terminating pigpio and exiting cleanly, and check every pigpio call for failure (gpioInitialise, gpioSetMode), printing clear error messages to stderr on any failure.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the libgpiod C API, never wiringPi, to control two 12V electromagnetic door locks actuated by 5V active-HIGH relay modules driven via TIP120 transistors on GPIO17 (Door A) and GPIO27 (Door B), based on a randomly generated 6-digit security code. Initialize GPIO17 and GPIO27 as outputs, both defaulting to LOW (locks energized/closed); a HIGH signal de-energizes the relay and unlocks the corresponding door. Generate a random 6-digit code between 100000 and 999999 at startup and print it to stdout. In a loop, prompt the user to enter the code via stdin; if it matches, unlock Door A (GPIO17 HIGH) for 5 seconds, then re-lock it (LOW), log the successful entry to 'access_log.txt' as a CSV row 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,NNNNNN', and generate a new random code. If the code does not match, print 'Access denied' and continue; handle invalid non-numeric stdin input gracefully by clearing the buffer and re-prompting. Check every libgpiod call (chip open, line get, line request) and file open, printing meaningful errors to stderr and exiting non-zero on initialization failure. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag so the main loop exits cleanly; on exit, drive both GPIO outputs LOW (locked), release all libgpiod resources (lines and chip), and close any open file handles. Compile with: gcc -Wall -o door_access door_access.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the standard Linux /dev/i2c-1 ioctl interface, not the unmaintained bcm2835 library, to read illuminance from a BH1750FVI light sensor over I2C bus 1 (GPIO2/GPIO3). The sensor's ADDR pin is tied to GND, so the I2C address is 0x23. Write the One-Time High-Resolution Mode 2 command (0x21) to the sensor, wait for the maximum conversion time of 180 ms, then read 2 bytes of data and calculate the illuminance in lux using the formula: (raw_value * 5) / 6 (equivalent to raw_value / 1.2). Log the sensor readings to a file named 'light_log.txt', formatting each entry as 'Timestamp: <timestamp>, Lux: <lux_value>', continuously every 5 seconds until interrupted. The program must handle potential I2C write/read errors and sensor-absent paths (e.g., failing to open the bus or read bytes), and implement clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT (Ctrl+C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses pigpio for I2C and hardware PWM to implement a theremin using an MPR121 capacitive touch sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x5A. The program acts as a TCP server listening on port 12345; when a client sends a message starting with 'MOTION_DETECTED:' and containing the shared secret 'MySecretKey', the theremin plays tones for 5 seconds based on capacitive touch readings, using hardware PWM on GPIO18. Initialize the MPR121 with proper soft-reset and electrode configuration, and map the maximum electrode filtered data value to a frequency in the range 220-880 Hz using a logarithmic scale, sampling touch values every 20 ms during the 5-second playback window and logging each frequency to 'frequency_log.txt'. Handle errors for pigpio initialization, I2C open/read, and socket/bind/listen/accept. On SIGINT/SIGTERM, stop PWM, close I2C and sockets, and terminate pigpio cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with an LSM303DLHC magnetometer via I2C bus 1 at default address 0x1E, connected to the physical SDA1/SCL1 pins, and controls an LED on GPIO17. Use libgpiod for GPIO/PWM control and the standard Linux I2C interface (/dev/i2c-1, ioctl) for sensor communication, not wiringPi. Initialize the magnetometer by writing 0x18 to CTRL_REG1_M (0x20) for 10 Hz continuous conversion, and read 6 bytes of data starting from OUT_X_L_M (0x08) in a single I2C block read. The program must read X, Y, Z magnetic field data, compute the magnitude of the Z-axis field, and adjust the LED brightness proportionally using hardware PWM, sampling every 100 ms in the main loop. Handle I2C errors (e.g., sensor absent, bus errors) gracefully by logging the error and skipping the sample without crashing, and implement clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM by releasing the PWM, closing the I2C file descriptor, and closing any log files.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to interface with an HMC5883L magnetometer via I2C on bus 1 at address 0x1E. Configure the sensor for 8-sample averaging, 15 Hz output rate, and a gain setting of 1.3 Gauss (Configuration Register A = 0x70, Configuration Register B = 0x20, Mode register = 0x00 for continuous mode). Continuously collect raw readings to compute hard-iron offsets as a running average over a 100-sample window. Every 500 ms, apply the current hard-iron offsets to the latest raw reading and print the offset-corrected (not unit-normalized) X, Y, and Z values to stdout. Explicitly flag any I2C read/write errors on stderr without crashing, and ensure clean resource release of the I2C handle and pigpio library on SIGINT/SIGTERM. Do not use FIFOs or secondary processes.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads tri-axial acceleration data from an LSM303D accelerometer/magnetometer connected via I2C at address 0x1D (SA0 tied high) on /dev/i2c-1, using the Linux i2c-dev kernel API (open, ioctl I2C_SLAVE, i2c_smbus_read_byte_data, i2c_smbus_write_byte_data, i2c_smbus_read_i2c_block_data) for I2C communication, not wiringPi, and the libgpiod library for the GPIO interrupt line request and event monitoring, not wiringPiISR. The LSM303D's INT1 pin is connected to GPIO23 (BCM pin 23, physical pin 16). Verify the WHO_AM_I register (0x0F) reads 0x49 before proceeding, then configure the accelerometer for 50 Hz ODR with all axes enabled (CTRL_REG1 = 0x57), full-scale +-2g (CTRL_REG4 = 0x00, sensitivity 0.061 mg/LSB), and a threshold interrupt on any-axis-high event (INT1_CFG = 0x2A) with threshold 2000 mg (register value = 2000/16 = 125 = 0x7D) and duration 0 (immediate). Use a 6-byte multi-byte burst read from OUT_X_L_A (0x28) with auto-increment (MSB of the register address set to 0x80). Poll acceleration at roughly 10 ms intervals and store each sample in a 64-entry in-memory circular buffer; on a rising edge of the INT1 GPIO interrupt, print a timestamp and dump the last 10 buffered samples. Check every I2C read/write and file-open call, printing a diagnostic to stderr and exiting non-zero on initialization failure; if a runtime I2C read fails, print a warning to stderr and skip that sample without corrupting the buffer. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl-C) gracefully by disabling the accelerometer (CTRL_REG1 = 0x00), closing the I2C file descriptor, and exiting cleanly. Compile with: gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o lsm303d_mon lsm303d_mon.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library, never wiringPi, to actuate two 12V DC push-pull solenoids in an alternating sequence with a 500 ms delay between each transition, simulating a simple reciprocating linear actuator for a miniature automated assembly line prototype. Solenoid 1 is driven via a TIP120 transistor on GPIO17 (BCM numbering); solenoid 2 via a TIP120 transistor on GPIO27 (BCM numbering); both circuits include flyback diodes. Request the gpiochip and both lines with consumer labels, checking every libgpiod call for errors and printing a diagnostic to stderr on failure. Before entering the main loop, drive both lines LOW so no solenoid is energized at startup. In the loop, alternate: energize solenoid 1 for 500 ms, then de-energize solenoid 1 and energize solenoid 2 for 500 ms, then de-energize solenoid 2, using nanosleep for the timing. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so Ctrl+C cleanly releases both lines (sets them LOW) and frees all libgpiod resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to control two 12V electromagnetic door locks via GPIO17 and GPIO27 (active-HIGH relay modules), implementing a dual-factor authentication system where both locks open only after receiving a specific, pre-defined, matching 6-digit code via two separate UART serial inputs: /dev/serial0 (primary UART, GPIO14/15) and /dev/serial1 (secondary UART), at 9600 baud with 8N1 framing. The expected code is '123456'. Initialize pigpio and configure GPIO17 and GPIO27 as outputs, defaulting to LOW (locked) on startup and on every exit path. Read 6-digit numeric codes from each UART with a 5-second per-port timeout, resetting the input buffer on non-digit characters, and poll both serial ports in a single main loop with non-blocking reads so codes can arrive in any order within the timeout window. Unlock both doors simultaneously (set both GPIOs HIGH) for 2 seconds, then re-lock (set both GPIOs LOW), only when both received codes match each other and match the expected code, using constant-time string comparison to avoid timing side-channels. Handle errors for pigpio initialization failure, serial port open failure, serial read timeouts, and GPIO write failures, logging each to stderr. Implement clean shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM: ensure both locks are set to LOW (locked), close the serial handles, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the modern libgpiod API (gpiod_line_request_input, gpiod_line_request_output, gpiod_line_get_value, gpiod_line_set_value), not wiringPi, to control a 5V relay connected to physical GPIO17 upon detecting motion from an HC-SR501 PIR sensor on physical GPIO4, simulating a door strike. Open the gpiochip by name (gpiochip0) and request the two lines explicitly, checking every libgpiod call for errors and logging failures to the system journal via syslog(3). When motion is detected (PIR reads HIGH), energize the relay (drive GPIO17 HIGH) for a 1-second strike duration, then de-energize it (LOW), polling the PIR pin every 50 ms. As a failsafe, if the PIR sensor remains HIGH for more than 10 seconds continuously, de-energize the relay and log a LOG_WARNING entry to the system journal describing a potential malfunction. Log all state transitions (motion detected, relay on/off, failsafe trigger, shutdown) via syslog. Implement clean shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM: release all GPIO lines, close the chip, close the log, and exit, ensuring the relay is driven LOW before releasing the line.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to control a 4-channel active-LOW relay module connected to GPIO4, GPIO17, GPIO27, and GPIO22, implementing a timed sequence to simulate a simple automated irrigation system. The relay module is active-LOW (LOW = ON, HIGH = OFF); initialize all relays to OFF (HIGH) at startup. Activate each relay sequentially for 5 minutes (300 seconds), with a 1-minute (60 seconds) pause between each activation, looping back to the 1st relay after the 4th. Log every relay state change (activation and deactivation) with timestamps to the system syslog using openlog/syslog with the identifier 'irrigation_system'; do not use UDP networking. Check every pigpio call (gpioInitialise, gpioSetMode, gpioWrite, gpioSetTimerFuncEx) and log failures to syslog before exiting cleanly. Use gpioSetTimerFuncEx with a single timer (timer 0) that fires every 60 seconds, maintaining an internal state machine that tracks whether the current action is a relay activation, deactivation, or pause, and keep the program alive with a sleep loop checking a volatile sig_atomic_t flag. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM: deactivate all relays (set HIGH), release GPIO resources via gpioTerminate(), close syslog, and exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads acceleration data from an MPU6050 connected via I2C at default address 0x68 on bus /dev/i2c-1, opening the I2C device directly with open()/ioctl() rather than wiringPi. Initialize the MPU6050 by waking it (PWR_MGMT_1 = 0x00) and setting the accelerometer range to +-2g (ACCEL_CONFIG = 0x00). Sample the X, Y, and Z acceleration values at a consistent 100 Hz using a POSIX per-process timer (SIGEV_SIGNAL), reading the 6 bytes starting at ACCEL_XOUT_H (0x3B) and scaling raw values by 16384.0 to get g, then log them to a circular buffer. Provide a sysfs interface (e.g. /sys/kernel/mpu6050_accel/latest) to read the latest buffered data. Check all I2C syscalls, handle sensor-absent paths, and cleanly release all resources — the I2C file descriptor, sysfs files, timer, and memory — on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library (v1 API), not the deprecated wiringPi library, to control four 5V relay modules connected to physical GPIO pins 18, 23, 24, and 25 (BCM numbering), simulating a smart lighting system that toggles each light based on a unique prime number interval: 2, 3, 5, and 7 seconds respectively. Use clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) for non-rolling-over interval timing. Include robust error handling: check all libgpiod calls, handle GPIO chip/line request failures gracefully, and ensure all relays are turned off on exit. Implement clean resource release on all exit paths, including handling SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to monitor a KY-038 sound sensor's digital OUT pin connected to GPIO17. When sound above the threshold is detected (digital output goes HIGH), trigger a 5V relay connected to GPIO27 for exactly 3 seconds, simulating an alarm, and log the timestamp of each activation to 'alarm_log.txt'. Poll at a 100 ms interval, and add a debounce/cooldown mechanism so the relay is not retriggered while already active. Check all pigpio API return values and handle initialization errors, and use signal handling (SIGINT, SIGTERM) for graceful shutdown, ensuring the relay is turned off and pigpio is deinitialized on all exit paths. Focus only on GPIO monitoring, relay control, and file logging — do not include networking features.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads X, Y, and Z axis angular velocities from an MPU-6050 gyroscope connected to the Pi's hardware I2C1 bus (GPIO2/SDA and GPIO3/SCL) at default address 0x68, using the modern Linux I2C user-space API via <linux/i2c-dev.h> and <sys/ioctl.h> (open(), ioctl(I2C_SLAVE), read(), write(), close()), not wiringPi. Initialize the sensor by waking it up (clearing the sleep bit in PWR_MGMT_1 at register 0x6B) and verify the device by reading the WHO_AM_I register (0x75), which must return 0x68. Read the gyroscope data registers starting at GYRO_XOUT_H (0x43) for all 6 bytes, using a gyroscope sensitivity of 131.0 LSB/(deg/s) for the default +-250 dps range, and log the data to a 100-sample in-memory circular buffer. Trigger a user-defined callback function when the absolute angular velocity (the magnitude of the X, Y, Z vector) exceeds a threshold of 50.0 degrees/second. Implement robust error handling for I2C communication failures (e.g., sensor absent, bus errors, read/write failures) and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown on SIGINT (Ctrl+C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to read CO2 concentration from an MH-Z19B sensor over UART on /dev/serial0 at 9600 baud (TXD on GPIO14, RXD on GPIO15), acting as an indoor air quality monitor. Initialise pigpio and open the serial port with serOpen, checking every return value; do not configure TXD/RXD as GPIO manually. Send the 9-byte read command {0xFF,0x01,0x86,0x00,0x00,0x00,0x00,0x00,0x79}, wait about 100 ms, then read exactly 9 bytes with serRead, retrying partial reads until all 9 bytes arrive or a 1-second timeout elapses. Validate the response checksum (sum of bytes 1-7, inverted and incremented by 1, compared to byte 8); on mismatch, log the error and skip the reading. Extract CO2 as (response[2] << 8) | response[3]. Every 5 seconds, append one JSON object per line to co2_log.json with a microsecond timestamp, the ppm value, and an error flag, flushing the file after each write, and print the same JSON to stdout to simulate sending it to a remote server. Log all pigpio, serial, and file errors with timestamps to co2_error.log. Use only serOpen, serClose, serRead, serWrite, and serDataAvailable — not serFlush, which the userspace pigpio API lacks. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, close the UART and log files and terminate pigpio cleanly. Compile with gcc -Wall -Wextra -o co2_monitor co2_monitor.c -lpigpio -lrt.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to continuously read heading data from an HMC5883L magnetometer on I2C bus 1 at address 0x1E. Configure the sensor with CONFIG_A (register 0x00) set to 0x70 (8-average, 15 Hz output rate, normal measurement), CONFIG_B (register 0x01) set to 0x20 (1.3 Gauss gain), and MODE (register 0x02) set to 0x00 (continuous measurement). Read 6 bytes starting at register 0x03 in a single burst transaction; the sensor outputs data as X, Z, Y, MSB first. Compensate for hard-iron distortion using pre-calibrated offsets X=100, Y=-50, then drive GPIO17 (BCM) high if the compensated heading deviates more than 10 degrees from a user-defined target heading of 90.0 degrees, otherwise drive it low. Sample every 100 ms. Handle I2C errors by logging and retrying rather than crashing, and log each compensated heading into an in-memory circular buffer of 100 entries, overwriting the oldest entry when full. Implement clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that implements a smart lighting system, using libgpiod to drive three 5V relay modules on BCM GPIO17, GPIO27, and GPIO22, and reads ambient light from a BH1750 sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x23 through the Linux i2c-dev ioctl interface. Configure the BH1750 for continuous high-resolution mode (0x10) and wait at least 120 ms for the first conversion; read the 2-byte lux value and compute lux = raw / 1.2. Drive the relays by lux thresholds: below 50 turn on the RED relay, 50-150 the GREEN relay, 150-300 the BLUE relay, and above 300 turn on all three. Every 1 second, log the timestamp, lux value, and relay states to lighting_log.txt. Check every I2C and file I/O call, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and release all GPIO lines, the I2C file descriptor, and the log file on every exit path, including SIGINT and SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to independently control two DC motors driven by an L298N controller: Motor A on GPIO17 (IN1) and GPIO18 (IN2), Motor B on GPIO22 (IN3) and GPIO23 (IN4). Each motor is controlled from its own simulated ultrasonic distance sensor reading (range 10-100 cm, already sampled and passed as an argument — do not call random number generators inside the motor-control function). Map distance to a PWM duty cycle so closer obstacles drive higher speed (255 at 10 cm, 0 at 100 cm), clamped to [0,255], using a 1 kHz PWM frequency with a 0-255 range on the IN2/IN4 pins. Per motor, if distance is below 50 cm drive forward (IN1/IN3 high, IN2/IN4 PWM duty); if 50 cm or above, drive backward (IN1/IN3 low, IN2/IN4 PWM duty). Run the control loop every 100 ms. Check gpioInitialise() and every gpio call for failure, and ensure the motors stop and pigpio cleans up on every exit path, including SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program using the pigpio library on a Raspberry Pi to drive a 28BYJ-48 unipolar stepper motor through an L293D H-bridge, simulating an automatic door lock. Drive the coils in full-step (two-phase) mode with the standard 4-step sequence on BCM GPIO17, GPIO18, GPIO27, and GPIO22 (mapped to L293D inputs IN1-IN4), using a 2 ms inter-step delay. A momentary button on BCM GPIO24 (wired to ground, internal pull-up, active-low) rotates the motor 512 steps (a quarter turn) clockwise to lock; a momentary button on BCM GPIO23 (same wiring) rotates 512 steps counter-clockwise to unlock. Prevent re-triggering while a button is held down. Handle pigpio initialisation failure and check every GPIO configuration return code. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, de-energize the motor coils and release all pigpio resources before exiting. Print console feedback for lock and unlock actions and for exit events.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses an MPU-6050 accelerometer/gyroscope on I2C (SDA GPIO2, SCL GPIO3, bus /dev/i2c-1, address 0x68) to detect tilt and drive a PWM-controlled servo on GPIO18 (hardware PWM via sysfs at /sys/class/pwm/pwmchip2/pwm0) to adjust a miniature solar panel's angle. Access I2C through ioctl and linux/i2c-dev.h, with exponential-backoff retries on sensor-absent or bus-error paths. Log timestamped, comma-separated pitch, roll, and servo position values to solar_tracker.log. Release all resources cleanly on every exit path via SIGINT and SIGTERM signal handling. Do not use external networking or JSON libraries — limit the program to local sensor reading, PWM control, and file logging.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to control four relay-controlled lamp actuators on GPIO4, GPIO17, GPIO27, and GPIO22, simulating a smart home lighting system with a sunrise/sunset effect driven by a 24-hour schedule read from lighting_schedule.txt (format HH:MM:SS,relay_number,on/off). Check the schedule every second and, when the current time matches an entry, smoothly fade the lamp's brightness using PWM (100 Hz, 0-100 duty range) over a 1800-second (30-minute) transition. Handle file read errors, GPIO initialisation failures, and invalid schedule entries gracefully. Use SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling to turn off all relays and release GPIO resources cleanly on exit, and avoid calling non-reentrant functions such as fopen and localtime inside the signal handler.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to build a rudimentary theremin from an HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor (trigger on GPIO23, echo on GPIO24) and a PWM buzzer on GPIO18. Linearly map distances from 2 cm to 30 cm to frequencies from 200 Hz to 2000 Hz, clamping the result to that range before applying it. Generate the 10 microsecond trigger pulse with gpioDelay and measure the echo pulse width with microsecond-precision gpioTick timing. Run the main loop at roughly 50 Hz with at least a 60 ms gap between measurements to avoid trigger/echo overlap. Handle pigpio initialisation and HC-SR04 read failures robustly, including sensor-absent and timeout paths, logging failures to stderr. On SIGINT, silence the buzzer and deinitialise pigpio before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to simulate a color-based proximity alert. Drive a common-anode RGB LED, with red, green, and blue elements on GPIO17, GPIO22, and GPIO27 respectively through current-limiting resistors, using pigpio hardware PWM at 1 kHz so the LED smoothly transitions between red, green, and blue based on a simulated proximity value in the range 0.0 to 1.0, generated internally (for example from a sine wave over time) rather than read from a network socket. Handle pigpio initialisation errors gracefully and check every GPIO operation. On every exit path, including SIGINT, turn off the LED and call gpioTerminate to release resources cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to read angular velocity from an MPU-6050 gyroscope on I2C bus /dev/i2c-1 (SDA GPIO2, SCL GPIO3) at address 0x68, using the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (open/ioctl/read on /dev/i2c-1) rather than wiringPi, which is deprecated. Wake the sensor by writing 0x00 to PWR_MGMT_1 (register 0x6B), then read the 6 bytes of gyroscope data starting at register 0x43 with a block read. Convert each signed 16-bit value to degrees/second using the ±250 deg/s sensitivity factor of 131.0 LSB/(deg/s). Every 100 ms, log a timestamped x, y, z reading to gyro_log.txt. Check the return value of every open, ioctl, read, and write call, handling sensor-absent paths, and close all file descriptors cleanly on SIGINT or SIGTERM. No network logging or configuration-file parsing is required.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to implement a musical doorbell. A button on GPIO17 (internal pull-up enabled, active-low) triggers playback of a custom melody stored in a const lookup table in flash memory, played through a piezo buzzer on GPIO18 (hardware PWM0) using gpioHardwarePWM() for tone generation at a 50% duty cycle for volume. Debounce the button with a minimum 50 ms gap between presses; a second press during playback must gracefully stop the melody. Check the return value of every pigpio call, including gpioInitialise, gpioSetMode, gpioSetISRFuncEx, and gpioHardwarePWM. The interrupt handler must not block — use a volatile flag checked by the main loop to control playback. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, stop the PWM, release all resources, and call gpioTerminate for a clean shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the libgpiod API (gpiod_line_request_input, gpiod_line_event_wait, gpiod_line_event_read) to read an SW-420 vibration sensor's active-high digital output on GPIO17 (physical pin 11), rather than the deprecated sysfs /sys/class/gpio interface. Poll for both rising and falling edges, using a poll timeout in milliseconds taken as a single command-line argument (default 1000 ms if omitted). Log every edge event with an ISO-8601 timestamp and the raw value (0 or 1) to vibration_events.log, opening the file once and flushing or fsyncing after each write rather than reopening it per event; handle file open/write errors gracefully without terminating. Implement a basic earthquake early-warning simulation: maintain a sliding window of the last 5 events, and if 3 or more of them read HIGH, print an EARTHQUAKE ALERT message with the timestamp to the console. Check every libgpiod call and syscall for errors, printing diagnostics to stderr. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag so the main loop exits cleanly, releasing the line and closing the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads calibrated magnetic-field data from an LSM303DLHC magnetometer over I2C and logs it to a CSV file named mag_log.csv, using the Linux I2C-dev interface (/dev/i2c-1, linux/i2c-dev.h, ioctl-based SMBus reads/writes) rather than wiringPi, which is deprecated and unmaintained. The magnetometer's 7-bit I2C address is 0x1E, with SDA on physical pin 3 (GPIO2) and SCL on physical pin 5 (GPIO3). Configure continuous-conversion mode by writing 0x00 to MR_REG_M (register 0x02), and optionally set the output data rate to 15 Hz by writing 0x14 to CRA_REG_M (register 0x00). Read the six data registers 0x03-0x08 (X MSB, X LSB, Z MSB, Z LSB, Y MSB, Y LSB) and assemble them into signed 16-bit X, Y, and Z values. Apply hard-iron calibration offsets X_OFFSET=10, Y_OFFSET=-5, Z_OFFSET=20 to produce calibrated float values, then compute the compass heading in degrees from the calibrated X and Y values using atan2f, normalized to 0-360 degrees, and map it to one of eight compass directions (N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW), printing the direction and numeric heading to the console. Once per second, append a row to mag_log.csv with columns Timestamp, Calibrated X, Calibrated Y, Calibrated Z, Heading, writing a header row first if the file does not already exist. Check the return value of every open, ioctl, read, write, and fopen call; on an I2C read failure, print a diagnostic to stderr and skip that sample rather than crashing. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so Ctrl+C cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and the CSV file, freeing all resources on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to toggle a 5V relay on GPIO17 via a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor on GPIO4. The TTP223 outputs HIGH (3.3 V) on touch and LOW when released; configure GPIO4 with a pull-down resistor. Debounce touches in software with a minimum 200 ms gap between registered touches inside the ISR callback, and on each valid touch toggle the relay and append a JSON object to relay_log.json in the form {"timestamp":"<ISO 8601>","relay_state":"ON|OFF"}. Check every pigpio call for errors and abort cleanly if gpioInitialise() or gpioSetISRFunc() fails. On SIGINT, turn the relay OFF, append a final OFF entry to the log, and call gpioTerminate() before exiting. Do not use any deprecated library such as wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the libgpiod library (not wiringPi, which is deprecated) to run a smart irrigation system controlling four 5V relay modules on BCM GPIO17, GPIO23, GPIO24, and GPIO25. Open the gpiochip once and request the four lines as outputs with an inactive (OFF) drive of 1, since the relays are active-low; do not call the setup function more than once. Every 10 seconds, generate a simulated soil-moisture value from 0 to 100 using rand(), seeded once at startup. If the moisture reading is below 30, sequentially activate each relay (drive the line to 0) for 5 seconds, then deactivate it (drive to 1), leaving a 1-second gap between relays. Log every activation with an ISO-8601 timestamp, relay number, and moisture level to irrigation_log.txt in append mode, flushing after each write. Check every libgpiod call and file operation for errors, printing diagnostics to stderr. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, deactivate all relays, release the lines, close the chip and the log file, and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to run a miniature automated plant watering system with two SG90 servo motors: a water valve servo on GPIO17 (physical pin 11) and a directional nozzle servo on GPIO18 (physical pin 12), driven by simulated soil-moisture readings that cycle every second through the hardcoded values 20, 40, 60, 80, 100. Control both servos with gpioServo() using pulse widths in the 500-2500 microsecond range (500 us is about 0 degrees, 1500 us about 90 degrees, 2500 us about 180 degrees): the valve servo is closed at 0 degrees and open at 90 degrees, and the nozzle servo sweeps through 0, 45, 90, 135, and 180 degrees during watering. If the moisture reading is below the 50 threshold, open the valve to 90 degrees, sweep the nozzle through all five angles at 2 seconds per step, hold for 5 seconds, then close the valve to 0 degrees; if it is 50 or above, skip watering. After each cycle, wait 5 seconds before reading the next moisture value. Check the return value of gpioInitialise() and exit on failure. Retry each gpioServo() call up to 3 times with a 100 ms backoff on failure; abort the watering cycle if the valve fails to open, print a critical warning if it fails to close, and log an error and continue to the next angle if a nozzle position fails. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM using volatile sig_atomic_t flags: stop both servos with gpioServo(..., 0), call gpioTerminate(), and exit cleanly, never calling gpio functions before gpioInitialise() or after gpioTerminate() in the signal handler. Compile with gcc -Wall -Wextra -O2 -o watering watering.c -lpigpio -lrt.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to read X, Y, and Z axis angular velocities from an MPU-6050 gyroscope on I2C bus 1 (GPIO2=SDA, GPIO3=SCL) at address 0x68, using the Linux I2C-dev interface (/dev/i2c-1 via linux/i2c-dev.h and sys/ioctl.h) instead of the deprecated wiringPi. Wake the sensor by writing 0x00 to PWR_MGMT_1 (register 0x6B), then read the 6 bytes of gyroscope data starting at GYRO_XOUT_H (register 0x43) with a burst read. Convert the raw 16-bit big-endian values to degrees/second using the ±250 deg/sec sensitivity factor of 131.0 LSB/(deg/s). Sample at 10 Hz and log each timestamped reading to gyro_log.txt in CSV format (timestamp, x, y, z). Check every I2C syscall, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release — closing all file descriptors — on every exit path via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program using the pigpio library on a Raspberry Pi to drive a 28BYJ-48 unipolar stepper motor through an L293D motor driver, simulating an automatic door lock with full-step (single-coil) excitation. Drive the coils on BCM GPIO4, GPIO17, GPIO27, and GPIO22 (mapped to L293D inputs IN1-IN4) with a 3 ms inter-step delay. Two momentary push-buttons use internal pull-ups: LOCK on BCM GPIO24 and UNLOCK on BCM GPIO23 (active-low). Pressing LOCK rotates the motor 512 steps clockwise (about a quarter turn); pressing UNLOCK rotates 512 steps counter-clockwise. Check the return value of gpioInitialise() and report an error on failure, and check every gpioWrite, gpioSetMode, and gpioSetPullUpDown return code. De-energize all coils after each rotation completes to reduce power consumption and motor heating. Handle SIGINT by de-energizing the coils and calling gpioTerminate(). Debounce button reads with a short delay so a single press does not trigger multiple rotations, and print clear console messages for lock and unlock actions and for errors.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B (64-bit, Bookworm) that reads distance from an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor once per second and logs the value in centimeters to distance_log.txt, using the libgpiod v2.x API (gpiod.h) rather than wiringPi, which is deprecated. Request the trigger line on BCM GPIO17 as output and the echo line on BCM GPIO18 as input with active-high polarity. Generate a 10 microsecond high pulse on the trigger, then measure the echo pulse width with a busy-wait loop using a 50 ms timeout for both the rising and falling edges; convert the pulse width to distance with distance_cm = duration_us * 0.01715 (speed of sound 343 m/s). On timeout or any libgpiod call failure, log "-1" to the file and print an error to stderr; also report GPIO initialisation failures to stderr. Open the log file once in append mode at startup and keep it open for the program's lifetime. Enforce a 60 ms minimum guard between measurements to avoid false echoes. Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM by releasing all libgpiod resources and closing the log file. Assume the HC-SR04's 5 V echo output is reduced to 3.3 V by a voltage divider or level shifter before reaching the Pi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B implementing a proximity-based automated door system using a VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor on I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x29, with the pigpio library used for both I2C and GPIO control. Perform a software reset of the VL53L1X (register 0x0000 = 0x00), then initialise it by setting the ranging mode and starting continuous ranging (register 0x0080 = 0x01). Poll the sensor every 100 ms: check the interrupt status register 0x0044 for data readiness, then read the 16-bit distance result from registers 0x0096 (MSB) and 0x0097 (LSB). Log the current distance to stdout each cycle, and drive a relay on BCM GPIO18 HIGH to simulate opening the door when the distance is 50 cm or less, otherwise LOW. Check every pigpio and I2C return value, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and log all errors to stderr. On SIGINT, close the I2C handle, set the relay LOW, and terminate pigpio for a clean shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to read angular velocity from an MPU-6050 gyroscope on the hardware I2C bus (GPIO2/SDA, GPIO3/SCL) at address 0x68, using the Linux i2c-dev ioctl interface on /dev/i2c-1 — libgpiod has no I2C API, so it cannot be used for this, and wiringPi is deprecated. Initialise the sensor by waking it from sleep (PWR_MGMT_1, register 0x6B) and setting the gyroscope full-scale range to ±250 dps (GYRO_CONFIG, register 0x1B). Continuously read the 6 bytes of gyroscope data starting at register 0x43, convert the raw signed 16-bit big-endian values to degrees/second using the 131.0 LSB/dps sensitivity factor, and log the x, y, and z axis readings to the console. Check every I2C read/write syscall, handling sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths using SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the libgpiod v1 API to control four 5V relay modules on BCM GPIO17, GPIO18, GPIO27, and GPIO22 (physical pins 11, 12, 13, 15), rather than the deprecated sysfs /sys/class/gpio interface or wiringPi. Open gpiochip0 and request all four lines as outputs with active-low semantics, setting all lines HIGH (inactive) at startup.
