Simulate an automated plant watering system that activates each relay sequentially for 5 seconds every 86400 seconds (24 hours), starting immediately on launch, and log each watering cycle's start time in 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS' format to watering_log.txt. Run the main loop on a 60-second polling interval. Check every libgpiod call and file I/O operation for errors, including the case where the GPIO chip cannot be opened. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that releases all GPIO lines, closes the chip, and exits cleanly. Compile with gcc -o watering watering.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library (rather than the deprecated wiringPi) to control four SRD-05VDC relay modules on BCM GPIO17, GPIO18, GPIO27, and GPIO22 (equivalent to wiringPi pins 0, 1, 2, 3), simulating a smart lighting 'sunrise' effect that gradually raises light intensity over 30 minutes using hardware PWM to simulate dimming. Run the sunrise simulation in 1-second steps, incrementing the duty cycle progressively across all four relays simultaneously, using a 1 kHz PWM frequency with duty cycles from 0 to 255. Check the return value of gpioInitialise(), verify each GPIO pin's mode setup, and handle PWM initialisation failures gracefully. Log every event with a timestamp to smart_lighting.log. Implement clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT and SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) for both I2C and GPIO to read angular velocity from a single MPU-6050 gyroscope on I2C bus 1 (address 0x68, GPIO2=SDA, GPIO3=SCL). Initialise the sensor by writing 0x00 to PWR_MGMT_1 (register 0x6B) to wake it, 0x07 to SMPLRT_DIV (register 0x19) for a 1 kHz sample rate, and 0x00 to GYRO_CONFIG (register 0x1B) for the ±250 deg/s full-scale range (131 LSB/deg/s sensitivity); do not configure the accelerometer. Verify the WHO_AM_I register (0x75) reads 0x68 during initialisation to confirm the sensor is present. At 20 Hz (a 50 ms period), read the 6 bytes of gyroscope data starting at GYRO_XOUT_H (register 0x43), convert the signed 16-bit big-endian values to degrees/second, and store each reading with its timestamp in a 100-entry in-memory circular buffer. Turn on an LED on GPIO17 whenever the absolute value of any axis exceeds 250 deg/s, and turn it off when all axes drop below that threshold. Check every pigpio call for errors: if I2C initialisation fails, print an error and exit; if a read fails, attempt re-initialisation up to 3 times before exiting. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, close the I2C handle, set the GPIO low, and call gpioTerminate() for a clean shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to read X, Y, and Z axis angular rates from an MPU-9250 gyroscope over SPI, using the standard Linux spidev interface with libgpiod for chip-select control rather than the unmaintained bcm2835 library. Open /dev/spidev0.0 and configure SPI at 1 MHz, mode 0, 8 bits per word, MSB first. Manually control chip select on GPIO8 (CE0) via libgpiod (/dev/gpiochip0, line offset 8), asserting it LOW during transfers and HIGH otherwise. Every 10 ms, read gyroscope data from registers 0x43-0x48 (GYRO_XOUT_H through GYRO_ZOUT_L) as a single 6-byte burst, and convert the raw 16-bit two's-complement values to degrees per second using a scale factor of 131.0 for the ±250 dps range. Log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp including nanoseconds to gyro_log.txt in CSV format: timestamp,x_rate,y_rate,z_rate. Retry SPI communication errors up to 3 times; on persistent failure, log to stderr and continue. Handle file write errors gracefully, and check every system and library call. Clean up the SPI handle, the GPIO chip-select line, and the log file on SIGINT/SIGTERM. The program should run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to read angular velocity from an InvenSense MPU-6050 gyroscope over SPI (SPI mode, not I2C), using the Linux spidev interface with libgpiod for manual chip-select control on GPIO8 (CE0) — not bcm2835, which is unmaintained, and not wiringPi. Configure SPI at approximately 3.9 MHz, mode 0, asserting the CE0 chip-select line via libgpiod for each transfer. Read gyroscope X, Y, and Z axis data from registers 0x43, 0x45, and 0x47 (high bytes) with auto-increment disabled, using single-byte reads, and convert the raw 16-bit two's-complement values to degrees per second using the 131.0 LSB/(deg/s) sensitivity factor. Store each reading, with its timestamp, in a 64-entry in-memory circular buffer. If any axis exceeds ±200 deg/s, blink an LED on GPIO17 (physical pin 11) with 500 ms on/off intervals. Handle SPI initialisation failures and sensor read failures (check for zero or invalid data). On SIGINT (Ctrl+C), print the entire circular buffer as CSV with columns Timestamp, X, Y, Z, then release the SPI handle and GPIO resources on every exit path. The program should simulate a basic stability monitoring system.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library (not wiringPi) — pigpio has no support for the Raspberry Pi 5's RP1 I/O controller, so the earlier Pi 4 Model B is used instead — to read tilt from an MPU-6050 accelerometer/gyroscope on I2C bus 1 at address 0x68. Wake the sensor by writing 0x00 to PWR_MGMT_1 (register 0x6B) and set the accelerometer full-scale range to ±2g by writing 0x00 to ACCEL_CONFIG (register 0x1C), verifying successful configuration. Every 100 ms, read the 6 bytes of raw accelerometer data from registers 0x3B-0x40, and compute roll = atan2(y, z) * 180/pi and pitch = atan2(-x, sqrt(y^2 + z^2)) * 180/pi. Turn on an LED on GPIO21 if the absolute roll exceeds 45 degrees or the absolute pitch exceeds 45 degrees, otherwise turn it off. Log each reading to tilt_log.txt in CSV format with a timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS), roll, and pitch, and print roll and pitch to the console each cycle. Check the I2C open, sensor initialisation, and every read operation; on a sensor read failure, log the error and continue without crashing. On SIGINT (Ctrl+C), turn off the LED, close the I2C handle, and terminate pigpio, with signal handling and resource cleanup on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to interface with a Si1145 optical biometric sensor (assumed register-compatible with the Si1182-A-GM) over I2C, using the Linux I2C-dev interface (/dev/i2c-1, ioctl, read/write) for the sensor and libgpiod (gpiod_line_set_value, etc.) for GPIO — not wiringPi and not pigpio. The sensor is at I2C address 0x5A (8-bit). Read the 2-byte little-endian ambient-light value from register 0x20 and the 2-byte little-endian proximity value from register 0x22 every 100 ms. Log each timestamped reading in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,AmbientLight:XXXX,Proximity:XXXX' to biometric_log.txt in append mode. If the proximity value exceeds 100, set GPIO17 high to simulate a presence-detected LED; otherwise set it low. Handle I2C communication errors with up to 3 retries and a 10 ms delay between attempts. Install SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handlers for graceful cleanup: close the I2C file descriptor, close the log file, and turn off the LED.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library for SPI and GPIO (not wiringPi) to read angular rate data from an Analog Devices ADXRS290 dual-axis gyroscope on SPI channel 0 (CE0, GPIO8) at a 1 MHz clock, SPI mode 0 (CPOL=0, CPHA=0). The X and Y axis angular-rate registers are at addresses 0x02 and 0x04; each returns 16-bit two's-complement data, high byte first. To read a register, send its address OR'd with 0x80 (the read bit) followed by a dummy byte — the response is the second byte of the transfer. The sensitivity is 200 LSB/deg/s. Sample both axes at approximately 100 Hz (a 10 ms delay between samples) and log each sample to gyro_data.csv with columns: timestamp (seconds since epoch, microsecond precision), X rate (raw int16), and Y rate (raw int16). If a read fails, attempt to reinitialise SPI up to 3 times before exiting. Check every pigpio call (gpioInitialise, spiOpen, spiXfer) and file operation for errors. Use a SIGINT handler to cleanly close SPI, flush and close the file, and terminate pigpio, releasing all resources on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to detect seismic activity with two Omron D7E-2 tilt sensors on BCM GPIO23 and GPIO24. The D7E-2 is a normally-open mechanical tilt switch that closes to ground when tilted beyond about 60 degrees; wire each sensor between its GPIO pin and 3.3V with a 10 kOhm pull-down resistor to ground, so the GPIO reads HIGH when tilted. Register edge-triggered pigpio callbacks for both rising and falling edges on each sensor. When both sensors simultaneously read HIGH for a continuous duration of at least 500 milliseconds, trigger an alert by setting GPIO17 HIGH for 2 seconds, then LOW. Log each seismic event to seismic_events.txt with an ISO-8601-style timestamp, e.g. '2024-01-15 14:30:00 - Seismic event detected!'. Check pigpio initialisation, the log file open, and callback registration for errors. Install SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handlers that close the log file, set the alert pin LOW, and terminate pigpio. The program should run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads an Analog Devices ADXRS290 dual-axis MEMS gyroscope over the hardware SPI0 bus (CE0 on GPIO8, SCLK on GPIO11, MOSI on GPIO10, MISO on GPIO9) using only the pigpio library, not wiringPi. Continuously read the 16-bit two's-complement X-axis angular-rate register (RATE_XL at address 0x02 and RATE_XH at address 0x03), combine the bytes, and convert to degrees per second using the 200 LSB/deg/s sensitivity. For each SPI read, set the MSB (bit 7) of the register address to 1 to indicate a read, transmit the address, and read the data payload, using a 1 MHz SPI clock and mode 0 (CPOL=0, CPHA=0). Timestamp each reading with clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) and store it in a thread-safe, in-memory circular buffer with a capacity of 100 entries. If the absolute angular velocity exceeds a threshold of 20.0 deg/s, turn on an LED on GPIO17 as a visual warning, turning it off again once the rate drops back below the threshold. Check the return values of all pigpio initialisation and SPI transfer calls, and on SIGINT or SIGTERM exit gracefully with proper resource cleanup: close SPI, turn off the LED, and terminate pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W implementing a 'smart sunset simulator' with three relay-controlled dimmable lamps on GPIO17, GPIO18, and GPIO27 (physical pins 11, 12, 13), using the pigpio library's hardware PWM rather than the sysfs PWM interface. Accept a single command-line argument: the total fade duration in seconds (integer, 1-3600). Fade each lamp sequentially from full brightness (100% PWM duty cycle) to off (0%) over the specified duration, with each lamp starting its fade only after the previous one completes, using a PWM range of 0-255 at 100 Hz. Validate the user-supplied duration and check every pigpio initialisation call. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully by turning off all lamps and releasing resources, ensuring proper cleanup on every exit path. Print status messages at startup, during each lamp's fade, and upon completion or termination.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using libgpiod (not wiringPi, which is deprecated) to drive four 5V relay modules on BCM GPIO17, GPIO22, GPIO23, and GPIO24 as a traffic light simulator. The relays are active-low (LOW turns a relay ON, HIGH turns it OFF). Cycle through the states red (10 seconds), red+yellow (2 seconds), green (10 seconds), and yellow (3 seconds), then repeat indefinitely. Check libgpiod initialisation, the chip open, the line request, and every GPIO operation for errors. Use SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling to gracefully release all GPIO lines and exit. Print each state transition to stdout. The program should run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library — chosen because pigpio has no support for the Raspberry Pi 5's RP1 I/O controller — to control a 5V relay on GPIO17, triggered by a capacitive touch sensor MPR121 on I2C bus 1 at address 0x5A. The relay simulates a light switch: touching electrode 0 toggles it on or off. Initialise pigpio and set GPIO17 as output, default LOW. Open the I2C device at address 0x5A on bus 1 and configure the MPR121 by writing: reset (register 0x80 = 0x63), stop mode (0x5E = 0x00), enable electrode 0 (0x5D = 0x01), touch threshold (0x41 = 0x0A), release threshold (0x42 = 0x08), debounce (0x5B = 0x21), charge time (0x5C = 0x0D), and run mode (0x5E = 0x0D). Read the touch status from registers 0x00 (LSB) and 0x01 (MSB) every 10 ms, debouncing touch events with a 100 ms delay. Log all I2C, GPIO, and configuration errors with timestamps to touch_relay.log. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to cleanly close the I2C handle, the GPIO, and the log file. Use only pigpio functions, not wiringPi, and check every initialisation and I2C operation for errors, logging and exiting gracefully on failure.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the libgpiod GPIO interface — not the deprecated sysfs /sys/class/gpio interface, and not wiringPi — to monitor a KY-026 flame sensor's digital output on GPIO17 (active-low: LOW means flame detected). When flame is detected, activate a buzzer on GPIO18 and an LED on GPIO23; both remain active for as long as flame is detected and turn off once it clears. Debounce the sensor reading with three consecutive reads at 50 ms intervals. Log each flame-detection event with a timestamp and the message 'Flame Detected' to flame_log.txt. Implement robust error handling for all GPIO operations, release all resources on any error exit path, and handle SIGINT/SIGTERM for graceful cleanup by releasing the GPIO lines and closing the log file. The program simulates a basic fire alarm.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to control two 12V push-pull solenoids connected through TIP120 Darlington transistors to GPIO17 and GPIO27, simulating a simple pneumatic dispensing system. Initialise pigpio, handling initialisation failure by printing an error and exiting, and configure GPIO17 and GPIO27 as outputs with error checking. On each dispense cycle, activate solenoid 1 for half of a 1000 ms total dispense duration, then activate solenoid 2 for the remaining half, then deactivate both, using gpioDelay() (microseconds) for timing; repeat the dispense every 5 seconds in a continuous loop. Log each dispense event, with timestamp, solenoid pins, and duration in milliseconds, to dispense_log.txt, handling file open failures. Each function should return 0 on success and non-zero on failure, with main checking every return value and printing error messages to stderr. Register a SIGINT handler to gracefully deactivate both solenoids, terminate pigpio, and exit on Ctrl+C. Compile with -lpigpio.

Develop a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that controls two DC motors via an L298N dual H-bridge using only the pigpio library (gpioInitialise, gpioSetMode, gpioPWM, gpioWrite, gpioDelay, gpioTerminate — no wiringPi or other deprecated API). Motor A uses GPIO17 (forward) and GPIO18 (backward); Motor B uses GPIO22 (forward) and GPIO23 (backward); the L298N's enable pins ENA (GPIO24) and ENB (GPIO25) must be held HIGH to allow PWM control, with all motor speeds clamped to +/-255. Simulate a self-balancing robot: an internal PID controller (Kp=1.0, Ki=0.01, Kd=0.1) generates motor commands every 50 ms from a simulated tilt error (a random float between -10.0 and 10.0 degrees). Also simulate an ultrasonic distance sensor returning a random value between 2.0 and 400.0 cm; if the distance is below 20 cm, reverse both motors at 50% speed for obstacle avoidance. Handle pigpio initialisation failure by printing an error and returning 1; handle log file open failure by printing an error, terminating pigpio, and returning 1; on an invalid motor character, log the error and skip. On SIGINT, stop the motors, close the log file, and terminate pigpio gracefully. Log every control cycle to balance_log.txt with columns: timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS), tilt_error, distance, motor_a_speed, and motor_b_speed.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library (not wiringPi, which is deprecated) to toggle a 5V relay on GPIO17 (physical pin 11) using a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor on GPIO4 (physical pin 7), simulating a smart light switch: each touch toggles the relay on or off. The TTP223 outputs logic HIGH when touched; assume an external pull-down resistor, or configure the internal pull-down via pigpio. The relay is active-high, energized when GPIO17 is HIGH. Debounce each touch with a delay of at least 50 ms after detection. Check every pigpio initialisation call and GPIO operation, handling sensor-absent or bus-error conditions gracefully, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling. The program should run indefinitely until terminated by Ctrl+C.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to implement a 'mood light' driven by ambient noise from ALSA audio capture. Drive a common-cathode RGB LED on GPIO17 (red), GPIO18 (green), and GPIO27 (blue), each with a current-limiting resistor, using pigpio software PWM (gpioPWM) for smooth color control. Configure ALSA to capture from the 'default' device at 8000 Hz, 16-bit signed little-endian, 1 channel, with a period size of 1024 frames. Continuously read samples, compute the RMS amplitude, and map it to RGB PWM values using a non-linear transition — cool colors for low amplitude, warm colors for high amplitude. Accept an optional command-line sensitivity-scaling argument (default 1.0, must be positive). Check every pigpio and ALSA call: recover from buffer overruns (EPIPE) with snd_pcm_prepare, and from a suspended state (ESTRPIPE) with snd_pcm_resume. Include a 10 ms delay between updates, print status messages to stdout and errors to stderr, and release all resources — pigpio, ALSA, and allocated memory — on exit via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handlers. Gate ALSA support behind an ALSA_AVAILABLE compile-time macro: when ALSA is unavailable, simulate the audio input with a sine-wave amplitude so the mood light still cycles through colors, and ensure all exit paths remain clean with no resource leaks in either mode.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a TCS34725 color sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x29, using the pigpio library for both I2C and timing (gpioDelay for the 500 ms interval), simulating a color-based sorting system. Initialise the sensor with power-on and RGBC enable (register 0x80 = 0x03) and set the integration time to 154 ms (register 0x81 = 0xD5). Every 500 ms, read the calibrated clear, red, green, and blue values from the data registers starting at 0x14 (clear low byte) through 0x1A (blue high byte). Log the Unix-epoch timestamp and the four C, R, G, B values as a comma-separated line to color_data.csv, writing a header row first. Check every I2C open, write, and read operation; on failure, print an error to stderr, set the sensor's values to 0 for that cycle, and continue without crashing. Register SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handlers to close the I2C handle, close the file, and terminate pigpio cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library to implement a sunrise/sunset lighting simulator controlling four independent 5V relay modules connected to lamps. The relays are active-low and wired to physical pins 11, 13, 15, and 17 (BCM GPIO17, GPIO27, GPIO22, GPIO23). Cycle repeatedly and indefinitely through four phases: sunrise, a gradual brightness increase over 1 hour; daytime, full brightness for 6 hours; sunset, a gradual brightness decrease over 1 hour; and nighttime, off for 14.4 hours. Simulate brightness with PWM-like relay toggling rather than true PWM, using an increasing duty cycle during sunrise and a decreasing duty cycle during sunset, with all four lamps running the same phase simultaneously. Use only the libgpiod functions gpiod_chip_open_by_name, gpiod_line_get, gpiod_line_request_output, gpiod_line_set_value, gpiod_line_release, and gpiod_chip_close. Handle initialization failures from gpiod_chip_open_by_name and gpiod_line_request_output with clear error messages and a graceful exit. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, turn off all relays and release GPIO resources cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to detect motion with a Keyes KY-033 IR Obstacle Avoidance Sensor on GPIO 17 (physical pin 11), which outputs an active-low digital LOW signal when an obstacle is detected. On motion detection, execute raspivid to record a 5-second video saved to /home/pi/videos/ with a timestamp-based filename such as 20250321_143022.h264, and log each event with an ISO 8601 timestamp to /home/pi/logs/motion_log.txt. Implement debouncing with a 200 ms minimum interval between triggers. Handle errors gracefully by checking pigpio initialization, file operations, and system command execution. Install a SIGINT signal handler for clean shutdown that closes the log file and terminates pigpio, and keep the program running continuously until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read X, Y, and Z angular velocities from an MPU-6050 gyroscope over I2C bus 1 at address 0x68 (AD0 pin low), for a basic vibration monitoring system. Initialize the sensor by writing 0x00 to register 0x6B to wake it, 0x07 to register 0x19 to set the sample rate divider to 125 Hz, and 0x00 to register 0x1B to set the gyroscope full-scale range to ±250°/s. Read the raw signed 16-bit gyroscope values from registers 0x43-0x48 (X_H, X_L, Y_H, Y_L, Z_H, Z_L) using a combined I2C block read, and convert them to degrees per second using a sensitivity of 131.0 LSB/(°/s). Sample at 100 Hz (10 ms interval) and log each reading to gyro_log.csv with columns timestamp (Unix epoch seconds with millisecond precision), X_degps, Y_degps, Z_degps. On a read failure, attempt sensor re-initialization (re-wake and re-configure) up to 3 times before logging an error and continuing. Check every pigpio call (gpioInitialise, i2cOpen, i2cWriteByteData, i2cReadI2CBlockData). Use a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler to close the log file and release the I2C handle, and run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to control four SainSmart 5V relay modules on BCM GPIO pins 4, 17, 27, and 22 for a simulated smart greenhouse irrigation system. Each relay corresponds to one irrigation zone, and a simulated moisture sensor using rand() % 101 produces readings from 0 to 100 every 5 seconds, with the random generator seeded from time(NULL). If a zone's reading is below 30, drive its relay LOW to activate it, since the relays are active-low; otherwise drive it HIGH to deactivate it. Append each sensor reading, relay state, and a timestamp to irrigation_log.txt. Check pigpio initialization, the log file open, and every GPIO operation. On SIGINT or any error, safely deactivate all relays (drive HIGH), close the log file, and terminate pigpio, installing the handler with signal().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to read accelerometer data from an Analog Devices ADXL345 over I2C at address 0x53. Configure the sensor for ±2g range with full resolution by writing 0x0B to the DATA_FORMAT register (0x31), and enable measurement mode by writing 0x08 to the POWER_CTL register (0x2D). Every 100 ms, read 6 bytes starting from the DATAX0 register (0x32) for the X, Y, Z axis data, and convert the raw signed 16-bit values to g-force using a scale factor of 256 LSB/g. Detect a freefall event when all three axes have an absolute value below 0.2g for a continuous 0.5 seconds, confirmed by reading twice with a 0.5 second delay. On a confirmed freefall, drive GPIO27 high to simulate an alarm, hold it for 5 seconds, then set it low. Log each freefall event to freefall.log in CSV format with a timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS) and x, y, z values to 3 decimal places. Handle I2C errors by printing to stderr and continuing operation, checking every pigpio and I2C call. Use a SIGINT handler to close the I2C handle, set GPIO low, and terminate pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to measure distance with an interrupt-driven HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor, TRIG on GPIO4 and ECHO on GPIO18 (BCM numbering). Send a 10 µs trigger pulse every 200 ms and measure the echo pulse width using rising-edge and falling-edge interrupt callbacks, correctly handling wrap-around of the 32-bit tick counter, which wraps roughly every 71.6 minutes. If the echo pulse width exceeds 23200 µs (about 4 meters, the sensor's maximum range) or no echo arrives within 100 ms of the trigger, discard the reading. Log each valid distance measurement in centimeters with a nanosecond-precision timestamp to distance_log.txt in CSV format: timestamp_ns,distance_cm. Protect the shared pulse-timing variables, which are updated from interrupt context, with a mutex. Handle pigpio initialization failure, file open failure, invalid pulse widths, and sensor timeouts. Use a SIGINT handler to cancel callbacks, close the file, terminate pigpio, and destroy the mutex, and run the measurement loop indefinitely.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the pigpio library to read acceleration data from an Adafruit LIS3DH accelerometer over I2C bus 1 at address 0x18, implementing a basic fall detection system that triggers a buzzer on GPIO17. Initialize pigpio and I2C with error checking, and configure the LIS3DH for a 100 Hz data rate and ±2g full scale by writing 0x77 to CTRL_REG1 and 0x00 to CTRL_REG4. Continuously read 16-bit signed acceleration values starting from register OUT_X_L (0x28), converting to g using a sensitivity of 16384 LSB/g. Detect freefall when the acceleration magnitude drops below 0.2g, then detect impact when it exceeds 1.5g; on impact, activate the buzzer for 1 second. Accept optional command-line freefall and impact thresholds. Handle I2C communication failures with up to 3 retries and perform graceful cleanup on SIGINT. Handle sensor absence and bus errors robustly, and ensure resources are released on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to precisely control two 28BYJ-48 stepper motors, each driven through a ULN2003 board, simulating a basic CNC plotter that draws a simple square. Motor 1 (X-axis) uses IN1=GPIO4, IN2=GPIO17, IN3=GPIO27, IN4=GPIO22; Motor 2 (Y-axis) uses IN1=GPIO5, IN2=GPIO6, IN3=GPIO13, IN4=GPIO19. Assume the 28BYJ-48's 1/64 gear ratio gives 2048 steps per revolution, use a 1000 microsecond step delay, and drive the coils with a 4-step wave drive (single-coil excitation) sequence. Draw a square with 50 mm sides using a conversion factor of 10 steps per mm. Set all GPIO pins as outputs, checking the return of every gpioWrite and gpioSetMode call, and check pigpio initialization. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to safely stop both motors and release resources, handle any motor movement failures gracefully, and set all GPIO pins low before termination.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the pigpio library to read X, Y, and Z acceleration data from a single Adafruit LIS3DH accelerometer over I2C at address 0x18 (overridable via a -a hex argument, valid range 0x08-0x77). Configure the sensor for ±2g range, high-resolution mode (12-bit left-justified), and 100 Hz output data rate by writing 0x57 to CTRL_REG1 and 0x88 to CTRL_REG4. Read acceleration at 10 Hz (100 ms interval), computing g as the 16-bit signed raw value shifted right 4 bits, then scaled by 0.0009765625 (2g / 2048). If the absolute acceleration on any axis exceeds a user-defined threshold in g (default 2.0g, overridable via a -t float argument), log the event with timestamp and axis values to /var/log/high_acceleration.log, then immediately trigger a system shutdown via `sudo shutdown -h now`. Use the pigpio I2C functions i2cOpen, i2cReadI2CBlockData, and i2cWriteI2CBlockData, but use i2cWriteByteData for single-byte register writes since i2cWriteI2CBlockData returns 0 on success rather than a byte count. Support only one sensor. Handle I2C open/configuration errors with cleanup and exit, handle sensor read errors gracefully by returning zeros and continuing, and validate the I2C address range (0x08-0x77) and threshold (greater than 0) from the command line. Register a SIGINT handler that closes I2C and terminates pigpio, and allow a graceful exit with code 0 when pigpio initialization or I2C open fails in a non-hardware environment.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod API to autonomously navigate a line-following robot using a SunFounder 3-Way Tracking Sensor (IR reflectance, digital GPIO). Sensor pins are LEFT=GPIO4, CENTER=GPIO17, RIGHT=GPIO27, where 0 means a line is detected and 1 means no line; an alert pin on GPIO22 drives an active-high LED or buzzer. Poll the sensors every 10 ms and log each reading (left, center, right) into a circular buffer of size 5. If the center sensor reads 'no line' for 5 consecutive readings, drive GPIO22 HIGH for 2 seconds as an alert. Implement line-following logic: move forward when the center sensor detects a line, turn left when the left sensor detects a line, turn right when the right sensor detects a line, and stop when all three sensors read 'no line'; motor control functions may be placeholders. Check every libgpiod initialization and line-request return value, handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release on every exit path via SIGINT and SIGTERM handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read magnetic field data from a Silicon Labs Si7210 Hall effect sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x30, and trigger a relay on GPIO 17 (active high) when the field strength exceeds a 5.0 mT threshold, sampling every 100 ms. Perform a one-shot measurement by writing 0x01 to register 0xC1 to start a conversion, polling register 0xC1 until it reads 0x00, then reading 2 bytes from register 0xC0 (byte 0 LSB, byte 1 MSB) and combining them into a signed 16-bit value: field_raw = (msb << 8) | lsb. Convert to milliTesla units of 0.01 mT with field_mT_x100 = field_raw * 25 / 1000, and compare against threshold * 100. If register 0xC1 does not clear after 50 poll attempts, log a timeout error and skip the cycle. Check every pigpio call (gpioInitialise, i2cOpen, i2cReadByte, i2cWriteByte, i2cReadByteData, i2cWriteByteData); if i2cOpen fails, log the error and exit, and on any read/write failure, log the error, deactivate the relay, and retry on the next cycle. Append timestamped entries in ISO 8601 format to magnetic_events.txt for every field reading, relay state change, and error. Install a SIGINT handler that closes the I2C handle, deactivates the relay, terminates pigpio, and logs the shutdown.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library for GPIO control and listens for TCP commands on port 5000 to trigger a KY-019 relay module connected to GPIO 18 (BCM numbering). Accept the commands "ON" and "OFF", case-insensitive and ignoring trailing whitespace, to control the relay. Log every activation, deactivation, and invalid-command event with a timestamp to relay_log.txt. Implement comprehensive error handling for socket operations (socket creation, bind, listen, accept, read) and for GPIO initialization. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM so the server shuts down gracefully: close all sockets, close the log file, turn off the relay, and terminate pigpio, ensuring clean resource release on every exit path.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library, not wiringPi, to interface with two Sensirion SLF3S-1300F liquid flow sensors (40 ml/min version) on I2C bus 1: sensor 1 at address 0x08 and sensor 2 at 0x09. Initialize pigpio and open both I2C handles with flags=0, checking for errors and cleaning up partially-initialized resources on failure. Send the SLF3S start-measurement command (bytes 0x36, 0x08) to each sensor and verify the write returns 0, aborting with full cleanup on failure. Configure GPIO 18 (BCM) as an output and initialize it low (de-energized), checking the return code. In a 100 ms polling loop, read 3 bytes (2 data + 1 CRC-8) from each sensor and validate the CRC-8 (polynomial 0x31, init 0xFF, no final XOR); on a read error or CRC mismatch, log a warning to stderr and skip that cycle without updating the relay. Convert each signed 16-bit big-endian raw value to ml/min using the scale factor 1/1500.0. If both reads succeed and either sensor reports flow below 5.0 ml/min, energize GPIO 18 (active-high relay, write 1); de-energize (write 0) when both sensors are at or above 5.0 ml/min. Log every successful cycle's flow rates with millisecond timestamps to flow_log.txt in append mode, flushing after each write. Install a single SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that sets a volatile flag so the main loop can exit cleanly; on shutdown, de-energize the relay, close both I2C handles if open, call gpioTerminate(), and print a shutdown message. The code must compile cleanly with gcc -Wall -Wextra.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the pigpio library to implement a single-process rain-actuated window controller. A Seeed Studio Rain Sensor v1.0 on GPIO 17 (BCM), configured as input with a pull-up, pulls its DO pin LOW when rain is detected and HIGH when dry; poll it every 200 ms. An L298N drives the window-closing DC motor via ENA on GPIO 22, IN1 on GPIO 23, and IN2 on GPIO 24 (all BCM). Only trigger the close-window sequence on a rising-edge dry-to-wet transition, never re-triggering while rain persists: set ENA HIGH, IN1 HIGH, IN2 LOW, hold for 5 seconds, then set ENA LOW and both IN1/IN2 LOW to stop, verifying each gpioWrite call. After completing the sequence, suppress further triggers until the sensor reads dry for at least 3 consecutive polls (about 600 ms). Check gpioInitialise()'s return value, logging and exiting on failure, and check every gpioWrite return code, logging warnings on failure. Log via syslog (facility LOG_USER, identifier "rain_window") using LOG_INFO for startup, rain detected, motor start/stop, and shutdown, and LOG_ERR/LOG_WARNING for failures. Implement everything in a single process with one main loop, with no fork(). Use gpioDelay() or usleep(), never busy-waiting, for the 200 ms poll interval and the 5-second motor run. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown: stop the motor (all GPIOs LOW), call gpioTerminate(), close syslog, and exit cleanly.

Write a C program that uses the pigpio library to control a door-lock servo on a Raspberry Pi. The servo is connected to GPIO 18 (physical pin 12, BCM 18). Two momentary push-buttons are wired to GPIO 21 (BCM) and GPIO 22 (BCM), each connecting its pin to ground when pressed, so internal pull-ups must be enabled. Pressing the GPIO 21 button drives the servo to the locked position with a 2000 µs pulse width; pressing the GPIO 22 button drives it to the unlocked position with a 1000 µs pulse width. Check the return value of gpioInitialise() and exit with an error message on failure, and verify that gpioServo() succeeds for both pulse-width commands. Implement button debouncing so a single press is not registered multiple times, waiting for release plus a short debounce delay, and poll the buttons in a tight loop with a small sleep to avoid high CPU usage. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so Ctrl+C cleanly stops the servo (pulse width 0) and calls gpioTerminate() before exiting. Print status messages to stdout for lock, unlock, and shutdown events.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to implement a smart security light. Monitor a PIR motion sensor on GPIO 4 (physical pin 7, input). On a rising edge (motion detected), activate a relay-controlled 12V LED floodlight on GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, output) for exactly 60 seconds, then turn it off. Log every activation event with an ISO-8601 timestamp and every deactivation event with timestamp and measured duration in seconds to security_log.txt in append mode. Check pigpio initialization, every gpioSetMode/gpioWrite/gpioRead return code, and every fopen/fprintf/fclose result; on a file error, turn off the floodlight before exiting. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so Ctrl+C cleanly turns off the floodlight, releases pigpio resources, and exits with code 0. Poll at a 100 ms interval to avoid busy-waiting, and ensure the floodlight is off on every exit path. Do not use wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the pigpio library to toggle a 5V relay on GPIO17 via an MPR121 capacitive touch sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x5A. Perform a full MPR121 initialization: issue a soft-reset, configure baseline filtering (MHD/NHD/NCL/FDL), set debounce (register 0x5B), set FFI/SFI/CDT (register 0x2C), set auto-config (registers 0x7B-0x7D), and enable exactly 12 electrodes by writing 0x0C to register 0x5E. Read touch status from register 0x00, a 16-bit word whose lower 12 bits are the electrode touch states. Toggle the relay only on a fresh (rising-edge) touch of electrode 0, with a 200 ms debounce. Include robust error handling for every pigpio/I2C call, checking return values and handling sensor-absent and bus-error paths, with clean resource release on every exit path via SIGINT/SIGTERM handling, and set the relay to a known OFF state on both startup and shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the modern libgpiod API, not wiringPi, for all GPIO operations and listens for TCP commands on port 5000 to control a servo motor (BCM GPIO17) and read a PIR sensor (BCM GPIO4). Drive the servo with a software PWM thread that toggles the line via gpiod_line_set_value at 50 Hz with a 1-2 ms pulse width spanning 0-180°. Parse commands of the form 'SERVO <angle>' (0-180) and 'PIR', which returns 'PIR:0' or 'PIR:1' over the socket. Log all activation events, commands, and errors to both syslog (LOG_USER facility) and a local file named security.log with ISO 8601 timestamps. Check every libgpiod call, socket syscall, and file I/O operation; if GPIO initialization fails, log the error and exit with a non-zero status. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, releasing all libgpiod resources, closing the socket, and closing the log file. Include stdarg.h for variadic functions so the code compiles cleanly with -Wall -Wextra.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to read ambient light levels from a BH1750 sensor at I2C address 0x23 on I2C1 (GPIO2=SDA, GPIO3=SCL). Trigger a relay on GPIO23 to activate a grow light when the lux reading falls below 150, and deactivate it when lux is 150 or above. Use the BH1750 One-Time High-Resolution mode (command 0x20) and wait at least 120 ms for the conversion before reading the 2-byte result, converting to lux with lux = raw / 1.2. Log timestamps and lux values to grow_log.txt, sampling every 2 seconds. Implement robust error handling for I2C communication failures by checking the return codes of i2cOpen, i2cWriteByte, i2cReadDevice, and file operations, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths by logging errors and retrying on the next cycle. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths — close the I2C handle, close the log file, deactivate the relay, and call gpioTerminate — with SIGINT and SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library, not wiringPi, to read weight from a TAL220B load cell via an HX711 amplifier, with DOUT on GPIO23 (physical pin 16) and SCK on GPIO24 (physical pin 18), and to trigger a solenoid lock on GPIO25 (physical pin 22), which is driven HIGH for 200 ms whenever the measured weight exceeds a threshold of 1000 grams. Implement the HX711 bit-bang read protocol: wait for DOUT to go LOW (data ready), clock out 24 bits MSB-first, then send one additional clock pulse to select Channel A / Gain 128, and convert the 24-bit two's-complement reading to a signed 32-bit integer. Average 5 readings per measurement cycle and compute weight as (average_raw - tare_offset) / scale, performing a startup tare by averaging 10 readings. Check every libgpiod call; if DOUT does not go LOW within 1 second, log an error and retry up to 3 times before exiting. Release all GPIO lines and chips, close syslog, and ensure the solenoid is set LOW on every exit path, handling SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown. Log informational and error messages via syslog. Accept optional command-line arguments --threshold <grams>, --scale <factor>, and --duration <ms>, and poll weight every 500 ms in the main loop.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running Raspberry Pi OS that subscribes to the MQTT topic home/lights/control via the libmosquitto client library and controls a relay module on GPIO17 (physical pin 11, BCM) using pigpio. Initialize pigpio, configure GPIO17 as an output, and drive it LOW (relay OFF) at startup. Connect to an MQTT broker at localhost:1883 with client ID relay_controller_1, clean-session enabled, and a 60-second keepalive, logging every connection, subscription, disconnection, and error event to syslog (facility LOG_USER, tag mqtt_relay). On a successful connect, subscribe to home/lights/control at QoS 0; on failure, log the connack string and keep the process alive for retry. In the message callback, treat the payload as a NUL-terminated string: ON sets GPIO17 HIGH (relay energized) and OFF sets it LOW (relay de-energized); log every received message, and if the payload is empty or anything other than ON/OFF, log an error via syslog(LOG_ERR, ...) and leave the relay state unchanged. Run mosquitto_loop in the main thread; if it returns an error or the broker disconnects unexpectedly, destroy the client, wait 5 seconds, and reconnect automatically, never exiting on transient MQTT failures. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown: stop the loop, set GPIO17 LOW, disconnect and destroy the mosquitto client, call mosquitto_lib_cleanup(), gpioTerminate(), and closelog(). Check every pigpio and mosquitto return code and report errors via syslog. Build with: gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o relay_controller relay_controller.c -lmosquitto -lpigpio -lrt.

Write a C program that uses the pigpio library to control 5 hobby servos connected to BCM GPIO pins 7, 8, 9, 10, and 11 on a Raspberry Pi, moving each to a different predefined position: 1000, 1500, 2000, 500, and 2500 microseconds respectively. Use the standard 50 Hz PWM frequency (20 ms period) with a pulse width between 500 and 2500 microseconds. Initialize pigpio and verify the return code, set the PWM frequency and range appropriately for each pin, apply the pulse widths, hold the signals for 3 seconds so the servos can reach their positions, then cleanly stop the PWM and release the library resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to implement a closed-loop speed control system for two DC motors driven by a DRV8833 H-bridge. The DRV8833 uses two input pins per motor (IN1/IN2 for A, IN3/IN4 for B); drive one pin high and PWM the other for forward motion. Motor A uses GPIO 17 (PWM on IN1) and GPIO 18 (direction on IN2); Motor B uses GPIO 22 (PWM on IN3) and GPIO 23 (direction on IN4). Quadrature encoders with 64 ticks per revolution, one count per rising edge, and an assumed 1:1 encoder-to-output-shaft ratio are attached: Encoder A on GPIO 4 (A-phase) and GPIO 5 (B-phase); Encoder B on GPIO 6 (A-phase) and GPIO 12 (B-phase). Target speed is 50 RPM for both motors. Implement a PI controller (Kp=0.5, Ki=0.05) running at a 100 ms period, with anti-windup clamping and PWM duty cycle clamped to [0, 255], using a 10 kHz PWM frequency. Check every pigpio initialization and ISR registration call and exit cleanly on failure, handle SIGINT by stopping the motors and releasing resources, detect encoder stall (zero ticks for more than 2 seconds) and print a warning, and print motor RPM and PWM duty cycle each control iteration. Ensure the code compiles cleanly with -Wall and uses atomic operations for the shared encoder counters.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to implement a smart chicken coop lighting system. Control a 12V relay-connected LED strip via GPIO 17 (active-high) based on ambient light read from a BH1750 sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x23. The relay activates at dusk, when lux falls below 50, and deactivates at dawn, when lux exceeds 200, using a hysteresis loop to prevent rapid toggling. Poll the sensor every 5 seconds, waiting at least 180 ms after issuing the One-Time High-Resolution Mode 2 command (0x21) before reading the 2 bytes of lux data, and convert the raw data to lux by dividing by 1.2. Log all sensor readings and relay state changes to chicken_coop_log.txt in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS: Lux = XXX, Relay = ON/OFF'. Implement comprehensive error handling for pigpio initialization, I2C bus communication, and file I/O; if the sensor fails to respond, log the error and safely turn off the relay. Ensure clean resource release of the I2C handle, the relay GPIO, and the log file on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown via SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to control a 5V relay on GPIO 17 (physical pin 11) via a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor on GPIO 4 (physical pin 7); each valid touch toggles the relay state. Initialize pigpio and check for errors, configure GPIO 4 as input and GPIO 17 as output, and implement software debouncing with a 50 ms stabilization delay, toggling only when the sensor reads HIGH both before and after the delay. Wait for the touch sensor to return LOW before allowing the next toggle (edge detection on touch-release). Log every relay state change to the console with an ISO-8601 timestamp and the new state (ON/OFF). Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for graceful shutdown by turning the relay OFF, releasing pigpio resources, and printing an exit message. Check the return value of every pigpio call (gpioInitialise, gpioSetMode, gpioWrite) and report errors to stderr. Use a 10 ms main-loop sleep to reduce CPU usage, and do not include MQTT or networking code.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the pigpio library to read flow rate from a YF-S201 water flow sensor on GPIO 17 (physical pin 11), computing liters per minute (LPM) from its 450 pulses-per-liter calibration as LPM = (pulses / 450.0) * 60.0. Trigger a solenoid valve on GPIO 27 to shut off when the rate exceeds 5.0 L/min, reopening only when it drops below 4.5 L/min (0.5 L/min hysteresis); the solenoid is open (HIGH) by default and closes (LOW) above the threshold. Initialize pigpio and validate all return codes (gpioInitialise, gpioSetMode, gpioWrite, gpioSetISRFuncEx), using a 1-second ISR debounce timeout on the flow sensor pin. Protect the shared pulse counter with a pthread mutex; sample the pulse count every 1 second and reset it after computing LPM. Log every LPM reading and every solenoid state change with timestamps to water_flow.log; if the log file cannot be opened, clean up all initialized resources and exit with a non-zero status. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by logging the event, reopening the solenoid to its safe state, closing the log file, destroying the mutex, and calling gpioTerminate.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the pigpio library, not bcm2835 or wiringPi, to read data from an HX711 load cell amplifier connected to GPIO 23 (DATA) and GPIO 24 (SCK), calibrate the readings using a known weight, and control an SG90-style servo motor on GPIO 18 via hardware PWM to dispense a pre-determined amount of ingredient based on the weight. The program must act as a TCP server listening on 127.0.0.1:12345: receive a target weight in grams from a client, open the servo to dispense, wait 1 second for the load cell to stabilize, read the actual weight from the HX711, send the actual weight back to the client, and log each dispensing event (date, time, target weight, actual weight, and any error message) as a JSON object appended to dispensing_log.json. Implement robust error handling for pigpio initialization, HX711 communication timeouts (sensor absent or not ready), servo control failures, file I/O, and network errors. Use signal handlers (SIGINT, SIGTERM) for clean shutdown of GPIO, sockets, and the servo. Read calibration_factor, server_ip, and server_port from a config.ini file, falling back to defaults if the file is missing or malformed. Read the HX711 using bit-banged GPIO with a 1 µs clock pulse width, timing out if DATA stays HIGH for more than 1000 attempts. Map the target weight to the servo's 1000-2000 µs pulse-width range.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to toggle a 5V relay on GPIO 17 upon detecting a touch on a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor on GPIO 4, implementing a touch-controlled on/off switch for a desk lamp. The TTP223 module idles LOW and drives HIGH while touched. Implement a 50 ms polling-based software debounce with stable-level confirmation, overridable via an optional command-line argument -d <milliseconds>, and robust error handling for every pigpio call (gpioInitialise, gpioSetMode, gpioWrite). On each valid rising edge (LOW to HIGH), toggle the relay. Log every relay state change to the console with a timestamp in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS Relay: ON' or '... Relay: OFF'. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers for graceful shutdown: turn the relay OFF, release pigpio resources, and exit cleanly. Keep the program self-contained, with no networking, Redis, or ZeroMQ code.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 (40-pin header) that uses the pigpio library, not WiringPi or direct /dev/mem register access, to control a standard hobby servo such as an SG90 connected to GPIO18 (physical pin 12) via hardware PWM. The user increments or decrements the servo angle via keyboard input without pressing Enter (raw terminal mode): '+' increases the angle by 10°, '-' decreases it by 10°, and 'q' quits, with the angle clamped to 0-180°. Use 50 Hz PWM (20 ms period) with a pulse width of 500-2500 µs spanning 0-180°, starting at 90° (1500 µs), and drive it with gpioServo() rather than raw register writes. Check the return value of gpioInitialise(), printing to stderr and exiting non-zero on failure, and validate that computed pulse widths stay within [500, 2500] µs. On 'q' or SIGINT (Ctrl-C), stop PWM pulses on GPIO18, call gpioTerminate(), and restore the terminal settings, saving and restoring termios even on an unexpected exit. Print the current angle after each change.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the modern libgpiod API, not wiringPi, to monitor a conveyor-belt motor using an A3144 Hall-effect sensor on GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, BCM). A two-pole magnet on the motor shaft produces one pulse per revolution, detected on the rising edge. Configure GPIO 17 as input with the internal pull-up enabled via the GPIOD_LINE_REQUEST_FLAG_BIAS_PULL_UP bias flag, since the A3144's open-collector output requires a pull-up. Use edge-triggered event detection (gpiod_line_event_wait) to count pulses, with a 2 ms debounce window to reject contact bounce and double-edge noise. Every 5 seconds, compute RPM = (pulseCount / 5.0) * 60.0, append the sample to motor_rpm.log in CSV format (timestamp in ISO 8601, rpm_value to 2 decimal places), flushing after every write, and print the current RPM to stdout. Check the return values of gpiod_chip_open, gpiod_chip_get_line, and gpiod_line_request_input_flags, printing clear diagnostics to stderr and exiting non-zero on failure. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown: stop the main loop, release the GPIO line, close the chip, close the log file, and exit cleanly. Use the monotonic clock (clock_gettime with CLOCK_MONOTONIC) for timing, not clock().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the pigpio library to control a 5V relay on GPIO17 based on a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor on GPIO4, which outputs 3.3V logic HIGH when touched and LOW otherwise; the relay module is active-HIGH. On the rising edge of a touch, toggle the relay state, polling the sensor every 50 ms. Implement a failsafe: if the touch sensor remains continuously HIGH for more than 10 seconds, force the relay OFF and ignore further toggles until the sensor is released. Check the return value of gpioInitialise() and every gpioSetMode()/gpioWrite()/gpioRead() call; if gpioRead() returns PI_BAD_GPIO, log the error and exit. Install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that set a volatile flag so the main loop can exit cleanly; perform the actual cleanup — releasing the relay (set OFF) and calling gpioTerminate() — in main() after the loop exits, not inside the signal handler itself.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library, not wiringPi, to implement a closed-loop flow control system for an ASCO RedHat 8210 series proportional solenoid valve. Drive the valve via PWM on GPIO 18 (BCM, hardware PWM 0), with enable/direction control on GPIO 23 (BCM), active-high, and count pulses from a YF-S201 flow sensor on GPIO 24 (BCM) via an interrupt-driven, rising-edge pulse counter. Accept the target flow rate in L/min as a command-line argument (-t, e.g. -t 5.0), validating it and exiting with an error message if missing or invalid. Sample the flow rate every 100 ms, computing L/min from the pulse count accumulated over the interval using the YF-S201 calibration of 450 pulses per liter, and use a proportional controller (Kp = 1.0) to adjust the valve PWM duty cycle (0-255), clamped to [0, 255], to maintain the target flow rate. Log timestamp_ms, flow_rate, and valve_position to flow_log.csv on every control iteration, logging only to this local file with no UDP or network logging. Enable the valve (GPIO 23 high) at startup; on shutdown, set PWM to 0, drive GPIO 23 low, close the log file, and cleanly terminate pigpio. Check pigpio initialization, GPIO mode setup, ISR registration, and file open, exiting with a diagnostic on any failure, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown and resource release.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to implement a two-factor authentication system controlling two YLI YM-180 electromagnetic lock actuators on GPIO 17 and GPIO 27. The locks are normally engaged (powered = locked); disengage them by driving their GPIO pins LOW for 5 seconds, then re-engage them (HIGH). Authentication requires both factors in sequence: a valid RFID tag read via SPI channel 0 at 100 kHz, where the reader returns 10 bytes and an all-zero response means 'no tag present' rather than an error, matched against the 10-byte valid tag {0x01..0x0A}; then a button press on GPIO 22 (active-low with internal pull-up, 50 ms debounce). On successful two-factor authentication, drive both lock pins LOW for 5 seconds, then re-engage. Log all access attempts — successful, invalid tag, RFID read failure, and button press without a valid tag — with ISO-8601 timestamps to /var/log/door_access.log. Check gpioInitialise(), spiOpen(), spiXfer(), gpioWrite(), and the log file open, handling SPI read failures gracefully without crashing. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler for clean shutdown: close SPI, release both locks to the engaged state, close the log file, and call gpioTerminate(). Use a non-blocking polling loop with gpioDelay, avoiding busy-wait.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the libgpiod library, not wiringPi, to control two L298N-driven DC motors, implementing a PID controller (KP=1.0, KI=0.1, KD=0.01, 100 ms sample time) to maintain a target rotational speed for each motor, measured by quadrature encoders with 600 pulses per revolution. Motor 1 uses ENA on GPIO 23, IN1 on GPIO 24, IN2 on GPIO 25; Motor 2 uses ENB on GPIO 12, IN3 on GPIO 16, IN4 on GPIO 20. Encoder 1 uses A on GPIO 5, B on GPIO 6; Encoder 2 uses A on GPIO 26, B on GPIO 19. Decode the quadrature signals using libgpiod BOTH_EDGES edge events on each A pin, reading the corresponding B pin to determine direction, and drive each motor with software PWM via libgpiod line toggling at a fixed frequency such as 100 Hz, with duty cycle proportional to the PID output. Target RPMs may be hardcoded, for example 60 RPM for both motors. Log motor speeds (RPM), the PID P/I/D components, and the PID output to motor_log.csv with a header row, flushing after each write. Check all libgpiod calls (chip open, line request, edge event setup) and file operations, and handle encoder read failures gracefully. Use threads for encoder event monitoring so it does not block the main control loop, protecting shared encoder counts with mutexes. Install signal handlers (SIGINT, SIGTERM) that stop the motors, release the GPIO lines, close the chips, and close the log file, and run the control loop indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library for both I2C and GPIO control to interface with a single MPR121 capacitive touch sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x5A, toggling a 5V relay module on GPIO 17. Implement a robust MPR121 initialization sequence: a soft reset, configuring filtering, setting touch and release thresholds for all 12 electrodes, and enabling run mode. In the main loop, poll the MPR121 touch status registers 0x00 and 0x01 every 50 ms; if any electrode is touched, activate the relay (GPIO 17 HIGH), otherwise deactivate it (GPIO 17 LOW). Log every relay state change to a timestamped text file, relay_log.txt. Include comprehensive error handling: check pigpio initialization and every I2C open/read/write operation, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to shut down the relay and close the I2C handle properly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the libgpiod library, not wiringPi or pigpio, to control two Adafruit Solenoid Valves (Product ID 997), each a 12V, 0.7A valve switched through a relay module rather than driven directly, implementing a timed water distribution schedule for a miniature automated greenhouse. Valve 1's relay is on GPIO 17 (BCM) and Valve 2's relay is on GPIO 18 (BCM), where GPIO HIGH means the relay is ON and the valve is open, and GPIO LOW means the relay is OFF and the valve is closed. Run the schedule indefinitely until interrupted: activate Valve 1 for 500 ms, then pause 5 seconds; activate Valve 2 for 1000 ms, then pause 10 seconds. Implement robust error handling for GPIO chip initialization failures, gpiod_line_request_output failures, and file I/O errors for logging. Log every valve activation event with an ISO 8601 timestamp to valve_log.txt. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to ensure clean GPIO release and file closure, releasing all GPIO lines and closing the log file on exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library, not wiringPi, to toggle a 5V relay on GPIO17 upon each successful touch event from an MPR121 capacitive touch sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x5A (SDA=GPIO2, SCL=GPIO3). Initialize the MPR121 in stop mode, set the touch threshold (0x10) and release threshold (0x0A) for all 12 electrodes, configure the filter/charge time (0x20) and electrode current (0x01), then enter run mode with ELE_EN=1 (0x20) and wait 100 ms for stabilization. Set the relay pin as output, initially off. In a loop with a 100 ms delay, read the touch status registers (0x00-0x01); if any electrode is touched (touch_status > 0), toggle the relay and print the status. Include robust error handling for all I2C operations, GPIO operations, and initialization failures, opening the I2C bus with error handling. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown by closing I2C and terminating pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the pigpio library to detect motion via an HC-SR501 PIR sensor on GPIO 17 (input with pull-down). On a rising-edge motion detection (0 to 1), activate a 5V relay on GPIO 18 (output) for 500 ms to momentarily unlock an electric door strike. Implement rate limiting: ignore subsequent motion events for 2 seconds after each unlock. Log all events — motion detected, door unlocked, and rate-limited events — with millisecond-precision timestamps to door_events.log. Handle pigpio initialization failure gracefully with a clear error message and exit code 1. Ensure proper cleanup on SIGINT or normal exit: close the log file, terminate pigpio, and set the relay off. Use a single thread with non-blocking polling at a 50 ms interval and edge detection, using no sensors or GPIOs beyond the ones specified.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to modulate the speed of two eccentric rotating mass (ERM) vibration motors, Precision Microdrives 310-101, on GPIO pins 17 and 27, generating randomized haptic feedback patterns. Each pattern consists of a sequence of 5 to 15 steps, where each step specifies a PWM duty cycle from 0 to 255 for each motor and a duration of 50-200 ms. Use gpioPWM for PWM control and gpioDelay for timing. Implement robust error handling: check the gpioInitialise return value, verify GPIO mode setting, handle memory allocation failures, and ensure graceful shutdown on SIGINT (Ctrl+C) by stopping the motors and releasing resources, using a volatile sig_atomic_t shutdown flag. Seed the random number generator with time(NULL), and run indefinitely, generating and playing patterns until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library, not wiringPi, to read weight from an HX711 load cell amplifier with its data pin on GPIO4 and clock pin on GPIO17, and control a solenoid lock on GPIO27 (active high to lock). Initialize pigpio with error checking, then load calibration data (scale_factor and offset, space-separated) from calibration.txt, or use defaults of scale=1.0 and offset=0.0 if the file is missing or invalid. Perform a one-time startup calibration by averaging 100 readings to determine the offset, assuming zero load, and save the calibration data back to the file. In a loop, read the sensor every 500 ms, convert the raw value to weight using the calibration, and if it exceeds a calibrated threshold of 10.0 kg, drive the solenoid pin high to engage the lock, otherwise drive it low to release it. Log each reading with a timestamp to weight_log.txt. Handle HX711 read timeouts of 0.5 seconds gracefully by skipping that iteration. Handle SIGINT for a clean shutdown that releases the GPIO and closes the files.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to automatically close a window when rain is detected by a Seeed Studio Grove Rain Sensor on GPIO4 (BCM), driving an L298N motor driver connected with IN1 to GPIO17, IN2 to GPIO18, and PWM enable to GPIO27. The rain sensor outputs LOW when rain is detected and HIGH when dry; debounce by taking 5 readings at 50 ms intervals and treat rain as detected when at least 3 readings are LOW. To close the window, set IN1=1, IN2=0, and drive the PWM enable at 1000 Hz with duty cycle 150 out of 255; run the motor for 5 seconds, then stop it by setting IN1=0, IN2=0, and PWM=0. Check the sensor every 60 seconds, and after closing the window wait 60 seconds before checking again. Log every rain event and motor action with a timestamp to /var/log/window_control.log via syslog. Handle all GPIO initialization failures with error messages and exit codes. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, stop the motor, release GPIO resources, and close the log before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to monitor a kitchen ingredient stock level with a single TAL220B load cell read through an HX711 amplifier, with the amplifier's DT line on GPIO23 and SCK line on GPIO24. Check the weight every 1 second; when it drops below 100 g, activate a solenoid lock on GPIO17 for 5 seconds. Log each activation event with a timestamp to stock_events.txt. Implement robust error handling for HX711 reads, including timeout and data-line-stuck-high conditions, for GPIO control by checking every return value, and for file I/O. The program must run continuously and perform a clean shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read weight from an HX711 load cell amplifier over its bit-banged GPIO protocol (the HX711 is not an I2C device) and control a solenoid door lock. Connect the HX711 data pin to GPIO4 and clock pin to GPIO17, with clock high and low delays of at least 1 microsecond, and read raw 24-bit signed values with correct timing. At startup, calibrate the load cell by prompting the user to place a known weight, reading the raw value, computing a calibration factor as raw divided by the known weight in kilograms, and saving it to calibration.txt. Continuously read the weight; whenever it exceeds 5.0 kg, log the event with a timestamp and the weight to security.log, drive the solenoid lock on GPIO27 high for 5 seconds, then set it low to unlock. Handle pigpio initialization failure, file open and write failures, calibration read errors, and HX711 communication timeouts where the data line stays high for more than 100 ms. Install a SIGINT handler to gracefully unlock the solenoid and terminate pigpio, and release all resources, including closing files and terminating pigpio, on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library to monitor a Keywish KY-022 IR obstacle avoidance sensor on GPIO16 (BCM) and toggle a Songle SRD-05VDC-SL relay module on GPIO20 (BCM). The sensor is active-low, reporting an obstacle by driving its output LOW, and the relay trigger is active-high. Continuously monitor the sensor; each time an obstacle is detected, toggle the relay state from ON to OFF or OFF to ON, and log the new relay state together with a timestamp in ISO 8601 format to relay_events.log. Use only libgpiod APIs — gpiod_chip_open_by_name, gpiod_chip_get_line, gpiod_line_request_bulk_inputs/outputs, gpiod_line_get_value, gpiod_line_set_value, gpiod_line_release, and gpiod_chip_close. Handle GPIO initialization errors such as a missing chip or a failed line request, sensor read errors, and log file write errors, printing descriptive error messages and cleaning up resources. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, release all GPIO lines and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the libgpiod library to detect motion from an HC-SR501 PIR sensor on GPIO17 (BCM numbering), which is active-high, and activate a 5V buzzer, also active-high and driven through a transistor or relay rather than directly from GPIO, on GPIO18 for exactly 2 seconds before deactivating it. Use gpiod_line_set_value with usleep for the 2-second timing rather than a busy-wait loop. Append each motion event's timestamp, formatted as YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, to motion_log.txt. The program must run continuously until interrupted. Check every libgpiod call, including gpiod_chip_open and gpiod_line_request_input/output, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths by printing an error and exiting cleanly. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers to turn off the buzzer, close the log file, and release all GPIO resources before exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library to run a timed watering system controlling a Parker Hannifin Series 9 General Purpose Miniature Solenoid Valve (12V, 1.6W). Since the Pi cannot drive a 12V, 1.6 W solenoid directly, the valve is driven through an external N-channel MOSFET or relay module connected to GPIO18 (BCM numbering). Initialize the libgpiod chip and line, requesting GPIO18 as output with active-low set to 0 and a default output value of 0 (valve off). Read the watering duration from a configuration file 'watering.conf' containing a single line in the format 'duration=<seconds>', where seconds must be a positive integer between 1 and 3600; reject empty files, malformed lines, and out-of-range values. Activate the valve by setting the line high, wait for the configured duration using a signal-safe sleep that SIGINT or SIGTERM can interrupt early, then set the line low. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag; the main loop must check this flag and turn the valve off before exiting. On every exit path — normal completion, signal, or error — release the GPIO line and close the chip, ensuring the valve is always left off. Check every libgpiod call for errors and print descriptive messages to stderr, and print status messages to stdout showing the configured duration and each valve on/off transition.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to implement a line-following robot with a Keywish 3-Way Infrared Tracking Sensor and two DC motors driven through an L298N motor driver. The three active-low IR sensors are connected to GPIO4, GPIO17, and GPIO27; the motor driver's PWM inputs are connected to GPIO22, GPIO23, GPIO24, and GPIO25 and run at 1 kHz. Initialize pigpio with error checking, then read all three sensors every 10 ms and apply this control law: if the middle sensor reads low, drive straight at a base speed of 150 out of 255; if only the left sensor reads low, turn right by halving the left motor's speed; if only the right sensor reads low, turn left by halving the right motor's speed; if no sensor reads low, stop both motors. Log each control cycle to trace_log.txt with an ISO 8601 timestamp, the three sensor states as 0 or 1, and the left and right motor speeds. Include robust error handling for pigpio initialization, file opening, and GPIO operations, use only the pigpio API and never wiringPi, and on SIGINT stop the motors, close the log file, terminate pigpio, and release all GPIOs before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read illuminance from a BH1750 light sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x23, using continuous high-resolution mode (command 0x10) with a 180 ms measurement delay. Trigger a relay connected to GPIO23 to activate a grow lamp whenever the lux reading falls below 150. Log every lux reading and every relay state change to grow_log.txt with millisecond-precision timestamps. Handle I2C errors gracefully: if the sensor is not detected or a read fails, log the error and continue without crashing. The program must run indefinitely until SIGINT is received, then cleanly release all resources — close the I2C handle, turn off the relay, and terminate pigpio. Use only C and standard POSIX APIs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that uses the pigpio library to control a door lock with a servo motor on GPIO18 (PWM-capable) and two push buttons, a lock button on GPIO21 and an unlock button on GPIO22, each using an external or internal pull-up so that pressing reads as active-low (0). When the lock button is pressed, move the servo to the locked position with a pulse width of 1000 microseconds (about 0 degrees); when the unlock button is pressed, move it to the unlocked position with a pulse width of 2000 microseconds (about 180 degrees). Debounce each button press with a 100 ms delay. Constrain the servo pulse width to the safe range of 500-2500 microseconds at all times. Handle initialization failures gracefully, print status messages, use only pigpio API calls and never wiringPi, and cleanly release all resources on exit through a SIGINT signal handler.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the libgpiod library to run a haptic feedback system pulsing two Precision Microdrives 310-101 vibration motors, which require 3 V at 60 mA typical and must not be connected directly to GPIO. Drive motor 1 through a driver circuit such as an NPN transistor with a flyback diode on GPIO17, and motor 2 the same way on GPIO27. Pulse motor 1 for 200 ms, then motor 2 for 300 ms, repeating this sequential pattern indefinitely. Use gpiod_line_request_output() and gpiod_line_set_value() with error checking on every call. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully stop the motors and release the GPIO lines, including robust handling of line request failures, value write failures, and signal handler registration, and call gpiod_line_release() for cleanup on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library to implement a sound-triggered alarm as a single executable with two modes selected by a command-line argument. In sound_sensor mode, poll an LM393 sound sensor's active-low DO pin on GPIO17 every 10 ms (logic 0 means sound above threshold was detected) and publish alerts via ZeroMQ on tcp://*:5555 under topic SOUND_ALERTS. In alarm_node mode, subscribe to tcp://localhost:5555 on topic SOUND_ALERTS and light an alarm LED on GPIO27 for 1 second whenever a message arrives. Include robust error handling for every GPIO and ZeroMQ call, handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for a clean shutdown, and release all resources — GPIO lines, the GPIO chip, and the ZeroMQ sockets and context — on every exit path. Do not use wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to decode NEC IR remote signals from an IR receiver such as a TSOP38238 connected to GPIO17 (BCM). Register a pigpio alert callback on the falling edge to capture pulse timings, and decode the 32-bit NEC frame using its 9 ms mark plus 4.5 ms space header, 560 microsecond bit marks, 1690 microsecond spaces for logic 1, and 560 microsecond spaces for logic 0. Validate the decoded command against its inverted copy — extended NEC frames are allowed, so inverted-address validation is not required — and log the decoded address and command to syslog. Publish each decoded command as JSON to an MQTT broker at localhost:1883 on topic ir/decoded, using paho-mqtt v2 callback semantics, with the MQTT client initialized once at startup and its network loop serviced from the main loop. Check pigpio initialization, handle GPIO initialization failures, guard against pulse buffer overflow, validate the NEC checksum, and cleanly release pigpio, MQTT, and syslog resources on SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads ambient light levels from four BH1750FVI sensors on the I2C-1 bus at 7-bit addresses 0x23, 0x24, 0x25, and 0x26, using the standard Linux I2C ioctl interface (<linux/i2c-dev.h> with open() and ioctl(I2C_SLAVE)) rather than wiringPi. Note that the BH1750 natively supports only addresses 0x23 and 0x5C via its ADDR pin, so addresses 0x24-0x26 require an I2C multiplexer or level-shifted address lines; assume the hardware is wired accordingly. For each sensor, open /dev/i2c-1 (a single shared file descriptor or one per sensor is acceptable), set the slave address with ioctl(I2C_SLAVE, addr) before each transaction, write the One-Time High-Resolution mode command byte 0x20, wait 180 ms for conversion, then read 2 bytes. Convert the big-endian result to lux using lux = ((data[0] << 8) | data[1]) / 1.2. Once per second, broadcast all four readings as a single UDP multicast packet to 239.255.255.250:5005, formatted as semicolon-separated sensor_id,lux pairs, e.g. 1,120.5;2,85.0;3,210.5;4,45.0. If any sensor fails — open error, address-set error, write error, read error, or partial read — report NaN for that sensor and continue. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by setting a flag to exit the loop cleanly, and close all file descriptors, both I2C and UDP socket, on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads airflow data from a Honeywell AWM7300V mass airflow sensor at I2C address 0x28 on /dev/i2c-1, using the Linux I2C character device interface (<linux/i2c-dev.h>, <sys/ioctl.h>, read() and write() syscalls) rather than wiringPi. To read flow data, issue a zero-length I2C write as a start condition followed by a 2-byte read; the sensor returns a 14-bit flow value in the first two bytes, masked with 0x3FFF. Convert the raw value to SLPM using flow = (raw - 3277) * 0.1, sampling once per second, and log each timestamped flow rate to airflow_log.txt. Check every syscall, retry transient I2C read failures up to 3 times with 100 ms delays between retries, and handle sensor-absent (ENXIO) and bus-error (EIO) conditions. Install a SIGINT handler that closes the I2C file descriptor and flushes the log file for a clean shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with an Adafruit AS7341 10-Channel Light/Color Sensor over I2C using the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface — opening /dev/i2c-1 and using ioctl with I2C_SLAVE to set the 7-bit address 0x39 — rather than wiringPi. Perform a proper initialization sequence: verify the WHO_AM_I/ID register at 0x24 equals 0x19, power the sensor on via the PON bit in the ENABLE register at 0x80, configure SMUX for spectral readings via the CFG6 register at 0xAF, and enable spectral measurement via the SP_EN bit. Read all 10 spectral channels — F1 through F8, Clear, and NIR — from their registers at 0x60-0x73, compute a simplified lux approximation, and log the results with a timestamp to spectral_log.csv every 5 seconds in comma-separated format. Check every I2C read and write return value, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release, closing both the I2C file descriptor and the log file, on all exit paths including SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with an Omron D7S seismic sensor over I2C using the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (opening /dev/i2c-1 and using ioctl I2C_SLAVE) rather than wiringPi. The sensor's default 7-bit I2C address is 0x37. Read the 6 bytes of tri-axial acceleration starting at register 0x28 — X_L, X_H, Y_L, Y_H, Z_L, Z_H, little-endian signed 16-bit — and convert to g using g = raw * 0.000244 for the ±8 g range. At 1-second intervals by default, log timestamped X, Y, Z values in g to seismic_data.csv with columns timestamp,x_g,y_g,z_g. Check every I2C read and write return value, retry transient failures up to 3 times with a 10 ms backoff, detect sensor-absent and bus-error conditions, and log all errors with timestamps to seismic_error.log. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C file descriptor and flushing and closing the CSV file on all exit paths. Support command-line options -a for the I2C address (default 0x37), -i for the interval in seconds (default 1), and -f for the output filename (default seismic_data.csv).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads ambient light from a BH1750 sensor at I2C address 0x23 on /dev/i2c-1, using the standard Linux I2C character-device API (open, ioctl(I2C_SLAVE), read, write) rather than wiringPi. Initialize the sensor by sending the power-on command 0x01 followed by the continuous high-resolution mode command 0x10. Every 1 second, read the 16-bit big-endian raw value, convert it to lux using lux = raw / 1.2, and broadcast the value as a floating-point string over UDP multicast to 239.255.255.250:5000 with TTL set to 1. Check every I2C write and read operation for failure, and on sensor absence or a bus error, print an error and retry after 1 second. Use a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM to properly clean up the I2C file descriptor and socket on exit, and run indefinitely using standard POSIX sockets until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library for UART access, never wiringPi, to interface with a Texas Instruments AWR1642 mmWave radar sensor over /dev/ttyS0 at 921600 baud. Continuously read the asynchronous TLV byte stream, synchronize on the 8-byte magic word 0x0204 0x0306 0x0805 0x0709 (little-endian), validate the TLV payload, and extract each detected object's range and velocity. For each detected object, write a row to radar_data.csv with columns timestamp, object_index, range_m, velocity_mps. Check every UART read, handle partial reads and buffer overflows gracefully, skip malformed frames, and log errors to stderr without crashing. On all exit paths, including SIGINT and SIGTERM, close the UART, flush and close the CSV file, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running a 64-bit OS that periodically reads range-detection data from a Texas Instruments AWR1642 mmWave radar sensor connected to the primary UART at /dev/serial0 (GPIO14/GPIO15). The radar emits ASCII lines in the format <unix_timestamp_seconds>,<range_meters> terminated by '\n' at 115200 baud, 8N1. Open and configure the UART using termios.h in non-canonical mode with a 0.5 s inter-byte timeout, use select() with a 2-second timeout to detect data availability and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths, and accumulate partial reads into a line buffer, parsing only complete newline-terminated lines. Log each valid detection to stdout as 'Timestamp: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Range: X.XX meters'. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, closing the UART on all exit paths, and check every syscall — open, tcgetattr, tcsetattr, read, select, strdup — printing errno-based diagnostics on failure. Use only standard POSIX C libraries: stdio, stdlib, string, fcntl, termios, unistd, errno, sys/select, signal, and time.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library, not wiringPi, to read a Keywish 3-Way Tracking Sensor (KY-033) with its left, middle, and right IR emitter/detector outputs connected to GPIO4 (pin 7), GPIO17 (pin 11), and GPIO27 (pin 13) respectively, each configured as an input with pull-up resistors enabled; the sensor's 5V and GND are wired to the Pi's 5V and GND pins. Each output reads digital LOW when an obstacle or line is detected and HIGH when clear. If pigpio initialization fails, print an error and exit with code 1; if a gpioRead call fails, print an error and continue rather than exiting. Running the main loop at 10 Hz (a 100 ms period), read all three sensors each cycle and log their states to the console with a timestamp, using 0 for obstacle detected and 1 for clear. If all three sensors read 0 simultaneously, send the string \"EMERGENCY STOP!\\n\" over the serial port /dev/ttyAMA0 at 115200 baud, 8N1, with no flow control, handling any serial write error by printing it and continuing rather than exiting. Register SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers to close the serial port and terminate pigpio before exit, and release all resources on any error path.
